kingdom-of-airgialla.t: Confederation of mid-Ulster peoples bound to the Uí Néill as hostage-givers, which survived under the MacMahons as Oriel until the settlement of Monaghan in 1591.
kingdom-of-airgialla.o: Airgialla means 'hostage-givers', and the name describes a group of peoples in mid-[[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]], in modern [[e:armagh|Armagh]], [[e:county-monaghan|Monaghan]], [[s:kingdom-of-tir-eoghain|Tyrone]], [[e:county-fermanagh|Fermanagh]] and [[e:county-louth|Louth]], who owed hostages and military service to the [[e:ui-neill|Uí Néill]]. Tradition says the [[e:three-collas|Three Collas]] destroyed [[e:emain-macha|Emain Macha]], the royal centre of the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]], and settled their descendants in the conquered land.
kingdom-of-airgialla.r: Airgialla was a federation of many small kingdoms, such as the Uí Chremthainn and the Uí Méith, under an over-king. Its people held the lands around [[e:armagh|Armagh]], whose church became the primatial see of Ireland. In the 12th century [[e:donnchad-ua-cerbaill|Donnchad Ua Cerbaill]], king of Airgialla, extended his realm into [[e:county-louth|Louth]] and founded [[e:mellifont-abbey|Mellifont Abbey]] in 1142, the first Cistercian house in Ireland.
kingdom-of-airgialla.e: [[e:anglo-normans|Anglo-Norman]] settlement took [[e:county-louth|Louth]], and the [[e:macmahons-of-oriel|MacMahons]], Mac Mathghamhna, became rulers of the remaining kingdom, known in English as Oriel, centred on [[e:county-monaghan|Monaghan]]. After the execution of [[e:hugh-roe-macmahon|Hugh Roe MacMahon]] in 1590, the English divided the lordship among MacMahon chiefs in 1591, creating County Monaghan.
kingdom-of-airgialla.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.t: The last independent Georgian kingdom in the east, created by Erekle II, which placed itself under Russian protection in 1783 and was annexed in 1801.
kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.o: [[e:erekle-ii|Erekle II]], king of the [[s:kingdom-of-kakheti|Kingdom of Kakheti]] since 1744, succeeded his father [[e:teimuraz-ii-of-kakheti|Teimuraz II]] in the [[s:kingdom-of-kartli|Kingdom of Kartli]] in 1762, uniting eastern [[s:georgia|Georgia]] under one crown for the first time since the 15th century. He had gained prestige fighting for [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] in [[e:india|India]] and against Dagestani raiders.
kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.r: [[e:erekle-ii|Erekle II]], ruling from [[e:tbilisi|Tbilisi]], modernised the army, encouraged trade and crafts and drew tribute from the khanates of [[s:ganja-khanate|Ganja]] and Erivan. In 1783 he signed the [[e:treaty-of-georgievsk|Treaty of Georgievsk]] with [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine the Great]], accepting a Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. [[e:russia|Russia]] failed to defend him, and in 1795 [[e:agha-mohammad-khan-qajar|Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar]] defeated the [[e:georgians|Georgians]] at [[e:battle-of-krtsanisi|Krtsanisi]] and sacked Tbilisi.
kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.e: After [[e:erekle-ii|Erekle]]'s death in 1798, his son [[e:george-xii-of-georgia|George XII]] asked for closer union with [[e:russia|Russia]]. When George died in 1800, [[e:paul-i-of-russia|Emperor Paul I]] and then [[e:alexander-i-of-russia|Alexander I]] annexed the kingdom in 1801, deposing the [[e:bagrationi-dynasty|Bagratid]] dynasty and making it a Russian province.

kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.t: The Artaxiad dynasty turned Armenia into a major power, and under Tigranes the Great it briefly ruled an empire stretching from the Caspian to the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.o: [[e:artaxias-i|Artaxias]], a [[e:seleucid-empire|Seleucid]] governor, broke away after the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]] lost the [[e:battle-of-magnesia|Battle of Magnesia]] in 190 BCE and proclaimed himself king of [[s:kingdom-of-armenia-arsacid|Greater Armenia]]. He united the Armenian-speaking lands, set boundary stones that still survive, and founded a new capital, [[e:artaxata|Artaxata]], on the [[e:aras-river|Araxes]], according to legend on the advice of [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]].
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.r: The kingdom combined an Iranian-style monarchy and great noble houses with Hellenistic court culture; Greek plays were staged at [[e:artaxata|Artaxata]]. [[e:tigranes-the-great|Tigranes II]], the Great, ruling from 95 BCE, seized northern [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]], took the title [[e:negus-nagast|King of Kings]] and built [[e:tigranocerta|Tigranocerta]], settling it with deportees. Wealth came from farming, horses and trade routes between [[e:parthia|Parthia]] and the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.e: [[e:lucius-licinius-lucullus|Lucullus]] defeated [[e:tigranes-the-great|Tigranes]] at [[e:tigranocerta|Tigranocerta]] in 69 BCE, and in 66 BCE he submitted to [[e:pompey|Pompey]], keeping only [[s:armenia|Armenia]]. His successors were caught between the [[s:roman-republic|Roman Republic]] and the [[s:parthian-empire|Parthian Empire]]; [[e:artavasdes-ii-of-armenia|Artavasdes II]] was killed in [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. After rival puppet kings, the line ended about 12 CE.
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.re: Armenian paganism with Iranian and Greek influence

koch-hajo.t: The eastern half of the divided Koch kingdom, ruled from Hajo in western Assam until it fell to the Mughals.
koch-hajo.o: The Koch kingdom reached its height under [[e:nara-narayan|Nara Narayan]] and his brother and general [[e:chilarai|Chilarai]] in the mid 16th century. In 1581 [[e:nara|Nara]] Narayan divided the realm, giving the lands east of the [[e:sankosh-river|Sankosh]] river to Chilarai's son [[e:raghudev-narayan|Raghudev]], who ruled from [[e:hajo|Hajo]] on the north bank of the [[e:brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]]. The western half became [[s:cooch-behar-state|Koch Bihar]].
koch-hajo.r: Koch [[e:hajo|Hajo]] was a [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] kingdom whose rulers patronised the Hayagriva Madhava temple at Hajo and the [[e:kamakhya-temple|Kamakhya]] temple near [[e:guwahati|Guwahati]], which the Koch had rebuilt. [[e:raghudev-narayan|Raghudev]] and his son [[e:parikshit-narayan|Parikshit Narayan]] were rivals of their [[s:cooch-behar-state|Koch Bihar]] cousins, who allied with the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]], while Koch Hajo looked to the [[s:ahom-kingdom|Ahom kingdom]] for support.
koch-hajo.e: Mughal armies, aided by [[s:cooch-behar-state|Koch Bihar]], defeated [[e:parikshit-narayan|Parikshit Narayan]] in 1613, and by 1616 Koch [[e:hajo|Hajo]] was annexed. The territory became a battleground between the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]] and the [[e:ahom-people|Ahoms]] until the Ahoms secured it after the [[e:battle-of-itakhuli|Battle of Itakhuli]] in 1682.

kingdom-of-kantipur.t: The Malla kingdom of Kathmandu, whose rulers built much of Hanuman Dhoka and Kathmandu Durbar Square before the Gorkha conquest.
kingdom-of-kantipur.o: Kantipur emerged in 1484 when [[e:ratna-malla|Ratna Malla]], a son of [[e:yaksha-malla|Yaksha Malla]] of the Malla dynasty, established himself at [[e:kathmandu|Kathmandu]] after his father's death. It became one of the three rival Malla kingdoms of the valley, alongside the [[s:kingdom-of-bhaktapur|Kingdom of Bhaktapur]] and, from the late 16th century, the [[s:kingdom-of-lalitpur|Kingdom of Lalitpur]].
kingdom-of-kantipur.r: [[e:pratap-malla|Pratap Malla]], in the mid 17th century, was the most celebrated king: a poet and builder who added to the [[e:hanuman-dhoka|Hanuman Dhoka]] palace and set up the [[s:rani|Rani]] Pokhari tank. [[e:kathmandu|Kathmandu]] profited from trade with [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], minting [[e:silver|silver]] coins used in [[e:lhasa|Lhasa]]. [[e:newar-people|Newar]] artisans produced fine metal images and painted scrolls, and the cult of the living goddess [[e:kumari-goddess|Kumari]] was associated with the court.
kingdom-of-kantipur.e: [[e:prithvi-narayan-shah|Prithvi Narayan Shah]] of the [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha Kingdom]] captured [[e:kathmandu|Kathmandu]] during the [[e:indra-jatra|Indra Jatra]] festival in 1768, while [[e:jaya-prakash-malla|Jaya Prakash Malla]] fled. Kathmandu became the capital of the new [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]].

kingdom-of-whydah.t: Coastal kingdom of present-day Benin whose port of Ouidah was one of the busiest slave-trading harbours in Africa around 1700.
kingdom-of-whydah.o: Whydah, or Hueda, was a kingdom of [[e:gbe-languages|Gbe]]-speaking people on the coast west of the [[s:kingdom-of-allada|Kingdom of Allada]], with its capital at Savi a few kilometres inland. It emerged as an independent state in the late 16th century and grew rapidly as European ships turned to its port.
kingdom-of-whydah.r: The king of Whydah opened the port to all European nations, and the English, French and Portuguese built forts at [[e:ouidah|Ouidah]]. By the early 18th century more than ten thousand enslaved people were shipped from Whydah in many years. The cult of the python, [[e:dangbe|Dangbe]], was central to the town's religion and is still practised.
kingdom-of-whydah.e: In 1727 [[e:agaja|Agaja]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-dahomey|Kingdom of Dahomey]] invaded and destroyed Savi, and King [[e:haffon|Haffon]] fled. [[e:kingdom-of-dahomey|Dahomey]] took control of [[e:ouidah|Ouidah]], which remained its main port. The town is now a centre of Vodun and of memory of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic slave trade]].

kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.t: The Napoleonic kingdom of southern Italy under Joseph Bonaparte and Joachim Murat, which abolished feudalism in the south.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.o: After the [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]] joined the coalition against [[e:france|France]], [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] sent an army in 1806. [[e:ferdinand-i-of-the-two-sicilies|King Ferdinand IV]] fled to [[e:sicily|Sicily]] under British protection, and Napoleon made his brother [[e:joseph-bonaparte|Joseph Bonaparte]] king of [[e:naples|Naples]].
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.r: Joseph abolished feudalism in 1806, closed monasteries and introduced French administration. In 1808 he became king of [[e:spain|Spain]] and was succeeded by [[e:joachim-murat|Joachim Murat]], [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] brother-in-law, who introduced the [[e:napoleonic-code|Napoleonic Code]], built roads and fought brigandage in [[e:calabria|Calabria]]. The kingdom never controlled [[e:sicily|Sicily]], which the [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbons]] held with British help.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.e: [[e:joachim-murat|Murat]] abandoned [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] in 1814, but in 1815 he declared war on [[e:austria|Austria]] with the [[s:lordship-of-rimini|Rimini]] Proclamation calling for Italian independence. Defeated at [[e:battle-of-tolentino|Tolentino]] in May 1815, he fled; landing in [[e:calabria|Calabria]] in October, he was captured and shot. Ferdinand returned to [[e:naples|Naples]].

cr.a: See File history below for details.

kingdom-of-ceredigion.t: Early Welsh kingdom on Cardigan Bay, named after its legendary founder Ceredig, which grew into Seisyllwg in the 8th century.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.o: Welsh tradition says the kingdom was founded by [[e:ceredig-ap-cunedda|Ceredig]], a son of [[e:cunedda|Cunedda]], who came from the north to drive Irish settlers out of [[e:wales|Wales]] in the 5th century, and that the land took its name from him. This story was recorded centuries later and is regarded with caution by historians, but Ceredigion as a district between the [[e:river-dyfi|Dyfi]] and the [[e:river-teifi|Teifi]] is ancient.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.r: Little is known of its rulers before the 8th century beyond genealogies. The kingdom covered the coastal lowlands and hills of modern Ceredigion, a region of small farms and [[e:cattle|cattle]]-rearing, and its church centres included [[e:llanbadarn-fawr|Llanbadarn Fawr]], associated with [[e:saint-padarn|St Padarn]], which became one of the leading monasteries of [[e:wales|Wales]].
kingdom-of-ceredigion.e: Around 730 its king [[e:seisyll-ap-clydog|Seisyll ap Clydog]] conquered the neighbouring [[s:kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi|Kingdom of Ystrad Tywi]], creating an enlarged realm known as [[s:kingdom-of-seisyllwg|Seisyllwg]]. This later passed to [[e:hywel-dda|Hywel Dda]] and became part of [[s:kingdom-of-deheubarth|Deheubarth]]. The name survives in the modern county of Ceredigion.

kingdom-of-guinala.t: Biafada kingdom on the Rio Grande de Buba in Guinea-Bissau, a busy port for Portuguese traders in the 16th century.
kingdom-of-guinala.o: Known mainly from Portuguese accounts. Guinala was one of several [[e:biafada|Biafada]] kingdoms along the rivers of present-day southern [[e:guinea-bissau|Guinea-Bissau]], and by the 16th century its port attracted Portuguese and Cape Verdean traders.
kingdom-of-guinala.r: Its rulers acknowledged the overlordship of the [[s:kaabu-empire|Kaabu Empire]] and traded slaves, kola, wax and cloth with Portuguese merchants, many of them based in [[s:portuguese-cape-verde|Portuguese Cape Verde]]. Portuguese writers such as [[e:andre-alvares-de-almada|Andre Alvares de Almada]] described its markets.
kingdom-of-guinala.e: Guinala declined in the 17th century as [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu's]] demands, raids and the shifting [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] weakened the [[e:biafada|Biafada]] states. Its lands later fell within [[s:portuguese-guinea|Portuguese Guinea]].

kingdom-of-di-206-bc.t: The northernmost of the Three Qins, given in 206 BCE to the former Qin officer Dong Yi and lost to Liu Bang within months.
kingdom-of-di-206-bc.o: [[e:dong-yi|Dong Yi]] was a [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] commander who urged [[e:zhang-han|Zhang Han]] to surrender to [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] in 207 BCE. As a reward, Xiang Yu made him King of Di, ruling the old [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] commandery in northern [[e:shaanxi|Shaanxi]] from Gaonu near modern [[e:yanan|Yan'an]], one of three kingdoms meant to contain [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]].
kingdom-of-di-206-bc.r: Di was a thinly populated frontier region on the Loess Plateau, facing the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]]. Its king had no local support, and the kingdom existed only a few months.
kingdom-of-di-206-bc.e: When [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]] broke out of [[e:hanzhong|Hanzhong]] in 206 BCE, [[e:dong-yi|Dong Yi]] surrendered and his kingdom became Han territory. Like [[e:sima-xin|Sima Xin]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-sai|Kingdom of Sai]], he later returned to [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] and killed himself after the Chu defeat on the Si River near [[e:battle-of-chenggao|Chenggao]] in 203 BCE.

kilwa-sultanate.t: The richest Swahili city-state of the Middle Ages, which controlled the gold trade of southern Africa from its island capital.
kilwa-sultanate.o: The [[e:kilwa-chronicle|Kilwa Chronicle]] traditionally dates the sultanate to c. 957, when Ali ibn al-Hasan, a prince said to come from [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] in [[e:persia|Persia]], bought the island of [[e:kilwa-kisiwani|Kilwa Kisiwani]] from a local ruler. Archaeology suggests a gradual rise from a fishing and trading settlement, with stone building and coinage appearing by the 11th century.
kilwa-sultanate.r: Kilwa grew rich by taking control of [[e:sofala|Sofala]], the port for gold from [[s:kingdom-of-zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]]. Under the Mahdali dynasty, from the late 13th century, [[e:sultan|Sultan]] al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman built the vast palace of [[e:husuni-kubwa|Husuni Kubwa]] and enlarged the [[e:great-mosque-of-kilwa|Great Mosque]]. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]], visiting in 1331, called Kilwa one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Its rulers minted [[e:copper|copper]] coins and traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], gold and slaves for Indian cloth and Chinese [[e:porcelain|porcelain]].
kilwa-sultanate.e: Dynastic quarrels weakened Kilwa in the 15th century, and in 1505 a Portuguese fleet under [[e:francisco-de-almeida|Francisco de Almeida]] sacked the city and built a fort there. Trade collapsed, and the town later fell under Omani rule. Its ruins are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

kingdom-of-qocho.t: A Uyghur kingdom of the Turfan oasis where Buddhism, Manichaeism and Christianity flourished and whose rulers submitted early to Genghis Khan.
kingdom-of-qocho.o: After the [[s:uyghur-khaganate|Uyghur Khaganate]] fell in 840, [[e:uyghurs|Uyghur]] groups moved south-west to the [[e:tian-shan|Tian Shan]] oases. By 856 they controlled [[e:turfan|Turfan]] and [[e:beshbaliq|Beshbaliq]], with Qocho ([[s:gaochang-kingdom|Gaochang]]) as a winter capital, establishing a kingdom under rulers with the title idiqut.
kingdom-of-qocho.r: The [[e:uyghurs|Uyghurs]] adapted to oasis life, with irrigated fields, vineyards and [[e:cotton|cotton]]. The court first favoured [[e:manichaeism|Manichaeism]], but [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] became dominant, and the [[e:bezeklik-caves|Bezeklik caves]] were decorated with murals of Uyghur donors. The Uyghur script, derived from Sogdian, was used for a large literature of Buddhist and other texts, and Uyghur scribes later served the [[e:mongols|Mongols]].
kingdom-of-qocho.e: The kingdom became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:qara-khitai|Qara Khitai]], and in 1209 the idiqut [[e:barchuq-art-tegin|Barchuq Art Tegin]] submitted to [[e:genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]]. Under the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] it remained a privileged vassal until rule passed to the [[e:chagatai-khanate|Chagatai Khanate]] in the 14th century.
kingdom-of-qocho.re: Buddhism, Manichaeism, Church of the East

kingdom-of-lalangina.t: A Betsileo kingdom of the southern Malagasy highlands, one of several small states absorbed by the expanding Merina Kingdom.
kingdom-of-lalangina.o: Lalangina was one of four main [[e:betsileo|Betsileo]] kingdoms that took shape in the southern highlands of [[e:madagascar|Madagascar]] in the 18th century, in the region around modern [[e:fianarantsoa|Fianarantsoa]]. Its ruling dynasty claimed descent from immigrant nobles, and its history is known mainly from oral tradition.
kingdom-of-lalangina.r: [[e:betsileo|Betsileo]] kings ruled over farming villages that built extensive terraced [[e:rice|rice]] fields in the highland valleys, and royal authority was tied to ancestral tombs and rituals. Lalangina competed with neighbouring kingdoms, including the [[s:kingdom-of-isandra|Kingdom of Isandra]], for land and [[e:cattle|cattle]].
kingdom-of-lalangina.e: Around 1811 the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]] under [[e:andrianampoinimerina|Andrianampoinimerina]] and his son [[e:radama-i|Radama I]] absorbed the [[e:betsileo|Betsileo]] kingdoms, and Lalangina came under Merina rule. The Betsileo remain one of [[e:madagascar|Madagascar's]] largest peoples.

kingdom-of-takrur.t: Kingdom of the middle Senegal valley whose ruler War Jabi was among the first in West Africa to adopt Islam, in the 11th century.
kingdom-of-takrur.o: Takrur grew up along the fertile middle valley of the [[e:senegal|Senegal]] river, where floodplain farming, fishing and herding supported a dense population. It was established by the 9th century and first described by Arab geographers such as al-Bakri, writing in 1068, as a trading town and kingdom on the route between the [[s:ghana-empire|Ghana Empire]] and the Saharan caravan trade.
kingdom-of-takrur.r: Its people were ancestors of the Pulaar-speaking [[e:toucouleur|Haalpulaar]] (Toucouleur). The ruler [[e:war-jabi|War Jabi]], who died around 1040, accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] and imposed Islamic law, and his son Labi fought alongside the [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]] against rebels in the western [[e:sahara|Sahara]]. Takrur traded gold, [[e:cotton|cotton]] cloth and grain for salt and North African goods, and the name 'Takrur' became a general Arabic word for Muslim West Africans.
kingdom-of-takrur.e: Takrur lost its independence in the 13th century, when it fell under the expanding [[s:mali-empire|Mali Empire]], traditionally around 1285. Its lands later formed part of the [[s:jolof-empire|Jolof Empire]] and the [[s:denianke-kingdom|Denianke Kingdom]], and the region kept its Islamic identity as [[s:imamate-of-futa-toro|Futa Toro]].

kel-ahaggar.t: The Tuareg confederation of the Hoggar mountains in southern Algeria, led by an amenokal and among the last Saharan peoples to submit to France.
kel-ahaggar.o: The Kel [[e:ahaggar-mountains|Ahaggar]] took shape as a confederation in the Ahaggar massif of the central [[e:sahara|Sahara]], with noble drum groups, especially the Kel Rela, providing the amenokal. Its organisation in recognisable form dates from around the mid-18th century.
kel-ahaggar.r: Noble warriors controlled [[e:vassal|vassal]] goat-herding tribes and cultivators of small oases, often of servile status. The Kel [[e:ahaggar-mountains|Ahaggar]] escorted and raided caravans, collected tribute and fought the [[s:kel-ajjer|Kel Ajjer]] in the 1870s. In 1881 they destroyed the [[e:flatters-expedition|Flatters expedition]] surveying a trans-Saharan railway.
kel-ahaggar.e: After their defeat by French forces at [[e:battle-of-tit|Tit]] in 1902, the amenokal [[e:moussa-ag-amastan|Moussa ag Amastan]] accepted French rule and befriended [[e:charles-de-foucauld|Charles de Foucauld]] at [[e:tamanrasset|Tamanrasset]]. The confederation survived under [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]] and independent [[e:algeria|Algeria]], where the traditional office of amenokal lost its role in the 1970s.

kydonia.t: Leading city of western Crete for much of antiquity, a rival of Knossos and Gortyn, on the site of modern Chania.
kydonia.o: Kydonia stood on a Minoan site on the north-west coast of [[e:crete|Crete]]. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] records that Samian exiles fleeing [[e:polycrates|Polycrates]] settled there in 524 BCE and built temples, before Aeginetans and Cretans defeated and enslaved them in 519 BCE. By the classical period it was an independent Cretan polis named after its legendary founder Kydon.
kydonia.r: Kydonia was governed, like other Cretan cities, by annual officials called [[e:kosmoi|kosmoi]] and a council of elders, with a warrior aristocracy and dependent rural labourers. It struck [[e:silver|silver]] coins, traded across the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] and supplied [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]], including famous [[e:archery|archers]]. In the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] it fought repeated wars with [[s:knossos|Knossos]], [[s:gortyn|Gortyn]] and [[s:polyrrhenia|Polyrrhenia]].
kydonia.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] intervened in [[e:crete|Crete]] during the wars against the Cretan [[e:piracy|pirates]]. [[e:quintus-caecilius-metellus-creticus|Quintus Caecilius Metellus]] besieged and took Kydonia in 69 BCE on his way to conquering the island, which became part of the province of Crete and [[s:republic-of-cyrene|Cyrene]]. Kydonia remained a free city under Rome and survives as Chania.

kingdom-of-venad.t: The southern Kerala kingdom centred on the port of Kollam, a pepper-trading state that was reshaped by Marthanda Varma into the kingdom of Travancore.
kingdom-of-venad.o: Venad emerged in the 9th century as a chiefdom under the [[s:chera-perumals-of-makotai|Chera Perumals of Makotai]]. The Tharisapalli [[e:copper|copper]] plates of 849, in which the Venad chief [[e:ayyanadikal-thiruvadikal|Ayyanadikal Thiruvadikal]] granted land and privileges to the [[e:saint-thomas-christians|Syrian Christian]] church at [[e:kollam|Kollam]], are among the earliest records of [[e:kerala|Kerala]]. After the Chera Perumal state broke up in the early 12th century, Venad became independent.
kingdom-of-venad.r: [[e:kollam|Kollam]] (Quilon) was a major [[e:indian-ocean|Indian Ocean]] port, visited by Chinese and Arab merchants and later by the Portuguese, who built a fort there in the early 16th century. [[e:ravi-varma-kulasekhara|Ravi Varma Kulasekhara]] (r. 1299–1314) briefly campaigned as far as [[e:kanchipuram|Kanchipuram]]. The ruling family split into several branches, and real power often lay with local nobles and temple corporations.
kingdom-of-venad.e: In the 1720s and 1730s [[e:marthanda-varma|Marthanda Varma]] crushed the nobles, absorbed neighbouring chiefdoms and transformed Venad into [[s:travancore|Travancore]], the register's successor state from 1729. Its rulers remained in power until 1949.

kuninda-kingdom.t: A Himalayan kingdom of the upper Sutlej and Yamuna, known from its fine silver coins and mentioned by Ptolemy.
kuninda-kingdom.o: The Kunindas, or Kulindas, appear in the [[e:mahabharata|Mahabharata]] as a mountain people, and Ptolemy places a land called Kulindrine near the sources of the [[e:beas|Beas]], [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]], [[e:yamuna|Yamuna]] and [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]]. They emerged as a state in the foothills of modern [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] and [[e:uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]] around the 2nd century BCE, after the fall of the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]].
kuninda-kingdom.r: The kingdom is known mainly from coins. The [[e:silver|silver]] coins of King [[e:amoghabhuti|Amoghabhuti]], modelled on [[e:indo-greek-kingdom|Indo-Greek]] drachms, carry legends in both Brahmi and Kharoshthi with a deer and a goddess, possibly [[e:lakshmi|Lakshmi]]. Later [[e:copper|copper]] coins show [[e:shiva|Shiva]] as Chatreshvara, lord of the parasol, suggesting a shift to [[e:shaivism|Shaiva]] worship. The economy probably depended on trade in forest and mountain products with the plains.
kuninda-kingdom.e: Kuninda coinage seems to have stopped during the expansion of the [[s:kushan-empire|Kushan Empire]] and resumed later. By the 4th century the Kunindas disappear from the record, possibly absorbed by the [[s:yaudheya-republic|Yaudheya republic]] or by the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]].

kutrigurs.t: Nomads of the steppe west of the Don whose raid under Zabergan in 559 reached the outskirts of Constantinople.
kutrigurs.o: The Kutrigurs are named by [[e:procopius|Procopius]] and [[e:agathias|Agathias]] in the 6th century as a Hunnic or [[e:bulgars|Bulgar]] people of the steppe between the [[e:don-river|Don]] and the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]], kin to the [[s:utigurs|Utigurs]] to their east. They emerged from the remnants of the [[s:hunnic-empire|Hunnic Empire]] and the [[e:oghurs|Oghur]] peoples who arrived after 463.
kutrigurs.r: As pastoral nomads under chiefs, they lived on herding and raids into the [[e:balkans|Balkans]], sometimes serving [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and sometimes, as in 551, allied with the [[e:gepids|Gepids]] against it. In 559 their khan Zabergan crossed the frozen [[e:danube|Danube]], raided [[e:thrace|Thrace]] and [[e:greece|Greece]] and threatened [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], until the aged general [[e:belisarius|Belisarius]] repelled him. Justinian then turned the [[s:utigurs|Utigurs]] against them.
kutrigurs.e: Weakened by war with the [[s:utigurs|Utigurs]], the Kutrigurs fell under the [[e:avars|Avars]] in the 560s; many joined the [[s:avar-khaganate|Avar Khaganate]] in [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]]. Others later joined [[e:kubrat|Kubrat's]] [[s:old-great-bulgaria|Old Great Bulgaria]].

kingdom-of-dotawo.t: The last Christian Nubian kingdom on the Nile, a rump of Makuria centred at Gebel Adda and Qasr Ibrim that survived into the late 15th century.
kingdom-of-dotawo.o: Dotawo was the [[e:old-nubian|Old Nubian]] name used in documents for the realm of [[s:makuria|Makuria]]. After Dongola was abandoned around 1365 amid [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] interventions and Arab raids, the surviving court moved north to Daw, generally identified with [[e:gebel-adda|Gebel Adda]] in [[e:lower-nubia|Lower Nubia]], and the reduced kingdom is known by this name.
kingdom-of-dotawo.r: The kingdom is known mainly from [[e:old-nubian|Old Nubian]] letters and legal documents found at [[e:qasr-ibrim|Qasr Ibrim]] and from scattered Arabic notices. It kept the Nubian Church with its [[e:bishop|bishops]], Greek and Old Nubian liturgy, and a court with eparchs and officials in the tradition of [[s:makuria|Makuria]], but its territory and resources were small.
kingdom-of-dotawo.e: The last known king, [[e:joel-of-dotawo|Joel]], is attested in 1484. Dotawo then disappears from the record, probably absorbed during the spread of [[e:islam|Islam]] and Arab tribes and the rise of the [[s:funj-sultanate|Funj Sultanate]], which ended Christian [[e:nubia|Nubia]].

kingdom-of-bau.t: A Fijian chiefdom ruled from a tiny island off Viti Levu, which became the strongest power in Fiji and under Cakobau led the islands into British rule.
kingdom-of-bau.o: Bau is an islet of a few hectares off the east coast of [[e:viti-levu|Viti Levu]]. In the mid-18th century chiefs of the [[e:kubuna-confederacy|Kubuna]] people settled there, and under the war-king title of [[e:vunivalu-of-bau|Vunivalu]] they built a maritime power using the island's fleets of large double canoes and alliances through marriage.
kingdom-of-bau.r: The [[e:vunivalu-of-bau|Vunivalu]] shared authority with the senior sacred chief, the Roko Tui Bau, but in practice the war kings came to dominate. In the early 19th century Naulivou used [[e:musket|muskets]] and European beachcombers such as [[e:charles-savage|Charles Savage]] to expand Bau's reach. Under [[e:tanoa-visawaqa|Tanoa Visawaqa]] and his son [[e:seru-epenisa-cakobau|Seru Epenisa Cakobau]], Bau dominated much of eastern [[e:fiji|Fiji]] through tribute and war. Cakobau's conversion to [[e:methodism|Methodism]] in 1854 and his victory at Kaba in 1855, with Tongan help, confirmed his power.
kingdom-of-bau.e: [[e:seru-epenisa-cakobau|Cakobau]], styling himself [[e:tui-viti|Tui Viti]], rivalled the Tongan chief [[e:enele-maafu|Maʻafu]] and his [[s:tovata-confederacy|Tovata Confederacy]]. In 1871 he became head of the [[s:kingdom-of-fiji|Kingdom of Fiji]], and in 1874 he ceded [[e:fiji|Fiji]] to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] as the [[s:colony-of-fiji|Colony of Fiji]]. Bau remains the seat of the [[e:kubuna-confederacy|Kubuna]] confederacy.

cr.a: The original uploader was Nevers at French Wikipedia.

kuban-soviet-republic.t: A Bolshevik republic proclaimed in the Kuban in spring 1918, contested by the Kuban Cossack government and the Volunteer Army.
kuban-soviet-republic.o: In March 1918 Red forces took [[e:krasnodar|Yekaterinodar]] from the [[e:kuban-rada|Kuban Rada]], the [[e:cossacks|Cossack]] regional government, which fled. The [[e:communist-party-of-the-soviet-union|Bolsheviks]] proclaimed the Kuban Soviet Republic in April 1918 as an autonomous part of the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]], governing the Kuban region and its large Cossack and non-Cossack peasant population.
kuban-soviet-republic.r: The republic was run by a council of commissars and relied on [[e:red-guards-russia|Red Guard]] units and non-[[e:cossacks|Cossack]] settlers, who resented Cossack privileges in land. It repelled [[e:lavr-kornilov|Kornilov]]'s [[e:volunteer-army|Volunteer Army]] at [[e:krasnodar|Yekaterinodar]] in April 1918, where Kornilov was killed. Grain requisitioning and conflict with the Cossacks undermined its support.
kuban-soviet-republic.e: In May 1918 it merged with the [[s:black-sea-soviet-republic|Black Sea Soviet Republic]] to form the [[s:kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic|Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic]], which the [[e:white-movement|Whites]] overran later that year. [[e:krasnodar|Yekaterinodar]] fell to the [[e:volunteer-army|Volunteer Army]] in August 1918.

kingdom-of-karangasem.t: East Balinese kingdom that conquered western Lombok and later built the famous water palaces of Ujung and Tirta Gangga.
kingdom-of-karangasem.o: Karangasem emerged in eastern [[e:bali|Bali]] as the central kingdom of [[s:kingdom-of-gelgel|Gelgel]] lost its hold over its lords in the 17th century. Its rulers, a branch of the Gusti dynasty, established an independent court at [[e:amlapura|Amlapura]] and by the late 17th century had sent forces across the [[e:lombok-strait|Lombok Strait]], where Balinese princes from Karangasem founded several realms in western [[e:lombok|Lombok]].
kingdom-of-karangasem.r: Society followed the Balinese [[e:caste|caste]] order, with a [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] court supported by [[e:brahmins|Brahmana]] priests and a peasantry organised in villages and irrigation societies (subak). Karangasem traded [[e:rice|rice]], slaves and [[e:cattle|cattle]], and its links with [[e:lombok|Lombok]] made it one of the most outward-looking Balinese states. Court culture favoured temple building, dance and palm-leaf literature.
kingdom-of-karangasem.e: Defeated by the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] expedition of 1849, Karangasem was handed to the Balinese rulers of the [[s:kingdom-of-mataram-lombok|Kingdom of Mataram (Lombok)]]. After the Dutch conquest of [[e:lombok|Lombok]] in 1894 it came under colonial control as a regency, and its last raja, [[e:anak-agung-anglurah-ketut-karangasem|Anak Agung Anglurah Ketut Karangasem]], governed it under Dutch supervision.

kamiros.t: Farming city on the west coast of Rhodes, one of the island's three ancient cities, whose terraced streets survive in remarkable condition.
kamiros.o: Kamiros was settled by [[e:dorians|Dorian Greeks]] in the early [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] on a slope above the west coast of [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]], facing [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] across the sea. It was one of the three Rhodian cities, with [[s:lindos|Lindos]] and [[s:ialysos|Ialysos]], and a member of the [[e:dorian-hexapolis|Dorian Hexapolis]].
kamiros.r: Unlike [[s:lindos|Lindos]], Kamiros relied mainly on farming of grain, figs, olives and wine. Its cemeteries have yielded rich finds of Archaic East Greek pottery and jewellery. The city fell under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] and then belonged to the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. Its acropolis held a temple of [[e:athena|Athena]] Kameiras.
kamiros.e: In 408 BCE Kamiros joined [[s:lindos|Lindos]] and [[s:ialysos|Ialysos]] to found the city of [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] and lost its political independence. It continued as a town; after earthquakes it was rebuilt in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]], and its houses and cistern can still be seen.
kamiros.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Kameiras

kingdom-of-daura.t: The spiritual home of the Hausa, where the Bayajidda legend places the founding of the Hausa royal lines.
kingdom-of-daura.o: [[e:daura|Daura]] is held by [[e:hausa|Hausa]] tradition to be the oldest Hausa town, ruled by a line of queens. The legend tells how [[e:bayajidda|Bayajidda]], a stranger from the east, killed the snake guarding the [[e:kusugu-well|Kusugu well]], married Queen [[e:daurama|Daurama]], and fathered Bawo, whose sons founded the other [[s:hausa-kingdoms|Hausa kingdoms]]. The state existed by the 11th century.
kingdom-of-daura.r: [[e:daura|Daura]] remained comparatively small, and its prestige rested on tradition rather than power. It traded with neighbouring [[s:katsina-kingdom|Katsina]] and [[e:kano|Kano]] and with Saharan merchants, and was assigned the role of trade in the legendary division of the [[e:hausa|Hausa states]]. For long periods it acknowledged the overlordship of the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]].
kingdom-of-daura.e: [[e:fula|Fulani]] forces took [[e:daura|Daura]] around 1806, creating the [[s:daura-emirate|Daura Emirate]] within the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]]. The old Hausa dynasty ruled in exile at [[e:zango|Zango]] and was later restored to Daura under British rule. The [[e:kusugu-well|Kusugu well]] is still shown to visitors.

kingdom-of-changshan.t: Zhang Er's kingdom in Hebei, carved from Zhao by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, which fell to his former friend Chen Yu within a year.
kingdom-of-changshan.o: [[e:zhang-er|Zhang Er]] had been chancellor of the revived state of Zhao during the rebellion against the [[s:qin-dynasty|Qin dynasty]]. In 206 BCE [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] made him King of Changshan, ruling most of Zhao from [[e:xingtai|Xiangguo]] (near Xingtai), while the Zhao king [[e:zhao-xie|Zhao Xie]] was moved north to the [[s:kingdom-of-dai-206-bc|Kingdom of Dai]] (206 BC).
kingdom-of-changshan.r: The kingdom was dominated by the bitter quarrel between [[e:zhang-er|Zhang Er]] and [[e:chen-yu|Chen Yu]], once sworn friends, who had fallen out during the siege of [[e:battle-of-julu|Julu]]. Chen Yu, given only a few counties, felt cheated by the settlement.
kingdom-of-changshan.e: In 205 BCE [[e:chen-yu|Chen Yu]], with troops from [[e:tian-rong|Tian Rong]] of Qi (206 BC), drove [[e:zhang-er|Zhang Er]] out; Zhang fled to [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]], and [[e:zhao-xie|Zhao Xie]] was restored as King of Zhao. After [[e:han-xin|Han Xin]] defeated Zhao at [[e:battle-of-jingxing|Jingxing]] in 204 BCE, Liu Bang made Zhang Er King of Zhao.

kingdom-of-calicut.t: The spice-trading kingdom of the Zamorins on the Malabar Coast, where Vasco da Gama landed in 1498 and where Arab, Chinese and European traders met.
kingdom-of-calicut.o: The [[e:zamorin|Zamorins]] (Samoothiri) were the rulers of Nediyiruppu, a small chiefdom that became independent after the fall of the [[e:chera-dynasty|Chera]] kingdom of [[e:mahodayapuram|Mahodayapuram]] in the early 12th century. They moved their seat to [[e:calicut|Calicut]] and, with the help of Arab and Muslim merchants, built it into the leading port of the [[e:malabar-coast|Malabar Coast]] by the 14th century.
kingdom-of-calicut.r: [[e:calicut|Calicut]] prospered on the [[e:pepper|pepper]], ginger and cardamom trade, and the [[e:zamorin|Zamorins]] guaranteed security to foreign merchants of all faiths; [[e:zheng-he|Zheng He's]] Chinese fleets called there in the early 15th century. The ruler presided over the [[e:mamankam-festival|Mamankam festival]] at [[e:thirunavaya|Thirunavaya]], and the court supported [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] scholarship. Muslim admirals of the [[e:kunjali-marakkar|Kunjali Marakkar]] family led the navy against the Portuguese.
kingdom-of-calicut.e: Decades of war with the Portuguese and their ally the [[s:kingdom-of-cochin|Kingdom of Cochin]] weakened [[e:calicut|Calicut]]. In 1766 [[e:hyder-ali|Hyder Ali]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799|Kingdom of Mysore]] invaded and the reigning [[e:zamorin|Zamorin]] died in his burning palace. [[e:malabar-coast|Malabar]] passed to the British in 1792, and the Zamorin family survived as landholders.

kingdom-of-glywysing.t: Kingdom of south-east Wales between the Usk and the Tawe, home of the great monasteries of Llantwit and Llancarfan, which became Morgannwg.
kingdom-of-glywysing.o: Glywysing took its name from Glywys, a legendary 5th-century king whose descendants, according to the Lives of the Welsh saints, included [[e:saint-cadoc|St Cadoc]]. It grew from the post-Roman communities of the [[s:lordship-of-glamorgan|Glamorgan]] lowlands, once the territory of the [[s:silures|Silures]], and was often joined with the neighbouring [[s:kingdom-of-gwent|Kingdom of Gwent]] under a single dynasty.
kingdom-of-glywysing.r: The [[e:book-of-llandaff|Llandaff charters]], a collection of land grants, show a society of kings, churchmen and landowners trading estates and gifts. [[e:meurig-ap-tewdrig|Meurig ap Tewdrig]] and his descendants ruled across Glywysing and [[s:kingdom-of-gwent|Gwent]] from the 7th century. The monasteries of [[e:llantwit-major|Llantwit Major]], founded by St [[e:illtud|Illtud]], and [[e:llancarfan|Llancarfan]], founded by [[e:saint-cadoc|St Cadoc]], were leading centres of learning. [[e:asser|Asser]] says Hywel ap Rhys submitted to Alfred.
kingdom-of-glywysing.e: In the 10th century [[e:morgan-ab-owain|Morgan Hen]] ruled both Glywysing and [[s:kingdom-of-gwent|Gwent]], and from around 942 his combined realm became known as [[s:kingdom-of-morgannwg|Morgannwg]], from which the name [[s:lordship-of-glamorgan|Glamorgan]] derives. The region later fell to the Normans under [[e:robert-fitzhamon|Robert Fitzhamon]] in the 1090s.

kingdom-of-amathus.t: Cypriot kingdom on the south coast that kept the island's pre-Greek Eteocypriot language alive into the 4th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.o: Amathus was founded c. 1050 BCE on a hill near modern [[e:limassol|Limassol]]. Ancient writers regarded its people as autochthonous Cypriots, and the city preserved the [[e:eteocypriot-language|Eteocypriot language]], written in the Cypriot syllabary, alongside Greek. It also had close links with [[e:phoenicia|Phoenicia]], and it was probably among the Cypriot kingdoms that paid tribute to [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] in the 7th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.r: The acropolis held a palace and a major sanctuary of the Cypriot goddess later called Aphrodite, with a giant stone vase now in the [[e:louvre|Louvre]]. The kingdom grew rich from [[e:copper|copper]] and agriculture. It was loyal to [[e:persia|Persia]]: in 498 BCE it refused to join the revolt led by [[e:onesilus|Onesilus of Salamis]] and was besieged.
kingdom-of-amathus.e: King Androcles sent ships to help [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]] at [[s:tyre|Tyre]] in 332 BCE. The monarchy was ended under [[e:ptolemy-i-soter|Ptolemy I]] c. 312 BCE, and Amathus continued as a city under the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]] and [[e:rome|Rome]]. It declined after the 7th century CE and was abandoned.

kingdom-of-the-rugians.t: A small East Germanic kingdom north of the Danube in Lower Austria, known chiefly from the Life of Saint Severinus and destroyed by Odoacer in 487.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.o: The Rugii originally lived on the Baltic coast, where [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] places them. After migrating south and serving under the [[e:huns|Huns]], they settled after [[e:attila|Attila's]] death in 453 on the north bank of the [[e:danube|Danube]] opposite the Roman province of [[s:kingdom-of-noricum|Noricum]], in the area later called Rugiland, in modern [[e:lower-austria|Lower Austria]].
kingdom-of-the-rugians.r: The Rugian kings were [[e:arianism|Arian Christians]] who dominated the remaining Roman towns of [[s:kingdom-of-noricum|Noricum]] Ripense, collecting tribute and controlling trade across the [[e:danube|Danube]]. [[e:eugippius|Eugippius]]' [[e:life-of-saint-severinus|Life of Saint Severinus]] portrays King [[e:flaccitheus|Flaccitheus]], his son [[e:feletheus|Feletheus]] and the harsh Queen [[e:giso|Giso]], whom the saint rebuked. Their power depended on balancing [[e:ostrogoths|Ostrogoths]], [[s:kingdom-of-the-heruli|Heruli]] and the Roman population.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.e: In 487 [[e:odoacer|Odoacer]], ruler of [[e:italy|Italy]], attacked Rugiland and captured [[e:feletheus|Feletheus]] and [[e:giso|Giso]]; in 488 his brother crushed their son Fredericus, and the Roman population of [[s:kingdom-of-noricum|Noricum]] was evacuated to Italy. Surviving Rugians joined Theodoric's [[e:ostrogoths|Ostrogoths]] and went with them to Italy, keeping a separate identity there into the 540s.

kurwai-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state of central India, founded by an Afghan officer of the Mughals near Vidisha.
kurwai-state.o: Kurwai was founded in 1713 by [[e:muhammad-diler-khan|Muhammad Diler Khan]], an Afghan officer in Mughal service, who received the territory near the [[e:betwa-river|Betwa]] river. His descendants ruled as Nawabs.
kurwai-state.r: The Nawabs ruled a small territory of farming villages, much of it lost to [[e:scindias|Sindhia]] and the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] in the 18th century. Under British paramountcy Kurwai was a minor state in the [[e:bhopal-agency|Bhopal Agency]]. Few further details are widely recorded.
kurwai-state.e: Kurwai joined [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 1956. The town lies in [[e:vidisha|Vidisha]] district.

kingdom-of-kuku.t: A Kabyle kingdom in the Djurdjura mountains whose founder, Ahmed Belkadi, defeated Hayreddin Barbarossa and briefly ruled Algiers.
kingdom-of-kuku.o: [[e:ahmed-belkadi|Ahmed Belkadi]], a judge from a family that had served the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsids]] in [[e:bejaia|Bejaia]], established himself in [[e:greater-kabylia|Greater Kabylia]] around 1515 after the Spanish captured Bejaia, with his stronghold at Kuku in the [[e:djurdjura|Djurdjura]] mountains.
kingdom-of-kuku.r: Belkadi first allied with the [[e:hayreddin-barbarossa|Barbarossa]] brothers, then turned against Hayreddin, defeated him and held [[e:algiers|Algiers]] from about 1520 until he was killed around 1527. His successors ruled the [[e:kabyles|Kabyle]] highlands, sometimes allied with the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]], sometimes with [[e:spain|Spain]], and competed with the [[s:kingdom-of-ait-abbas|Kingdom of Ait Abbas]]. Rule depended on mountain tribal alliances.
kingdom-of-kuku.e: The dynasty declined in the 17th century as [[e:kabyles|Kabyle]] tribes asserted their independence and [[e:algiers|Algiers]] extended its influence. By around 1638 the kingdom had broken up, though [[e:greater-kabylia|Greater Kabylia]] stayed largely self-governing until the French conquest.

kingdom-of-lazica.t: A western Georgian kingdom on the Black Sea coast, heir of ancient Colchis, over which Byzantium and Persia fought the long Lazic War of the 6th century.
kingdom-of-lazica.o: The Lazi, a Kartvelian people of the old [[s:kingdom-of-colchis|Kingdom of Colchis]], rose to dominance on the eastern [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] coast in the 2nd century CE. [[e:arrian|Arrian]], touring the coast for Emperor Hadrian in the 130s, recorded a Lazi king holding power by Roman appointment, and the Lazi gradually united neighbouring tribes.
kingdom-of-lazica.r: Kings ruled from the fortress of [[e:nokalakevi|Archaeopolis]], modern Nokalakevi, over a land of forests, river valleys and coastal forts. Lazica was a client of the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]] and then the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]], and King [[e:tzath-i|Tzath I]] was baptised in [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in 522, making [[e:christianity|Christianity]] official. The kingdom controlled trade routes and [[e:timber|timber]] vital to [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] navies.
kingdom-of-lazica.e: In 541 the Lazi invited Persian help, sparking the [[e:lazic-war|Lazic War]]; after King [[e:gubazes-ii-of-lazica|Gubazes II]] was murdered by Byzantine officers, a peace of 562 returned Lazica to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. Arab raids in the 7th century weakened it, and its lands passed into the [[s:kingdom-of-abkhazia|Kingdom of Abkhazia]].

kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.t: A brief sub-kingdom in the east Midlands created for Penda's son Peada, notable as the place where Christianity first entered Mercian lands.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.o: The [[e:middle-angles|Middle Angles]] were a group of peoples in the east [[e:midlands|Midlands]], around the [[e:the-fens|Fens]] and the [[e:river-nene|Nene]] and [[e:river-welland|Welland]] valleys. Around 653 [[e:penda-of-mercia|Penda]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Kingdom of Mercia]] made his son [[e:peada|Peada]] their king. Peada married [[e:alhflaed|Alhflaed]], a daughter of [[e:oswiu|Oswiu of Northumbria]], and accepted baptism as a condition of the marriage.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.r: [[e:peada|Peada]] brought four priests, including [[e:cedd|Cedd]] and [[e:diuma|Diuma]], who preached among the [[e:middle-angles|Middle Angles]], the first Christian mission in Mercian territory. Tradition links Peada to the foundation of [[e:peterborough-abbey|Medeshamstede]], later [[e:peterborough|Peterborough]] Abbey. The many small peoples of the region, listed in the [[e:tribal-hidage|Tribal Hidage]], kept their own identities.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.e: After [[e:penda-of-mercia|Penda's]] death in 655 [[e:oswiu|Oswiu]] let [[e:peada|Peada]] rule southern [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]], but he was murdered in 656, allegedly through his wife's treachery. The [[e:middle-angles|Middle Angles]] were absorbed into Mercia, though they later had their own bishopric at [[e:leicester|Leicester]].

kingdom-of-bhaktapur.t: One of the three Malla kingdoms of the Kathmandu Valley, whose palace square and five-storey temple are masterpieces of Newar architecture.
kingdom-of-bhaktapur.o: When [[e:yaksha-malla|Yaksha Malla]] of the Malla dynasty died in 1482, his kingdom was divided among his sons. [[e:raya-malla|Raya Malla]] kept [[e:bhaktapur|Bhaktapur]], the old capital in the east of the valley, while his brothers established the [[s:kingdom-of-kantipur|Kingdom of Kantipur]] and other seats, creating rival Malla kingdoms in a small area.
kingdom-of-bhaktapur.r: [[e:bhaktapur|Bhaktapur]] was the most traditional of the three [[e:newar-people|Newar]] kingdoms, rich in festivals and crafts such as pottery and woodcarving. [[e:bhupatindra-malla|Bhupatindra Malla]], around 1700, built the [[e:nyatapola-temple|Nyatapola]] temple and enlarged the fifty-five-window palace, and his son [[e:ranajit-malla|Ranajit Malla]] added the [[e:golden-gate-bhaktapur|Golden Gate]] in 1754. The kingdom controlled routes to [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] in the east and competed with [[e:kathmandu|Kathmandu]] and [[e:lalitpur-nepal|Patan]] for trade.
kingdom-of-bhaktapur.e: The [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]]'s [[e:prithvi-narayan-shah|Prithvi Narayan Shah]] conquered [[e:bhaktapur|Bhaktapur]] in 1769, after taking [[e:kathmandu|Kathmandu]] and [[e:lalitpur-nepal|Patan]]; [[e:ranajit-malla|Ranajit Malla]], its last king, went into exile at [[e:varanasi|Varanasi]]. Bhaktapur's medieval town survives as a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].

kazakh-khanate.t: The khanate of the Kazakh steppe, founded by Kerei and Janibek, which shaped Kazakh identity and law for nearly four centuries.
kazakh-khanate.o: Around 1465 the sultans [[e:kerei-khan|Kerei]] and [[e:janibek-khan|Janibek]], descendants of [[e:urus-khan|Urus Khan]] of the [[s:white-horde|White Horde]], broke away from [[e:abul-khayr-khan|Abu'l-Khayr]]'s [[s:uzbek-khanate|Uzbek Khanate]] and led their followers to [[e:moghulistan|Moghulistan's]] western pastures in the Chu valley. Their people became known as [[e:kazakhs|Kazakhs]], 'free wanderers', and after Abu'l-Khayr's death they took over most of the steppe.
kazakh-khanate.r: The khanate was a nomadic confederation led by Genghisid sultans, with clan elders and judges (biys). Under [[e:kasym-khan|Qasim Khan]] in the early 16th century it may have numbered a million people. [[e:tauke-khan|Tauke Khan]] in the late 17th century issued the code of law known as [[e:zhety-zhargy|Zhety Zhargy]]. The city of [[e:turkistan-city|Turkistan]], with the mausoleum of [[e:ahmad-yasawi|Ahmad Yasawi]], was a political and spiritual centre.
kazakh-khanate.e: Divided into the [[s:senior-juz|Senior Juz]], [[s:middle-juz|Middle Juz]] and [[s:junior-juz|Junior Juz]] in the 18th century, the [[e:kazakhs|Kazakhs]] suffered [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] invasions and turned to [[e:russia|Russia]]. Russia abolished the khans' power in the 1820s, and [[e:kenesary-kasymov|Kenesary Kasymov's]] revolt ended in 1847.

kingdom-of-the-franks.t: The Frankish realm founded by Clovis, the most lasting of the barbarian kingdoms and the common ancestor of France and Germany.
kingdom-of-the-franks.o: [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]] succeeded his father [[e:childeric-i|Childeric I]] as king of the [[s:salian-franks|Salian Franks]] at [[e:tournai|Tournai]] in 481. He destroyed the [[s:domain-of-soissons|Domain of Soissons]] in 486, defeated the [[s:alemanni|Alemanni]], accepted Catholic baptism at [[e:reims|Reims]] and in 507 crushed the [[s:visigothic-kingdom|Visigothic Kingdom]] at [[e:battle-of-vouille|Vouillé]], taking [[s:duchy-of-aquitaine|Aquitaine]]. He made [[e:paris|Paris]] his capital and absorbed the other [[e:frankish-kingdom|Frankish kingdoms]].
kingdom-of-the-franks.r: The Merovingian kings divided the realm among their sons as private inheritance, creating [[s:austrasia|Austrasia]], [[s:neustria|Neustria]] and [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]]. Gallo-Roman [[e:bishop|bishops]], counts and a Frankish warrior aristocracy ran it together. From the 7th century real power passed to the mayors of the palace, and [[e:charles-martel|Charles Martel]] halted an [[e:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad]] army near [[e:tours|Tours]] in 732.
kingdom-of-the-franks.e: In 751 [[e:pepin-the-short|Pippin the Short]] deposed the last Merovingian, Childeric III, and became king. His son [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] conquered [[e:saxony|Saxony]] and [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] [[e:italy|Italy]] and was crowned emperor in 800, ruling the [[s:carolingian-empire|Carolingian Empire]]. In 843 the [[e:treaty-of-verdun|Treaty of Verdun]] split the realm into [[s:west-francia|West Francia]], [[s:middle-francia|Middle Francia]] and [[s:east-francia|East Francia]].

kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.t: The mountain-based Kongo kingship of Kibangu, one of the rival courts that emerged from Kongo's civil wars and eventually reunited the kingdom in 1709.
kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.o: After the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kingdom of Kongo's]] defeat by Portugal at the [[e:battle-of-mbwila|Battle of Mbwila]] in 1665, the kingdom split among rival royal houses, and the capital [[e:mbanza-kongo|Sao Salvador]] was abandoned in 1678. One faction made its base on the fortified mountain of Kibangu, east of the old capital, where a line of claimants maintained the title of king of Kongo.
kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.r: The Kibangu kings ruled a small territory but kept the full ceremony and Catholic identity of the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kongo]] monarchy, hosting Italian Capuchin missionaries. [[e:garcia-iii-of-kongo|Garcia III]] and later [[e:pedro-iv-of-kongo|Pedro IV]] ruled from there. Pedro IV pursued reconciliation among the rival houses, while the prophet [[e:kimpa-vita|Kimpa Vita]] and her Antonian movement challenged him by reoccupying [[e:mbanza-kongo|Sao Salvador]]; he had her burnt in 1706.
kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.e: In 1709 [[e:pedro-iv-of-kongo|Pedro IV]]'s forces retook [[e:mbanza-kongo|Sao Salvador]], ending the separate Kibangu court and restoring a single, though much weakened, [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kingdom of Kongo]].

kaqchikel-kingdom.t: A highland Maya kingdom that broke from the K'iche' around 1470, allied with the Spanish in 1524 and then fought them for six years.
kaqchikel-kingdom.o: The [[e:kaqchikel-people|Kaqchikel]] had been allies and subjects of the [[s:kiche-kingdom|K'iche' kingdom]]. Around 1470, during disputes that followed the reign of K'iq'ab, Kaqchikel lords left [[e:qumarkaj|Q'umarkaj]] and founded their own capital at Iximche, on a ridge in the central highlands, becoming an independent and expanding power.
kaqchikel-kingdom.r: Iximche held palaces, temples and ballcourts in walled plazas for the leading lineages, whose two chief lords ruled jointly. The kingdom fought the [[e:kiche-people|K'iche']] and [[e:tzutujil-people|Tz'utujil]] kingdoms. Its history, from origin myths to the Spanish conquest, is recorded in the [[e:annals-of-the-kaqchikels|Annals of the Kaqchikels]], written in [[e:kaqchikel-people|Kaqchikel]] in the colonial period.
kaqchikel-kingdom.e: The [[e:kaqchikel-people|Kaqchikel]] kings [[e:kaji-imox|Kaji' Imox]] and [[e:beleheb-kat|Beleheb' Kat]] welcomed [[e:pedro-de-alvarado|Pedro de Alvarado]] in 1524, and Iximche briefly became the first Spanish capital. Harsh demands led to a revolt that ended in 1530; Kaji' Imox was hanged in 1540. Kaqchikel remains widely spoken.
