kingdom-of-sine.t: Serer kingdom of west-central Senegal, ruled by the Guelowar dynasty and long a stronghold of Serer religion against Muslim jihad.
kingdom-of-sine.o: [[e:serer|Serer]] tradition holds that around 1350 the [[e:guelowar|Guelowar]], a maternal lineage of [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] origin from [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu]], came to the Serer country and married into its old landholding families. [[e:maysa-wali|Maysa Wali]], remembered as the first Guelowar king, founded the line of rulers titled Maad a Sinig. The royal seat was later fixed at [[e:diakhao|Diakhao]].
kingdom-of-sine.r: The king ruled with a council of great chiefs and with the Lingeer, the queen mother or royal sister. [[e:serer|Serer]] religion, with its saltigue priests and rain rites, remained central, and Sine resisted conversion. The economy rested on [[e:millet|millet]], [[e:cattle|cattle]] and later [[e:groundnut|groundnuts]]. In 1867 its army defeated and killed the jihadist [[e:maba-diakhou-ba|Maba Diakhou Ba]] at [[e:battle-of-fandane-thiouthioune|Fandane-Thiouthioune]].
kingdom-of-sine.e: Sine became a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] and was absorbed into the colony of [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]] in 1891. Kings continued as colonial chiefs; the last, [[e:mahecor-diouf|Mahecor Diouf]], died in 1969, after which independent [[e:senegal|Senegal]] ended the monarchy.

kingdom-of-asturias.t: The first Christian kingdom in Iberia after the Muslim conquest, born at Covadonga and seen as the cradle of the Reconquista.
kingdom-of-asturias.o: After 711 the Visigothic noble [[e:pelagius-of-asturias|Pelagius]] led a revolt in the mountains of [[e:asturias|Asturias]] and defeated a Muslim force at [[e:battle-of-covadonga|Covadonga]], traditionally in 718 or 722. His small realm, based at [[e:cangas-de-onis|Cangas de Onís]], grew under Alfonso I, son of Duke Peter of the [[s:duchy-of-cantabria|Duchy of Cantabria]], who raided the [[e:douro|Douro]] valley and absorbed [[e:cantabria|Cantabria]].
kingdom-of-asturias.r: [[e:alfonso-ii-of-asturias|Alfonso II the Chaste]] made [[e:oviedo|Oviedo]] the capital and modelled his court on the Visigothic kingdom of [[e:toledo|Toledo]]. Under him the tomb of [[e:james-the-great|St James]] was proclaimed at [[e:santiago-de-compostela|Compostela]], starting a great pilgrimage. [[e:ramiro-i-of-asturias|Ramiro I]] built the pre-Romanesque churches of [[e:monte-naranco|Monte Naranco]]. [[e:alfonso-iii-of-asturias|Alfonso III]] the Great resettled the [[e:douro|Douro]] frontier, taking [[e:porto|Porto]] in 868 and [[e:coimbra|Coimbra]] in 878, and sponsored chronicles of a Gothic restoration.
kingdom-of-asturias.e: In 910 [[e:alfonso-iii-of-asturias|Alfonso III]] was deposed by his sons, who divided the realm into León, [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria|Galicia]] and [[e:asturia|Asturias]]. In 924 [[e:fruela-ii-of-asturias|Fruela II of Asturias]] succeeded his brother [[e:ordono-ii-of-leon|Ordoño II]] in León, reuniting the realms, and the Kingdom of [[e:asturias|Asturias]] gave way to the [[s:kingdom-of-leon|Kingdom of León]].

kingdom-of-provence.t: Short-lived Carolingian kingdom of the lower Rhône, carved out for the youngest son of Lothair I.
kingdom-of-provence.o: When [[e:lothair-i|Lothair I]] divided [[s:middle-francia|Middle Francia]] in 855, his youngest son Charles, still a boy, received [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]] and the duchy of [[e:lyon|Lyon]], stretching from the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] up the [[e:rhone|Rhône]] valley.
kingdom-of-provence.r: Charles suffered from epilepsy, and the kingdom was effectively run by Count [[e:gerard-of-roussillon|Girart of Vienne]], his guardian, who defended it against the ambitions of [[e:charles-the-bald|Charles the Bald]] and fought [[e:vikings|Viking]] raiders who had sailed up the [[e:rhone|Rhône]]. [[e:vienne|Vienne]] and [[e:lyon|Lyon]] were its main centres.
kingdom-of-provence.e: Charles died childless in 863, and his brothers [[e:lothair-ii|Lothair II]] and the emperor [[e:louis-ii-of-italy|Louis II]] divided the kingdom between them. The region later re-emerged as the [[s:kingdom-of-lower-burgundy|Kingdom of Lower Burgundy]] under [[e:boso-of-provence|Boso]] in 879.

kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.t: The last Herodian kingdom, briefly reuniting Herod the Great's realm under Agrippa I and surviving as a Roman client under Agrippa II until about 100.
kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.o: [[e:herod-agrippa-i|Herod Agrippa I]], grandson of [[e:herod-the-great|Herod the Great]] and friend of [[e:caligula|Caligula]], received the former [[s:tetrarchy-of-philip|Tetrarchy of Philip]] with the title king in 37. Caligula added [[e:galilee|Galilee]] and [[e:peraea|Peraea]] in 39, and [[e:claudius|Claudius]], whom Agrippa had helped to the throne, gave him [[e:judaea|Judea]] and [[e:samaria|Samaria]] in 41, restoring his grandfather's kingdom.
kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.r: [[e:herod-agrippa-i|Agrippa I]] courted Jewish opinion in [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]], began a third city wall and, according to [[e:acts-of-the-apostles|Acts]], executed the apostle James; he died suddenly at [[s:lordship-of-caesarea|Caesarea]] in 44, and [[e:judaea|Judea]] returned to Roman procurators. His son [[e:agrippa-ii|Agrippa II]] received [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]] and from 53 the northern lands, renaming [[e:banias|Caesarea Philippi]] as Neronias. He supervised the Temple, appointed high priests and heard the apostle Paul at Caesarea.
kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.e: [[e:agrippa-ii|Agrippa II]] urged his people not to revolt in 66 and fought on [[e:rome|Rome's]] side in the Jewish War. He kept his kingdom afterwards; its end is dated by his death, placed by some sources around 92-93 and by others around 100, after which the territory was annexed to [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]].

kiche-kingdom.t: The most powerful Postclassic Maya kingdom of the Guatemalan highlands, whose lords compiled the Popol Vuh, the great Maya book of creation.
kiche-kingdom.o: According to their own chronicles, the [[e:kiche-people|K'iche']] descended from warrior lineages that arrived in the highlands from the east, probably from the [[e:gulf-coast-of-mexico|Gulf Coast]] region, and conquered local peoples in the 13th century. They built fortified capitals and, in the 15th century, founded [[e:qumarkaj|Q'umarkaj]] (Utatlán) on a defensible plateau.
kiche-kingdom.r: Four great lineages shared power, headed by the Kaweq, whose leaders held the titles Ajpop and Ajpop K'amha. Under K'iq'ab, in the mid-15th century, the kingdom reached its greatest extent, ruling much of western [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] and the Pacific slope, before revolts, including the secession of the [[s:kaqchikel-kingdom|Kaqchikel kingdom]], weakened it. Temples, palaces and a ballcourt filled [[e:qumarkaj|Q'umarkaj]].
kiche-kingdom.e: In 1524 [[e:pedro-de-alvarado|Pedro de Alvarado]] defeated the [[e:kiche-people|K'iche']] near [[e:quetzaltenango|Quetzaltenango]], where tradition says the hero [[e:tecun-uman|Tecun Uman]] fell, then burnt the kings [[e:oxib-keh|Oxib Keh]] and [[e:beleheb-tzi|Beleheb Tz'i]] and destroyed [[e:qumarkaj|Q'umarkaj]]. The [[e:popol-vuh|Popol Vuh]] was written down in the 1550s, and K'iche' remains [[e:guatemala|Guatemala's]] most widely spoken Maya language.

kanesh.t: Kanesh, a central Anatolian city-kingdom near Kayseri that hosted the largest Assyrian trading colony, and whose name gave the Hittite language its own title.
kanesh.o: Kanesh, at Kültepe, was a native Anatolian city by the late 3rd millennium BCE. From c. 1950 BCE merchants from [[e:assur|Assur]] settled in a trading quarter, the karum, below its citadel, bringing [[e:tin|tin]] and woollen textiles by donkey caravan to exchange for Anatolian [[e:silver|silver]] and gold.
kanesh.r: Local kings and queens ruled the citadel and taxed the trade under treaties with [[e:assur|Assur]], while the merchants kept their own court and over 23,000 letters and contracts in Old Assyrian. The archives record Anatolian personal names that are the earliest evidence of Hittite, which its speakers later called nesili after Nesa, the local name of Kanesh.
kanesh.e: Around 1750 BCE [[e:pithana|Pithana]] and his son [[e:anitta|Anitta of Kussara]] captured Nesa and made it their seat. The trade colony faded c. 1700 BCE and the city lost importance as power shifted towards [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]] and the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]].

kingdom-of-gomma.t: One of the five Oromo kingdoms of the Gibe region in south-western Ethiopia, noted as an early centre of Islam among the Oromo.
kingdom-of-gomma.o: Gomma emerged around 1800 in the upper [[e:didessa-river|Didessa]] and [[e:gibe-river|Gibe]] valleys, one of the monarchies formed as [[e:oromo|Oromo]] settlers of the region replaced the egalitarian gadaa system with hereditary kingship. It bordered the [[s:kingdom-of-jimma|Kingdom of Jimma]], [[s:limmu-ennarea|Limmu-Ennarea]], the [[s:kingdom-of-gumma|Kingdom of Gumma]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-gera|Kingdom of Gera]].
kingdom-of-gomma.r: Its kings ruled through officials and governors in the manner of the other [[e:gibe-river|Gibe]] states, and its people farmed and grew [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] in the fertile valleys. Gomma was among the first Gibe states to adopt [[e:islam|Islam]], and Muslim scholars and traders from the north were active there. It took part in the trade in coffee, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and slaves.
kingdom-of-gomma.e: Weakened by wars with its neighbours, Gomma was conquered by the forces of [[e:menelik-ii|Menelik II]] and annexed to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] in 1886.

kingdom-of-sussex.t: The kingdom of the South Saxons on the English Channel coast, among the earliest Anglo-Saxon realms and the last major one to accept Christianity.
kingdom-of-sussex.o: The [[e:anglo-saxon-chronicle|Anglo-Saxon Chronicle]] says that [[e:aelle-of-sussex|Aelle]] and his three sons landed in 477 and fought the [[e:britons-celtic-people|Britons]] near the shore, later storming the Roman fort of [[e:pevensey-castle|Anderitum]] (Pevensey) in 491. [[e:bede|Bede]] names Aelle as the first overlord of the southern English. Settlement was hemmed in by the dense [[e:the-weald|Weald]] forest, which isolated the kingdom from its neighbours.
kingdom-of-sussex.r: Sussex was small and inward-looking, with a farming economy on the coastal plain and the chalk downs. Its kings often stood under Mercian or [[e:wessex|West Saxon]] overlordship. Paganism lasted until [[e:wilfrid|Wilfrid of York]] converted the South [[s:saxons|Saxons]] in the 680s, founding a monastery at [[e:selsey|Selsey]] on land given by King [[e:aethelwealh-of-sussex|Aethelwealh]]; Selsey later became the seat of the South [[e:saxons|Saxon]] bishopric. Several kings sometimes ruled at once.
kingdom-of-sussex.e: [[e:caedwalla|Caedwalla]] of [[s:kingdom-of-wessex|Wessex]] overran Sussex in the 680s, and in the 8th century it fell under [[e:offa-of-mercia|Offa of Mercia]]. After [[e:egbert-of-wessex|Ecgberht]]'s victory at [[e:battle-of-ellendun|Ellendun]] in 825, Sussex submitted to the [[e:wessex|Kingdom of Wessex]] and became a shire. The name survives in the modern counties of East and [[e:west-sussex|West Sussex]].

kazikumukh-khanate.t: A Lak khanate in the mountains of central Dagestan whose ruler Surkhay Khan briefly controlled Shirvan in the 1720s.
kazikumukh-khanate.o: When the shamkhals moved to [[e:tarki|Tarki]] around 1642, the [[e:lak|Lak]] heartland at [[e:kumukh|Kumukh]] became a separate state under its own rulers, who took the title khan. The khanate kept the prestige of Kumukh as an old centre of [[e:islam|Islam]] in [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]].
kazikumukh-khanate.r: The khans ruled [[e:lak|Lak]] villages known for craftsmen, traders and seasonal workers, and drew wealth from raids and [[e:mercenary|mercenary]] service. [[e:surkhay-khan-i|Surkhay Khan I]] joined the rebel [[e:hajji-davud|Hajji Davud]] in sacking [[e:shamakhi|Shamakhi]] in 1721, an event that helped trigger [[e:peter-the-great|Peter the Great's]] Persian campaign, and briefly ruled [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvan]] as an Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassal]]. [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] later defeated him.
kazikumukh-khanate.e: The khanate accepted Russian protection in 1820. Its khans, such as [[e:aslan-khan-of-kazikumukh|Aslan Khan]], sided with [[e:russia|Russia]] against the [[s:caucasian-imamate|Caucasian Imamate]], and in 1860 the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished it. Its lands became the Kazikumukh district of the [[e:dagestan-oblast|Dagestan Oblast]], the heart of today's [[e:lak|Lak]] region.

kamarupa.t: The ancient kingdom of Assam in the Brahmaputra valley, ruled by three successive dynasties for some 800 years.
kamarupa.o: Kamarupa, known in the epics as Pragjyotisha, emerged as a state in the mid-4th century under [[e:pushyavarman|Pushyavarman]], founder of the Varman dynasty. The [[e:prayagraj|Allahabad]] pillar inscription lists it among frontier kingdoms paying tribute to [[e:samudragupta|Samudragupta]] of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]]. Its kings claimed descent from the mythical [[e:narakasura|Naraka]] and [[e:bhagadatta|Bhagadatta]].
kamarupa.r: The greatest Varman king, [[e:bhaskaravarman|Bhaskaravarman]], allied with [[e:harsha|Harsha]] of the [[s:pushyabhuti-dynasty|Pushyabhuti dynasty]] and received the Chinese pilgrim [[e:xuanzang|Xuanzang]] around 643. After him the Mlechchha dynasty of [[e:salastambha|Salastambha]] ruled from Haruppeshvara, near [[e:tezpur|Tezpur]], followed by the [[s:pala-empire|Pala dynasty]] of Kamarupa. Kings made land grants to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] recorded on [[e:copper|copper]] plates; the kingdom traded [[e:silk|silk]], aloe wood and elephants, and the goddess shrine at [[e:kamakhya-temple|Kamakhya]] became a major centre of [[e:shaktism|Shakta]] worship.
kamarupa.e: Kamarupa fragmented in the 12th century after the [[s:pala-empire|Pala dynasty]] of [[e:bengal|Bengal]] installed its general [[e:vaidyadeva|Vaidyadeva]] as ruler. Smaller successor states, among them Kamata, took its place, and in the 13th century the [[s:ahom-kingdom|Ahom kingdom]] rose in the upper valley.

kingdom-of-slavonia.t: Habsburg crown land between the Drava and Sava rivers, reconquered from the Ottomans in 1699 and rebuilt with new settlers and baroque towns.
kingdom-of-slavonia.o: [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] armies drove the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] out of [[e:slavonia|Slavonia]] in the [[e:great-turkish-war|Great Turkish War]], and the [[e:treaty-of-karlowitz|Treaty of Karlowitz]] in 1699 confirmed the conquest. The reclaimed land was divided between a civilian part, organised as the counties of [[e:pozega-croatia|Požega]], [[e:virovitica|Virovitica]] and [[e:syrmia|Srijem]], and a southern strip along the [[e:sava|Sava]] placed in the [[s:military-frontier|Military Frontier]].
kingdom-of-slavonia.r: [[e:slavonia|Slavonia]] was depopulated by war, so the crown and new landowners brought in German, Hungarian, Slovak and [[e:serbs|Serb]] settlers. [[e:osijek|Osijek's]] fortress, [[e:tvrda|Tvrđa]], was rebuilt in the 1710s and 1720s, and the bishopric of [[e:dakovo|Đakovo]] revived Catholic life, while [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Serbs were organised around [[e:sremski-karlovci|Sremski Karlovci]]. From 1745 the civil counties were placed under the Croatian ban and [[e:croatian-parliament|Sabor]].
kingdom-of-slavonia.e: [[e:slavonia|Slavonia]] remained formally a separate kingdom within the [[e:lands-of-the-crown-of-saint-stephen|Lands of the Hungarian Crown]] until the [[e:croatian-hungarian-settlement|Croatian-Hungarian Settlement]] of 1868 joined it with [[e:croatia|Croatia]] as the [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia|Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia]]. The eastern part, [[e:syrmia|Srijem]], was divided between Croatia and [[s:serbia|Serbia]] after 1945.

khanate-of-kazan.t: A Tatar khanate on the middle Volga, successor to Volga Bulgaria, whose conquest by Ivan the Terrible in 1552 opened the East to Russia.
khanate-of-kazan.o: Around 1438 [[e:ulugh-muhammad|Ulugh Muhammad]], a deposed khan of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]], settled in the former lands of [[s:volga-bulgaria|Volga Bulgaria]] and established a khanate with [[e:kazan|Kazan]] as its capital. His son Mahmud consolidated it as an independent state.
khanate-of-kazan.r: [[e:kazan|Kazan]] ruled [[e:tatars|Tatars]], [[e:chuvash-people|Chuvash]], [[s:mari|Mari]], [[e:udmurts|Udmurts]] and [[e:bashkirs|Bashkirs]], with a farming and trading economy linked to the [[e:volga|Volga]] route. The khan shared power with a council of leading princely clans and religious leaders. The city had mosques, [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] and a strong merchant community. Rival factions favoured [[e:moscow|Moscow]] or the [[s:crimean-khanate|Crimean Khanate]], and Russian-backed khans such as [[e:shah-ali-khan|Shah Ali]] were repeatedly installed.
khanate-of-kazan.e: After several failed campaigns, [[e:ivan-iv-of-russia|Ivan IV]] besieged and stormed [[e:kazan|Kazan]] in 1552, annexing the khanate to [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Muscovy]]. Its [[e:tatars|Tatar]] population survived, and Kazan remained the centre of Tatar culture, now the capital of [[e:tatarstan|Tatarstan]].

kingdom-of-mauretania.t: The Berber kingdom of the Moors in Morocco and western Algeria, ending with Juba II's learned court at Caesarea.
kingdom-of-mauretania.o: The [[e:mauri|Mauri]], [[e:berbers|Berber]] peoples of northern [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], were united under kings by the late 3rd century BCE; the first well-known king, [[e:baga-of-mauretania|Baga]], provided an escort to [[e:masinissa|Masinissa]] in 206 BCE. The kingdom lay west of the [[e:moulouya-river|Mulucha]] (Moulouya) river and included old Phoenician towns such as [[s:lixus|Lixus]] and [[e:tangier|Tingis]].
kingdom-of-mauretania.r: The kings mixed [[e:berbers|Berber]], Punic and later Roman and Greek culture. [[e:bocchus-i|Bocchus I]] handed [[e:jugurtha|Jugurtha]] of [[s:numidia|Numidia]] to [[e:sulla|Sulla]] in 105 BCE, gaining western Numidia. After [[e:bocchus-ii|Bocchus II]] bequeathed the kingdom to [[e:rome|Rome]], Augustus installed [[e:juba-ii|Juba II]] in 25 BCE, and Juba married [[e:cleopatra-selene-ii|Cleopatra Selene]], daughter of [[e:cleopatra-vii|Cleopatra VII]]. Juba, a scholar, rebuilt [[e:caesarea-mauretaniae|Iol]] as [[s:lordship-of-caesarea|Caesarea]], and the kingdom exported purple dye, citrus wood and wild animals.
kingdom-of-mauretania.e: In 40 CE [[e:caligula|Caligula]] summoned [[e:juba-ii|Juba]]'s son Ptolemy to [[e:rome|Rome]] and had him executed. After a revolt led by [[e:aedemon|Aedemon]], [[e:claudius|Claudius]] annexed the kingdom, dividing it in 42 CE into [[s:mauretania-tingitana|Mauretania Tingitana]] and [[s:mauretania-caesariensis|Mauretania Caesariensis]].

kingdom-of-aragon.t: The Pyrenean kingdom that conquered the Ebro valley, joined Catalonia to form the Crown of Aragon and kept its own laws until 1707.
kingdom-of-aragon.o: Aragon began as a small Carolingian-era county around [[e:jaca|Jaca]]. In 1035 [[e:sancho-iii-of-navarre|Sancho III of Navarre]] left it to his son [[e:ramiro-i-of-aragon|Ramiro I]], who ruled as king in practice. His heirs [[e:sancho-ramirez|Sancho Ramírez]] and Peter I expanded south, taking [[e:huesca|Huesca]] in 1096, and [[e:alfonso-i-of-aragon|Alfonso I the Battler]] captured [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] in 1118.
kingdom-of-aragon.r: The kingdom developed strong traditions of noble privilege: its [[e:corte|Cortes]], its fueros and the [[e:justicia-de-aragon|Justicia de Aragón]], a judge who guarded the laws even against the king. Its economy rested on [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] valley farming, wool and the many Muslim farmers, later called mudéjares and [[e:moriscos|Moriscos]], who stayed on the land. [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] became its capital.
kingdom-of-aragon.e: The marriage of [[e:petronilla-of-aragon|Petronila]] to [[e:ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-barcelona|Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona]] created the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]]. Aragon kept its institutions under [[s:habsburg-spain|Habsburg Spain]] until Philip V abolished them by the [[e:nueva-planta-decrees|Nueva Planta decrees]] of 1707 after the [[e:war-of-the-spanish-succession|War of the Spanish Succession]].

kingdom-of-eguafo.t: Coastal Akan kingdom of the central Gold Coast whose lands held Elmina, where the Portuguese built their great fort in 1482.
kingdom-of-eguafo.o: Eguafo, called Commany by Europeans after the port of [[e:komenda|Komenda]], was a small [[e:akan|Akan]] kingdom inland from the central [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]]. It already existed when the Portuguese arrived in 1471, and the fishing town of [[e:elmina|Elmina]] lay within its territory, though its own chiefs dealt independently with the newcomers.
kingdom-of-eguafo.r: Eguafo's rulers profited from the trade in gold, and later slaves, passing through the coastal towns, charging rents and customs from European forts. In the 17th century the [[e:dutch|Dutch]], English and others competed for its favour, and the [[e:komenda-wars|Komenda Wars]] from 1694 to 1700 drew Eguafo into conflict between the Dutch and English companies.
kingdom-of-eguafo.e: Weakened by those wars and by rising inland powers such as the [[e:fante|Fante]] and the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]], Eguafo lost importance in the 18th century. Its people became part of the Fante coastal states, and Eguafo survives as a traditional area in [[e:ghana|Ghana's]] Central Region.

kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.t: Autonomous Croatian kingdom within the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary, where modern Croatian institutions and the idea of South Slav unity took shape.
kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.o: The [[e:croatian-hungarian-settlement|Croatian-Hungarian Settlement]] of 1868, known as the Nagodba, joined the kingdoms of [[e:croatia|Croatia]] and [[e:slavonia|Slavonia]] into one autonomous unit within the [[e:lands-of-the-crown-of-saint-stephen|Lands of the Hungarian Crown]]. Croatia kept its own [[e:croatian-parliament|Sabor]] and control of internal affairs, justice and education, while finance and defence were common with [[e:hungary|Hungary]]. The former [[s:military-frontier|Military Frontier]] was added in 1881.
kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.r: A ban appointed on the Hungarian prime minister's advice headed the government in [[e:zagreb|Zagreb]]. Ban [[e:ivan-mazuranic|Ivan Mažuranić]] modernised schools and courts in the 1870s, while Ban [[e:karoly-khuen-hedervary|Károly Khuen-Héderváry]], from 1883 to 1903, ruled by playing [[e:serbs|Serbs]] against [[e:croats|Croats]]. [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:josip-juraj-strossmayer|Strossmayer]] founded the [[e:croatian-academy-of-sciences-and-arts|Yugoslav Academy]] and helped open the [[e:university-of-zagreb|University of Zagreb]] in 1874. [[s:free-state-of-fiume|Fiume]] remained under [[e:hungary|Hungary]].
kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.e: From 1905 the [[e:croat-serb-coalition|Croat-Serb Coalition]] dominated politics. On 29 October 1918 the [[e:croatian-parliament|Sabor]] broke all ties with [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] and joined the [[s:state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs|State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs]], which in December merged into the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]].

kingdom-of-brycheiniog.t: Welsh kingdom of the Usk valley, founded according to legend by the Irish-descended Brychan, whose royal crannog at Llangorse was stormed by the Mercians in 916.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.o: Brycheiniog took its name, by tradition, from [[e:brychan|Brychan]], a legendary 5th-century ruler of Irish and British descent whose many saintly children are celebrated in Welsh and Cornish tradition. Ogham-inscribed stones in the region support Irish settlement in the post-Roman period. The kingdom occupied the upper [[e:river-usk|Usk]] valley and the uplands around modern [[s:lordship-of-brecknock|Brecon]].
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.r: Its kings were often under pressure from larger neighbours. [[e:asser|Asser]] records that Elisedd ap Tewdwr submitted to [[e:alfred-the-great|Alfred of Wessex]] in the 880s. The royal crannog on [[e:llangorse-lake|Llangorse Lake]], an artificial island built in the 890s, is the only one known in [[e:wales|Wales]]; in 916 the Mercians under [[e:aethelflaed|Æthelflæd]] attacked it and carried off the king's wife. Tewdwr ab Elisedd later witnessed English royal charters.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.e: Brycheiniog lost its independence in the 11th century, coming under the rulers of [[s:kingdom-of-deheubarth|Deheubarth]] and [[s:kingdom-of-morgannwg|Morgannwg]]. In 1093 the Norman [[e:bernard-de-neufmarche|Bernard de Neufmarché]] defeated and killed [[e:rhys-ap-tewdwr|Rhys ap Tewdwr]] near [[s:lordship-of-brecknock|Brecon]] and created the Norman lordship of Brecknock, which later became the county of [[e:brecknockshire|Brecknockshire]].

kingdom-of-tabanan.t: Rice-rich kingdom of south-western Bali whose ruling house ended in tragedy during the Dutch conquest of 1906.
kingdom-of-tabanan.o: Tabanan traced its ruling dynasty to Arya Kenceng, a noble said to have come to [[e:bali|Bali]] with the [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]] conquest of the 14th century. The house became an independent kingdom as the central [[s:kingdom-of-gelgel|Gelgel]] state broke apart in the 17th century, ruling the fertile slopes between [[e:mount-batukaru|Mount Batukaru]] and the south coast.
kingdom-of-tabanan.r: The kings, styled Cokorda, ruled through branches of the royal family and allied noble houses, with [[e:brahmins|Brahmana]] priests serving the court. The economy rested on wet-[[e:rice|rice]] farming organised by subak irrigation societies, and Tabanan became one of the granaries of [[e:bali|Bali]]. Its courts were active patrons of temple festivals and gamelan.
kingdom-of-tabanan.e: In 1906, after the puputan of the [[s:kingdom-of-badung|Kingdom of Badung]], [[e:dutch|Dutch]] troops advanced on Tabanan. The raja [[e:gusti-ngurah-agung|Gusti Ngurah Agung]] surrendered and took his own life in captivity with his son. The kingdom was annexed into the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]], though the royal house remains locally prominent.

karenni-states.t: A group of small Karenni principalities in the eastern hills of Burma whose independence Britain and Burma recognised in 1875.
karenni-states.o: The Karenni, or [[e:karenni-people|Red Karen]], lived in the hills between the Shan plateau and [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]]. In the early 19th century their chiefs organised several small states, the most important being [[e:kantarawaddy|Kantarawaddy]], alongside [[e:bawlake|Bawlake]] and [[e:kyebogyi|Kyebogyi]]. Their early history is known mainly from British and Burmese records.
karenni-states.r: Karenni chiefs, called saopha in the Shan style, ruled over [[e:rice|rice]] farmers, hill cultivators and teak forests, and traded and raided across the [[e:salween|Salween]]. In 1875 an agreement between [[e:mindon-min|King Mindon]] of the [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]] and the British recognised the Karenni states as independent of both, a status that made them unlike the Shan states.
karenni-states.e: From 1892 the Karenni chiefs accepted British protection, but the states remained outside [[s:british-burma|British Burma]] proper. In 1948 they joined the [[s:myanmar|Union of Burma]], and in 1952 the region became [[e:kayah-state|Kayah State]]. Claims of separate status fuelled a long Karenni insurgency.

kingdom-of-rhos.t: Early kingdom of the north Welsh coast east of the Conwy, guarded by the fortress of Deganwy, which became a cantref of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-rhos.o: Rhos lay between the [[e:river-conwy|River Conwy]] and the Clwydian hills, on the coast of modern Conwy county. Welsh tradition linked it with the sons of [[e:cunedda|Cunedda]], and in the 6th century [[e:gildas|Gildas]] denounced [[e:cuneglasus|Cuneglasus]], often identified as a king of Rhos, as the charioteer of the Bear's Stronghold, possibly the hillfort of [[e:bryn-euryn|Bryn Euryn]] near [[e:colwyn-bay|Colwyn Bay]].
kingdom-of-rhos.r: The fortress of [[e:deganwy|Deganwy]], on twin hills above the [[e:river-conwy|Conwy]] estuary, was associated with [[e:maelgwn-gwynedd|Maelgwn Gwynedd]] and with the rulers of Rhos, and excavation has found imported [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] pottery of the 5th and 6th centuries. The kingdom was closely tied to the [[s:kingdom-of-gwynedd|Kingdom of Gwynedd]] and its kings were probably a junior branch of Maelgwn's dynasty.
kingdom-of-rhos.e: In 822, according to the [[e:annales-cambriae|Annales Cambriae]], the Mercians destroyed [[e:deganwy|Deganwy]] and took control of [[s:kingdom-of-powys|Powys]]. Rhos was later firmly part of the [[s:kingdom-of-gwynedd|Kingdom of Gwynedd]] as a cantref of the [[e:perfeddwlad|Perfeddwlad]], contested with English kings, until the conquest of 1283.

korea-state.t: A Chauhan-ruled forest state of northern Chhattisgarh, its hills rich in coal, governed from Baikunthpur.
korea-state.o: [[e:korea|Korea]], or Koriya, was ruled by a [[e:chauhan|Chauhan]] family whose traditions say they took the territory from earlier Kol chiefs. The register dates the state to around 1600. It lay in the hilly north-west of the [[e:chota-nagpur-plateau|Chota Nagpur]] plateau.
korea-state.r: The Raja ruled a thinly settled land of forest and tribal villages. Under British paramountcy it was a [[e:chota-nagpur-plateau|Chota Nagpur]] tributary state, transferred to the [[e:central-provinces|Central Provinces]] in 1905 and later to the [[e:eastern-states-agency|Eastern States Agency]]. The coalfields around [[e:chirmiri|Chirmiri]] and [[e:manendragarh|Manendragarh]] were developed in the 20th century.
korea-state.e: [[e:korea|Korea]] merged into the [[e:central-provinces|Central Provinces and Berar]] in 1948, later [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]]. It is now Koriya district of [[e:chhattisgarh|Chhattisgarh]].

kingdom-of-vungu.t: A small kingdom north of the lower Congo River, remembered in Kongo tradition as the homeland of the founders of the Kingdom of Kongo.
kingdom-of-vungu.o: Vungu lay in the [[e:mayombe|Mayombe]] region north of the [[e:congo-river|Congo River]] and is known chiefly from oral traditions recorded by Portuguese and later writers. These say that the founder of [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kongo]], [[e:lukeni-lua-nimi|Lukeni lua Nimi]], was a younger son of a Vungu ruler who crossed the river in the 14th century to conquer lands to the south.
kingdom-of-vungu.r: Very little is known of its government. Like neighbouring [[e:kongo-language|Kikongo]]-speaking polities it was probably ruled by a sacred king drawn from leading lineages, with authority tied to ancestral and territorial spirits. Its prestige rested largely on its role as the ancestral source of [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kongo]] kingship, as Kongo traditions acknowledged.
kingdom-of-vungu.e: Vungu was gradually overshadowed by larger coastal kingdoms such as the [[s:kingdom-of-loango|Kingdom of Loango]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-kakongo|Kingdom of Kakongo]], and it faded from the record by around 1700. Its memory survives mainly in [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kongo]] origin traditions.

kawardha-state.t: A Raj Gond principality in the Maikal hills of Chhattisgarh, near the Bhoramdeo temple.
kawardha-state.o: Kawardha was founded in the mid-18th century by a [[e:raj-gond|Raj Gond]] family holding land at the edge of the [[e:maikal-range|Maikal range]]. It was subordinate to the [[e:bhonsles|Bhonsles]] of the [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Nagpur Kingdom]].
kawardha-state.r: After the British took over the [[e:nagpur|Nagpur]] territories, Kawardha became a feudatory state of the [[e:central-provinces|Central Provinces]] and later part of the [[e:chhattisgarh-feudatory-states|Chhattisgarh States]]. Its population was largely rural and partly Adivasi. The nearby 11th-century [[e:bhoramdeo-temple|Bhoramdeo temple]] is the best-known monument of the area.
kawardha-state.e: Kawardha acceded to [[e:india|India]] and on 1 January 1948 was merged into the [[e:central-provinces|Central Provinces and Berar]]. It is now the headquarters of [[e:kabirdham-district|Kabirdham district]] in [[e:chhattisgarh|Chhattisgarh]].

kotoko-kingdoms.t: Walled city-states on the Logone and Chari rivers south of Lake Chad, heirs to the ancient Sao culture.
kotoko-kingdoms.o: The [[e:kotoko-people|Kotoko]] are considered descendants of the Sao, who built walled settlements on the plains south of [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]] from the first millennium. By the 16th century a number of Kotoko towns, including Logone-Birni, [[e:kousseri|Kousseri]], [[e:makari|Makari]] and [[e:goulfey|Goulfey]], had become small kingdoms, each surrounded by thick earthen walls.
kotoko-kingdoms.r: Each town was ruled by its own sultan, or mra, with titled officials, and lived from fishing, farming and river trade. The [[e:kotoko-people|Kotoko]] states paid tribute to the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]], adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] between the 17th and 19th centuries, and were known for their brick architecture and bronze work.
kotoko-kingdoms.e: The warlord [[s:rabih-az-zubayrs-state|Rabih az-Zubayr]] overran the region in the 1890s, and the French defeated him at [[e:kousseri|Kousseri]] in 1900. The [[e:kotoko-people|Kotoko]] towns were then divided between [[s:kamerun|German Kamerun]] and French [[e:chad|Chad]], and their sultans survive as traditional rulers.

kurundwad-senior.t: The senior of two Patwardhan Brahmin states at Kurundwad on the Krishna, in the southern Maratha country.
kurundwad-senior.o: Kurundwad was one of the shares created when the [[e:patwardhan|Patwardhan family]], [[e:chitpavan-brahmins|Chitpavan Brahmin]] generals of the [[e:peshwa|Peshwas]], divided its lands in 1811. In 1855 the Kurundwad share was itself divided between two branches, forming the Senior and Junior states.
kurundwad-senior.r: Kurundwad Senior was a small state of the [[e:southern-maratha-country|Southern Maratha Country]], later the [[e:deccan-states-agency|Deccan States Agency]], ruled by a Chief from a palace at the confluence of the [[e:krishna|Krishna]] and [[e:panchganga-river|Panchganga]]. Its territory was small and scattered, mainly farmland.
kurundwad-senior.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Kurundwad Senior was merged into [[e:bombay-state|Bombay State]] in 1948 and has been part of [[e:maharashtra|Maharashtra]] since 1960; the town lies in [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] district.

kingdom-of-ketu.t: Ancient Yoruba kingdom on today's Benin-Nigeria border, a Yoruba outpost between the Oyo and Dahomey powers.
kingdom-of-ketu.o: Ketu traditions trace its royal line, the Alaketu, to a grandson of [[e:oduduwa|Oduduwa]] who left [[s:kingdom-of-ife|Ile-Ife]], and name Ede as the founder of the walled town of Ketu. The kingdom took shape in the western [[e:yoruba|Yoruba]] lands, and its massive town wall and gate, the Idena, became symbols of its antiquity.
kingdom-of-ketu.r: The Alaketu was chosen from royal houses in rotation and ruled with town chiefs and powerful religious societies. Ketu was a centre of [[e:yoruba|Yoruba]] religion, notably of the orisha cults later carried to [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]]. Lying between the [[s:oyo-empire|Oyo Empire]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-dahomey|Kingdom of Dahomey]], it was repeatedly raided by Dahomean armies from the late 18th century.
kingdom-of-ketu.e: In 1886 the forces of [[s:kingdom-of-dahomey|Dahomey]] under King [[e:glele|Glele]] destroyed Ketu and carried off much of its population. After the French conquest of [[e:kingdom-of-dahomey|Dahomey]] the town was resettled within [[s:french-dahomey|French Dahomey]], and the Alaketu still reigns at Ketou in [[e:benin-empire|Benin]].

kel-ewey.t: A powerful Tuareg confederation of the Aïr mountains, masters of the salt caravans between the Sahara and Hausaland.
kel-ewey.o: The Kel Ewey are thought to have entered the [[e:air-mountains|Aïr]] massif in the 15th or 16th century, displacing earlier [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] groups such as the [[s:kel-gres|Kel Gres]] southward. They established themselves in the central and eastern Aïr around [[e:timia|Timia]] and [[e:iferouane|Iferouane]], closely linked to the [[s:sultanate-of-agadez|Sultanate of Agadez]].
kel-ewey.r: The confederation was led by an anastafidet whose influence over the choice of sultan in [[s:sultanate-of-agadez|Agadez]] was considerable. Society was hierarchical, with noble, [[e:vassal|vassal]], religious and servile groups. The Kel Ewey organised the great caravans carrying salt and dates from [[e:bilma|Bilma]] and [[e:fachi|Fachi]] south to [[s:hausa-kingdoms|Hausaland]], returning with [[e:millet|millet]] and cloth.
kel-ewey.e: French troops occupied [[e:air-mountains|Aïr]] after 1900. In 1916 to 1917 [[e:kaocen-ag-mohammed|Kaocen ag Mohammed]], of a Kel Ewey section, led a major revolt and besieged [[s:sultanate-of-agadez|Agadez]], but French forces crushed the uprising in 1917. The Kel Ewey remain a major [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] group in [[e:niger-river|Niger]].

kingdom-of-ait-abbas.t: A Kabyle mountain kingdom in the Bibans, ruled from the fortress of Kalâa, that long resisted Ottoman Algiers and later led the 1871 Mokrani revolt.
kingdom-of-ait-abbas.o: After [[e:spain|Spain]] took [[e:bejaia|Bejaia]] in 1510, Hafsid-era notables of the region founded a principality in the Bibans mountains of [[e:lesser-kabylia|Lesser Kabylia]], with its stronghold at the Kalâa of the Ait Abbas. It controlled the [[e:iron-gates-algeria|Iron Gates]] pass on the route between [[e:algiers|Algiers]] and Constantine.
kingdom-of-ait-abbas.r: The kingdom's rulers drew on [[e:kabyles|Kabyle]] tribal levies armed with firearms and on the craft workshops of the Kalâa. Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]], its most famous ruler, alternately allied with and fought the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]] and the rival [[s:kingdom-of-kuku|Kingdom of Kuku]], and fell in battle against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] around 1559. Later the ruling family became known as the Mokrani.
kingdom-of-ait-abbas.e: The Mokrani accommodated Ottoman and then French rule as local lords. In 1871 [[e:mohamed-el-mokrani|Mohamed El Mokrani]] led a great uprising against [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]]; its defeat in 1872 brought confiscations and the end of the family's power.

kingdom-of-paphlagonia.t: Paphlagonia, a kingdom of the forested Black Sea hinterland, ruled by local dynasts under Persia and later a pawn of Pontus and Rome.
kingdom-of-paphlagonia.o: The Paphlagonians lived between [[s:kingdom-of-bithynia|Bithynia]] and [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Pontus]], along the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] coast and the forested mountains behind it, with [[e:cankiri|Gangra]] as an inland seat. By the early 4th century BCE they had kings, such as [[e:corylas|Corylas]], mentioned by [[e:xenophon|Xenophon]], who were nominally subject to the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]].
kingdom-of-paphlagonia.r: The rulers commanded cavalry and controlled [[e:timber|timber]] and the coastal towns. Thys defied [[e:persia|Persia]] until [[e:datames|Datames]] captured him c. 380 BCE. Later kings, often called Pylaemenes, sought alliances with [[e:rome|Rome]] while [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Pontus]] pressed them.
kingdom-of-paphlagonia.e: [[e:mithridates-vi-of-pontus|Mithridates VI]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Kingdom of Pontus]] occupied Paphlagonia in the 2nd century BCE. After [[e:rome|Rome's]] victory it was divided among client rulers; when [[e:deiotarus-philadelphus|Deiotarus Philadelphus]] died in 6 BCE, his kingdom was annexed to Roman [[s:galatia|Galatia]].

kingdom-of-maravi.t: The Chewa confederacy of the Kalonga at the southern end of Lake Malawi, which controlled the ivory trade of the lower Zambezi and gave Malawi its name.
kingdom-of-maravi.o: According to tradition, the Phiri clan migrated from the [[e:luba-empire|Luba]] lands of the [[e:congo-basin|Congo basin]] and settled south-west of [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]] in the late 15th century. Their leader took the title Kalonga and set up his capital at Mankhamba, near the lake. Related chiefs spread out to found the [[s:kingdom-of-undi|Kingdom of Undi]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-lundu|Kingdom of Lundu]].
kingdom-of-maravi.r: The Kalonga ruled a loose confederacy of chiefs bound by kinship and tribute. Wealth came from iron working, cloth and especially [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], sold to the Portuguese and [[e:swahili|Swahili]] on the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]]. Religion centred on the rain shrines of the high god [[e:chisumphi|Chisumphi]] and on the [[e:nyau|Nyau]] masked societies. [[e:kalonga-masula|Kalonga Masula]] in the early 17th century extended Maravi power towards the coast and in 1608 sent warriors to help the Portuguese support the [[e:mutapa-empire|Mutapa]] ruler against rebels.
kingdom-of-maravi.e: After [[e:kalonga-masula|Masula]]'s death the confederacy loosened, and by the early 18th century the Kalonga, Undi and [[s:kingdom-of-lundu|Lundu]] ruled separately. [[e:ngoni|Ngoni]] and Yao incursions in the 19th century completed the break-up. The name Maravi survives in modern [[e:malawi|Malawi]].

kingdom-of-tamassos.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom built on rich copper mines, whose last king sold his realm to the king of Kition for fifty talents.
kingdom-of-tamassos.o: Tamassos lay in the [[e:pedieos|Pediaios]] valley at the foot of the [[e:copper|copper]]-rich [[e:troodos-mountains|Troodos]] mountains and was settled from the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]]. Its copper may be the 'Temese' of [[e:homer|Homer's]] [[e:odyssey|Odyssey]]. By the 7th century BCE it was an independent kingdom; its king Admetus appears among the Cypriot rulers listed by [[e:esarhaddon|Esarhaddon of Assyria]].
kingdom-of-tamassos.r: The kingdom's wealth came from [[e:copper|copper]] mining and smelting. Its royal tombs of the 6th century BCE are built of fine ashlar masonry imitating wooden houses, and a sanctuary of [[e:apollo|Apollo]] and the Mother of the Gods has yielded much sculpture. Tamassos used Greek and Phoenician alongside each other.
kingdom-of-tamassos.e: In the 4th century BCE King Pasicyprus sold Tamassos to [[e:pumiyaton|Pumiyaton]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-kition|Kingdom of Kition]] for fifty [[e:talent|talents]]. [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]] later gave it to the king of [[e:salamis-cyprus|Salamis]]. Tamassos survived as a town under Ptolemaic and Roman rule.

kingdom-of-surrey.t: A short-lived Saxon territory south of the Thames whose name, the 'southern district', survives as the county of Surrey.
kingdom-of-surrey.o: Surrey, Suthrige, probably began as the southern part of a larger Middle [[e:saxons|Saxon]] territory on both sides of the [[e:river-thames|Thames]]. In the 7th century it lay between Kent, [[s:kingdom-of-wessex|Wessex]], [[s:kingdom-of-sussex|Sussex]] and [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]] and was ruled by local leaders under one or another of them.
kingdom-of-surrey.r: The only known ruler is [[e:frithuwold|Frithuwold]], a sub-king under [[e:wulfhere-of-mercia|Wulfhere]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Kingdom of Mercia]], who around 672 to 674 endowed [[e:chertsey-abbey|Chertsey Abbey]], founded by [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:eorcenwald|Eorcenwald]]. The charter shows estates, minsters and Mercian overlordship but no independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-surrey.e: Surrey never had a lasting royal line. Control passed between [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]] and [[s:kingdom-of-wessex|Wessex]], and in the 9th century it became a [[e:wessex|West Saxon]] shire, keeping its name and much of its boundary.

kingdom-of-morocco.t: The independent Moroccan monarchy, in which the Alaouite kings have kept central power through decades of political change and the Western Sahara dispute.
kingdom-of-morocco.o: After the [[s:french-protectorate-in-morocco|French protectorate in Morocco]] and the [[s:spanish-protectorate-in-morocco|Spanish protectorate in Morocco]] ended in 1956, [[e:mohammed-v-of-morocco|Sultan Mohammed]] V of the [[s:alaouite-sultanate|Alaouite Sultanate]] adopted the title of king in 1957. [[e:tangier|Tangier]], [[e:tarfaya|Tarfaya]] in 1958 and [[s:ifni|Ifni]] in 1969 were reintegrated.
kingdom-of-morocco.r: [[e:hassan-ii-of-morocco|Hassan II]], king from 1961 to 1999, introduced constitutions but kept firm control, surviving coup attempts in 1971 and 1972 and repressing opposition during the [[e:years-of-lead-morocco|Years of Lead]]. His [[e:green-march|Green March]] of 1975 began Moroccan control of most of [[s:spanish-sahara|Spanish Sahara]], leading to war with the [[e:polisario-front|Polisario Front]]. The economy rests on [[e:phosphate|phosphates]], agriculture, tourism and remittances.
kingdom-of-morocco.e: [[e:mohammed-vi-of-morocco|Mohammed VI]] succeeded in 1999, reforming family law in 2004 and approving a new constitution after the 2011 protests, though the king retains wide powers. [[e:morocco|Morocco]] remains a monarchy, claiming [[e:western-sahara|Western Sahara]].

kingdom-of-gera.t: The southernmost Gibe Oromo kingdom, remembered for holding the Italian explorers Cecchi and Chiarini captive in 1879 to 1880.
kingdom-of-gera.o: Gera emerged as a monarchy around 1835 in the forested highlands south of the [[e:gibe-river|Gibe]], bordering the [[s:kingdom-of-kaffa|Kingdom of Kaffa]]. Like the other Gibe states it was formed when [[e:oromo|Oromo]] settlers adopted hereditary kingship and settled government.
kingdom-of-gera.r: Gera's kings ruled from Chala through officials, with an economy of [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], honey, civet and slaves traded north to the markets of the [[s:kingdom-of-jimma|Kingdom of Jimma]]. The ruling family adopted [[e:islam|Islam]]. In 1879 the court seized the Italian explorers [[e:antonio-cecchi|Antonio Cecchi]] and [[e:giovanni-chiarini|Giovanni Chiarini]], who was held there until his death; Cecchi was freed in 1880 after Ethiopian intervention.
kingdom-of-gera.e: In 1887 Gera was conquered by the forces of [[e:menelik-ii|Menelik II]] and annexed to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]].

kalahandi-state.t: A Naga dynasty state in western Odisha, once known as Karond, whose Maharajas ruled from Junagarh and later Bhawanipatna until 1948.
kalahandi-state.o: Tradition holds that the [[s:nagas-of-padmavati|Naga dynasty]] was founded around 1005 by Raghunath Sai, with its capital at Junagarh. The early history of the state is known mainly from family tradition and later records.
kalahandi-state.r: Kalahandi was a largely rural state of [[e:rice|rice]] fields and forest with a large [[e:kondh|Kondh]] population. In the 18th century it became tributary to the [[e:bhonsles|Bhonsles]] of the [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Nagpur Kingdom]], and in 1849 the capital moved to [[e:bhawanipatna|Bhawanipatna]]. It passed to British supervision with [[e:nagpur|Nagpur]] in 1853, and a Kondh uprising in 1882 was put down by British troops.
kalahandi-state.e: [[e:maharaja|Maharaja]] Pratap Keshari Deo signed the merger agreement, and Kalahandi joined [[e:odisha|Orissa]] on 1 January 1948. It is now a district of Odisha.

kazakh-ssr.t: The vast Soviet republic of the Kazakhs, scene of the Virgin Lands campaign, nuclear testing at Semipalatinsk and the Baikonur space launches.
kazakh-ssr.o: The [[s:kazakh-assr|Kazakh ASSR]] became a union republic, the Kazakh SSR, under the Soviet constitution of December 1936, with its capital at [[e:almaty|Alma-Ata]]. It emerged from the famine of the early 1930s with [[e:kazakhs|Kazakhs]] a minority in their own land.
kazakh-ssr.r: The republic received deported peoples, including [[e:koreans|Koreans]], [[e:volga-germans|Volga Germans]] and [[e:chechens|Chechens]], and many [[e:gulag|Gulag]] camps such as [[e:karlag|Karlag]]. From 1954 [[e:nikita-khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] [[e:virgin-lands-campaign|Virgin Lands campaign]] ploughed millions of hectares of steppe for wheat, bringing in Russian and Ukrainian settlers. The Soviet nuclear test site near [[e:semey|Semipalatinsk]] carried out over 450 tests from 1949 to 1989, and [[e:baikonur-cosmodrome|Baikonur]] launched [[e:sputnik-1|Sputnik]] and [[e:yuri-gagarin|Yuri Gagarin]]. [[e:dinmukhamed-kunaev|Dinmukhamed Kunaev]] led the republic from 1964 to 1986.
kazakh-ssr.e: [[e:dinmukhamed-kunaev|Kunaev]]'s replacement by a Russian sparked the Jeltoqsan protests of December 1986. [[e:nursultan-nazarbayev|Nursultan Nazarbayev]] became leader in 1989, and on 16 December 1991 the republic, the last to leave the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], declared independence as [[s:kazakhstan|Kazakhstan]].

kingdom-of-kinda.t: A central Arabian tribal kingdom that briefly united the Bedouin of Najd under Himyarite patronage and produced the poet Imru al-Qays.
kingdom-of-kinda.o: Kinda was a tribe from the borders of [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]] that moved into central [[e:arabia|Arabia]]. In the 5th century the [[s:himyarite-kingdom|Himyarite Kingdom]] installed its chief [[e:hujr-akil-al-murar|Hujr Akil al-Murar]] as king over the [[e:maadd|Ma'add]] tribes of [[e:najd|Najd]], giving Himyar indirect control of the interior. [[e:qaryat-al-faw|Qaryat al-Faw]], a caravan town on the edge of the Empty Quarter, is often linked with the kingdom.
kingdom-of-kinda.r: Kindite kings ruled as overlords of shifting tribal alliances rather than through fixed institutions, collecting tribute and leading raids. Under [[e:al-harith-ibn-amr|al-Harith ibn Amr]] in the early 6th century, Kinda reached its peak and even held [[e:al-hira|al-Hira]] for a time at the expense of the [[s:lakhmid-kingdom|Lakhmid Kingdom]], reportedly installed there by the Sasanian king [[e:kavad-i|Kavad I]].
kingdom-of-kinda.e: After [[e:al-harith-ibn-amr|al-Harith]] was killed around 528, his sons divided the tribes and were defeated by the [[s:lakhmid-kingdom|Lakhmids]] and rival tribes. The kingdom had collapsed by about 540. Its memory survives through the poet [[e:imru-al-qais|Imru al-Qays]], son of al-Harith's son Hujr, whose ode is one of the [[e:muallaqat|Mu'allaqat]].

kingdom-of-tio.t: The Teke kingdom on the plateaus north of Malebo Pool, whose king signed the 1880 treaty that founded French rule on the Congo.
kingdom-of-tio.o: The Tio or [[s:teke|Teke]] kingdom formed on the sandy plateaus north of [[e:malebo-pool|Malebo Pool]] by the 15th century. Portuguese sources of the 16th century call it Anziku and describe wars with the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kingdom of Kongo]] for control of the Pool, the hub of river trade between the interior and the Atlantic coast.
kingdom-of-tio.r: The king, known as the Makoko, ruled from Mbe as a sacred figure whose power came from the national shrine of Nkwe Mbali and the royal nkobi, a box of sacred relics. Real power was shared with territorial lords who controlled trade at the Pool. The kingdom traded slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and [[e:copper|copper]] downriver in exchange for cloth, guns and shells, and was famed for its raffia textiles.
kingdom-of-tio.e: In 1880 [[e:makoko-iloo-i|Makoko Iloo I]] signed a treaty with [[e:pierre-savorgnan-de-brazza|Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza]] placing his lands under French protection, which gave [[e:france|France]] its foothold on the [[e:congo-river|Congo]] and its new post of [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]]. The kingship survives as a ceremonial office in the [[e:republic-of-the-congo|Republic of the Congo]].

kingdom-of-york.t: The Viking kingdom centred on Jorvik, a prosperous Anglo-Scandinavian town whose kings were often also rulers of Dublin.
kingdom-of-york.o: The [[e:great-heathen-army|Great Heathen Army]] captured York in 866 to 867, and in 876 [[e:halfdan-ragnarsson|Halfdan]] shared out the land of [[s:kingdom-of-northumbria|Northumbria]] south of the [[e:river-tees|Tees]] among his followers. Danish kings ruled from [[e:york|York]], with [[e:guthfrith-of-york|Guthfrith]] in the 880s accepting [[e:christianity|Christianity]]. Early in the 10th century the Norse dynasty of the [[s:kingdom-of-dublin|Kingdom of Dublin]] took over.
kingdom-of-york.r: [[e:york|Jorvik]] grew into a major town of craftsmen and traders, with goods from [[e:scandinavia|Scandinavia]] to the [[e:middle-east|Middle East]], as the [[e:coppergate|Coppergate]] excavations show. Its kings minted coins, some with Christian symbols, and cooperated with the archbishops of York. Scandinavian settlement left hundreds of place-names across [[e:yorkshire|Yorkshire]].
kingdom-of-york.e: Aethelstan seized York in 927, but Norse kings such as [[e:olaf-guthfrithson|Olaf Guthfrithson]], [[e:olaf-cuaran|Amlaib Cuaran]] and [[e:eric-bloodaxe|Eric Bloodaxe]] returned repeatedly. Eric's expulsion and death in 954 ended the kingdom, and York became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-england|Kingdom of England]] as an earldom.

klein-vrystaat.t: A tiny Boer republic on the Swazi border, created from a land grant by the Swazi king Mbandzeni.
klein-vrystaat.o: Around 1886 a group of [[e:boers|Boer]] farmers who had obtained grazing and land concessions from the Swazi king [[e:mbandzeni|Mbandzeni]] in the southwest of his kingdom set themselves up as an independent republic, the Little Free State, around the area of the later town of [[e:piet-retief|Piet Retief]].
klein-vrystaat.r: Very little is recorded beyond its small [[e:volksraad-dutch-east-indies|Volksraad]] and a population of a few dozen farming families. Its existence was one example of the concessions that left much of the [[s:swazi-kingdom|Swazi Kingdom]] in the hands of outsiders.
klein-vrystaat.e: Klein Vrystaat was incorporated into the [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]] in 1891.

kingdom-of-matamba.t: An Mbundu kingdom east of Ndongo, often ruled by women, which Queen Njinga made the base of her long resistance to Portugal.
kingdom-of-matamba.o: Matamba lay in the upper [[e:kwango-river|Kwango]] valley and was a tributary of the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kingdom of Kongo]] in the early 16th century. It was ruled by queens in the later 16th century. Around 1631 [[e:njinga-of-ndongo-and-matamba|Njinga Mbande]], driven out of the [[s:kingdom-of-ndongo|Kingdom of Ndongo]], conquered Matamba and made it the centre of her state.
kingdom-of-matamba.r: [[e:njinga-of-ndongo-and-matamba|Njinga]] ruled with the support of [[e:imbangala|Imbangala]] warriors, trading captives to the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] during their occupation of [[e:luanda|Luanda]] and later to the Portuguese after the peace of 1656. She accepted Christian missionaries, and Santa Maria de Matamba became her capital. After her death in 1663 her sister [[e:barbara-of-matamba|Barbara]] and later rulers continued the line, and the kingdom served as a slave-trading intermediary between the interior and [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]].
kingdom-of-matamba.e: Matamba remained independent through the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes at war with Portugal or the [[s:kingdom-of-kasanje|Kingdom of Kasanje]]. Portuguese forces finally occupied it in 1909, and it was absorbed into [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]].

kingdom-of-the-hwicce.t: An Anglo-Saxon sub-kingdom of the lower Severn valley around Worcester, ruled by its own kings under Mercian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.o: The Hwicce took shape in [[e:gloucestershire|Gloucestershire]], [[e:worcestershire|Worcestershire]] and western [[e:warwickshire|Warwickshire]] after the [[e:wessex|West Saxon]] victory at [[e:battle-of-dyrham|Dyrham]] in 577 opened the region to English settlement. By the 7th century the area was ruled by a local dynasty, possibly installed or confirmed by [[e:penda-of-mercia|Penda]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Kingdom of Mercia]].
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.r: Hwiccan kings such as Osric and [[e:oshere|Oshere]] endowed early minsters, Osric being credited with founding those at [[e:bath|Bath]] and [[e:gloucester|Gloucester]], and a bishopric was created at [[e:worcester|Worcester]] around 680 to serve the people. The territory was rich in salt from [[e:droitwich-spa|Droitwich]] and in farmland, and its charters are among the earliest English documents.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.e: Hwiccan rulers were downgraded from kings to ealdormen in the late 8th century under [[e:offa-of-mercia|Offa]]. The kingdom's boundaries survived as the medieval diocese of [[e:worcester|Worcester]], preserving its outline for centuries.

kingdom-of-kourion.t: Cypriot kingdom on a clifftop above the south coast, remembered for the sanctuary of Apollo Hylates and for its king's betrayal at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE.
kingdom-of-kourion.o: Kourion arose in the Episkopi area of southern [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]], near a [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]] settlement, in the 11th century BCE. Its Greek inhabitants claimed descent from settlers from [[s:argos|Argos]]. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the island's city-kingdoms, listed among the Cypriot rulers who paid tribute to the Assyrian king [[e:esarhaddon|Esarhaddon]].
kingdom-of-kourion.r: The kings ruled a fertile territory along the [[e:kouris-river|Kouris]] river. The sanctuary of [[e:sanctuary-of-apollo-hylates|Apollo Hylates]], god of the woodland, was its chief cult centre, and [[e:luigi-palma-di-cesnola|Luigi Palma di Cesnola]] claimed to have found a rich gold and [[e:silver|silver]] hoard there, the so-called Curium treasure, though its true findspots are doubtful. Kourion followed the Cypriot syllabary and Greek institutions, under Assyrian and then Achaemenid overlordship.
kingdom-of-kourion.e: In the [[e:ionian-revolt|Ionian Revolt]], King Stasanor deserted to the [[e:persians|Persians]] at the [[e:battle-of-salamis-in-cyprus|Battle of Salamis]] in 497 BCE. Later King Pasicrates aided Alexander at [[s:tyre|Tyre]]. The monarchy was abolished under [[e:ptolemy-i-soter|Ptolemy I]] c. 312 BCE, and Kourion flourished as a Roman and early Christian city until earthquakes in the 4th century CE.
kingdom-of-kourion.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Hylates

kingdom-of-corsica.t: The eight-month kingdom of Theodore von Neuhoff, a German adventurer crowned by Corsican rebels against Genoa in 1736.
kingdom-of-corsica.o: Corsicans had been in revolt against Genoese rule since 1729. In March 1736 [[e:theodore-von-neuhoff|Theodore von Neuhoff]], a Westphalian baron, landed with arms and money from [[e:tunis|Tunis]], and in April the rebel leaders crowned him king at the convent of Alesani, with a constitution limiting his power.
kingdom-of-corsica.r: Theodore set up a court at [[e:cervione|Cervione]], created orders of knighthood, minted coins and issued titles, but failed to take the Genoese-held coastal towns. Promised foreign aid did not arrive, and his support among the rebel chiefs waned.
kingdom-of-corsica.e: In November 1736 Theodore left [[s:corsican-republic|Corsica]] to seek help. His later attempts to return failed, and he ended in a [[e:london|London]] debtors' prison, dying in 1756. The revolt continued and later produced the Corsican Republic.

kingdom-of-tunisia.t: Tunisia's brief monarchy after independence, in which the last Husainid bey reigned as king while Habib Bourguiba held power.
kingdom-of-tunisia.o: When the [[s:french-protectorate-of-tunisia|French protectorate of Tunisia]] ended in March 1956, the bey [[e:muhammad-al-amin-bey|Muhammad al-Amin]], known as Lamine Bey, became head of an independent kingdom. [[e:habib-bourguiba|Habib Bourguiba]], leader of the [[e:neo-destour|Neo-Destour]] party, became prime minister after elections to a constituent assembly.
kingdom-of-tunisia.r: Real power lay with [[e:habib-bourguiba|Bourguiba]], who sidelined the monarchy and the rival Youssefist faction. In August 1956 the government issued the Code of Personal Status, abolishing polygamy and reforming divorce, among the most progressive family laws in the Arab world. Religious courts were unified and lands of religious endowments reformed.
kingdom-of-tunisia.e: On 25 July 1957 the constituent assembly abolished the monarchy and proclaimed a republic, with [[e:habib-bourguiba|Bourguiba]] as president. [[e:muhammad-al-amin-bey|Lamine Bey]] was placed under house arrest, ending the [[s:beylik-of-tunis|Husainid dynasty]], which had ruled since 1705.

kingdom-of-syunik.t: A south Armenian mountain kingdom that outlasted the fall of Ani, home to the great monastery of Tatev.
kingdom-of-syunik.o: The [[e:siunia-dynasty|Siunid]] family had governed the mountainous province of Syunik since antiquity. Around 987 Smbat, a prince of its Baghk branch, took the title king with the backing of [[s:bagratid-armenia|Bagratid Armenia]], forming a kingdom in the southern highlands between [[e:lake-sevan|Lake Sevan]] and the [[e:aras-river|Araxes]].
kingdom-of-syunik.r: Kings ruled from fortresses such as [[e:kapan|Kapan]] over a land of deep valleys, mines and pasture. The monastery of [[e:tatev-monastery|Tatev]], seat of the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of Syunik, held many villages and grew into a centre of learning. The kingdom acknowledged the kings of Ani and later paid tribute to the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] while defending its fortresses.
kingdom-of-syunik.e: Seljuk conquests stripped away fortress after fortress in the 12th century, and in 1170 the [[s:eldiguzids|Eldiguzids]] took [[e:baghaberd|Baghaberd]], ending the kingdom. Local princely families such as the [[e:orbelian-dynasty|Orbelians]] later restored Armenian rule in Syunik under Georgian and Mongol overlords.

kingdom-of-hana.t: Hana, a kingdom of the middle Euphrates centred on Terqa, which filled the gap left by Mari's fall and preserved its old traditions.
kingdom-of-hana.o: After the [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]] destroyed [[s:mari|Mari]] c. 1760 BCE, local rulers at [[e:terqa|Terqa]], some 70 kilometres upstream and long the seat of the god [[e:dagan|Dagan]], created the kingdom of Hana. It controlled the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] valley between the [[e:khabur-river|Khabur]] river and the Babylonian frontier.
kingdom-of-hana.r: Its kings, such as Isharlim and Kashtiliashu, issued land contracts in a distinctive Hana style and kept the Mari-era cult of [[e:dagan|Dagan]]. Excavations at [[e:terqa|Tell Ashara]] found a scribe's house with a jar of [[e:cloves|cloves]], which must have travelled from south-east [[e:asia|Asia]]. Some rulers bore names suggesting links with the [[e:kassites|Kassites]].
kingdom-of-hana.e: Hana fell under the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]] in the 15th century BCE and later the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]], surviving as a province and a regional name. Its successor on the middle [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] was the [[s:land-of-suhu|Land of Suhu]].

kingdom-of-nepal.t: The Himalayan kingdom of the Shah dynasty, created by the Gorkha conquest of the Kathmandu Valley and abolished in 2008.
kingdom-of-nepal.o: [[e:prithvi-narayan-shah|Prithvi Narayan Shah]] of the [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha Kingdom]] conquered the [[e:kathmandu-valley|Kathmandu Valley]] in 1768 to 1769 and made [[e:kathmandu|Kathmandu]] his capital. His successors extended the kingdom from the [[e:teesta-river|Teesta]] river to the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]], absorbing the [[s:kumaon-kingdom|Kumaon Kingdom]], the [[s:kingdom-of-palpa|Kingdom of Palpa]] and many hill states, before war with [[e:china|China]] in 1792 and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1814 to 1816 checked expansion.
kingdom-of-nepal.r: The [[e:treaty-of-sugauli|Treaty of Sugauli]] in 1816 fixed [[e:nepal|Nepal's]] borders and made it a semi-isolated buffer. From 1846 the Rana family held hereditary power as prime ministers, with the king a figurehead; [[e:jang-bahadur-rana|Jang Bahadur Rana]] issued the [[e:muluki-ain|Muluki Ain]] law code in 1854. [[e:gurkhas|Gurkha]] soldiers served in the British army. The monarchy regained power in 1951 and [[e:mahendra-of-nepal|Mahendra]] imposed the partyless panchayat system in 1960.
kingdom-of-nepal.e: Popular movements in 1990 restored multiparty democracy. A [[e:nepalese-civil-war|Maoist insurgency]] from 1996, the royal massacre of 2001 and [[e:gyanendra-of-nepal|King Gyanendra]]'s seizure of power in 2005 led to mass protests in 2006. The Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy in 2008, creating the [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-nepal|Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal]].

kwararafa.t: Jukun power of the Benue valley whose armies raided deep into Hausaland in the 16th and 17th centuries.
kwararafa.o: Kwararafa is the name used in [[e:hausa|Hausa]] and [[e:bornu|Bornu]] sources for a power centred on the [[e:jukun-people|Jukun people]] of the middle [[e:benue-river|Benue]]. Its origins are obscure; it emerged by the 14th century, perhaps as a confederacy of Jukun and neighbouring groups along the river valleys south of the Hausa states.
kwararafa.r: The [[e:jukun-people|Jukun]] king, the [[e:aku-uka|Aku Uka]], was a sacred ruler whose wellbeing was bound to the harvest and who was secluded from ordinary view. Kwararafa's strength was military: the [[e:kano-chronicle|Kano Chronicle]] records attacks that forced [[e:kano|Kano]] to pay tribute, and in the 17th century its armies raided [[s:katsina-kingdom|Katsina]], Kano and even threatened the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]].
kwararafa.e: Kwararafa declined in the 18th century under pressure from [[e:bornu|Bornu]], internal division and later the [[e:fulani-war|Fulani jihad]]. Its successor, the [[s:kingdom-of-wukari|Kingdom of Wukari]], kept the [[e:jukun-people|Jukun]] kingship, and the [[e:aku-uka|Aku Uka]] still reigns at Wukari in [[e:taraba-state|Taraba State]].

kolhapur-state.t: The senior surviving Maratha state of Shivaji's line, founded by Queen Tarabai and made famous by the social reformer Shahu Maharaj.
kolhapur-state.o: After the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] succession dispute that followed the release of Shahu in 1707, [[e:tarabai|Tarabai]], widow of [[e:rajaram-i|Rajaram]], set up a rival court for her son [[e:shivaji-ii|Shivaji II]], settling at Kolhapur by around 1710. The [[e:treaty-of-warna|Treaty of Warna]] in 1731 divided the Maratha kingdom between [[e:satara|Satara]] and Kolhapur.
kolhapur-state.r: The [[e:chhatrapati|Chhatrapatis]] of Kolhapur ruled the fertile [[e:panchganga-river|Panchganga]] valley. Shahu, who reigned from 1894 to 1922, founded schools and hostels, reserved posts for non-[[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] and backward [[e:caste|castes]] in 1902, and supported the [[e:satyashodhak-samaj|Satyashodhak]] movement. It was a nineteen-gun salute state.
kolhapur-state.e: Kolhapur merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1949 and became part of [[e:maharashtra|Maharashtra]] in 1960. The royal family remains influential in the city.

kharsawan-state.t: A small Singh Deo state of Chota Nagpur, remembered for the police firing on Adivasi protesters at its merger in 1948.
kharsawan-state.o: Kharsawan was founded by a younger branch of the Singh Deo family of Porahat, the line that also ruled [[s:seraikela-state|Seraikela State]]. The register dates its separate existence to around 1650.
kharsawan-state.r: The Rajas governed a small forested territory largely inhabited by Ho and other Adivasi communities, with some iron and [[e:copper|copper]] resources. It came under British protection in the early 19th century and later the [[e:eastern-states-agency|Eastern States Agency]].
kharsawan-state.e: On 1 January 1948, as Kharsawan was merged into [[e:odisha|Orissa]], police fired on an Adivasi gathering opposing the merger, killing many. The state was transferred to [[e:bihar|Bihar]] later that year and now lies in [[e:seraikela-kharsawan-district|Seraikela Kharsawan district]] of [[e:jharkhand|Jharkhand]].

karauli-state.t: The Jadaun Rajput state of eastern Rajasthan, whose rulers claimed descent from Krishna's Yadava clan and whose capital grew around the Madan Mohan temple.
karauli-state.o: The [[e:jadaun|Jadaun]] [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]], claiming descent from the [[e:yadava|Yadavas]], ruled around [[e:bayana|Bayana]] and Timangarh before the 14th century. In 1348 [[e:arjun-pal|Arjun Pal]] founded the town of Karauli, which became the capital of the state.
karauli-state.r: Karauli was a hilly, largely rural state on the [[e:chambal-river|Chambal]] ravines. Its [[e:maharaja|Maharajas]] accepted Mughal overlordship and later paid tribute to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]]. The temple of Madan Mohan, a form of [[e:krishna|Krishna]], made the town a pilgrimage centre, and red sandstone from local quarries was used for its palaces. In 1817 Karauli signed a treaty with the British.
karauli-state.e: Karauli joined the [[s:matsya-union|Matsya Union]] in 1948, which merged into [[e:rajasthan|Rajasthan]] in 1949. It is now a district of Rajasthan.

kingdom-of-fetu.t: Small Akan kingdom of the Gold Coast in whose lands Cape Coast Castle and other European forts were built.
kingdom-of-fetu.o: Fetu, or Efutu, was a kingdom of [[e:guan-people|Guan]] and [[e:akan|Akan]] speakers inland from present-day [[e:cape-coast|Cape Coast]]. It existed by the time Portuguese traders reached the coast in the late 15th century, and the coastal town of Oguaa, later Cape Coast, belonged to it.
kingdom-of-fetu.r: Its king drew wealth from renting land to European traders and taxing their commerce in gold and slaves. The Swedes built [[e:cape-coast-castle|Carolusborg]] at [[e:cape-coast|Cape Coast]] in 1653, later taken over by the English as Cape Coast Castle, and the [[e:danes|Danes]] built a fort on a nearby hill. Fetu's rulers played the companies against one another.
kingdom-of-fetu.e: Fetu declined around 1700 under pressure from the [[e:fante|Fante]] and wars among European companies, and its lands were absorbed into the Fante states. [[e:cape-coast|Cape Coast]] became the headquarters of the British on the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]].

khadga-dynasty.t: A Buddhist dynasty of Samatata in south-eastern Bengal, known from copper plates and the reports of Chinese pilgrims.
khadga-dynasty.o: The Khadgas emerged in the 7th century in [[e:samatata|Samatata]], the region around modern [[e:comilla|Comilla]] in south-eastern [[s:bangladesh|Bangladesh]], after the collapse of the [[s:gauda-kingdom|Gauda Kingdom]]. The line was founded by Khadgodyama, and its capital is named in inscriptions as Karmanta, probably modern Barakamta.
khadga-dynasty.r: The Khadgas were Buddhists and are known from [[e:copper|copper]] plates found at Ashrafpur, which record grants to Buddhist monasteries, and from a few other inscriptions. The Chinese pilgrim [[e:yijing|Yijing]] reported that King Rajabhata of [[e:samatata|Samatata]] supported thousands of monks and recited Buddhist texts daily. Samatata had trade links with the [[e:bay-of-bengal|Bay of Bengal]] coast.
khadga-dynasty.e: The Khadga line fades from the record in the early 8th century. [[e:samatata|Samatata]] later came under the Deva dynasty and then the [[s:chandra-dynasty|Chandra dynasty]] and the [[s:pala-empire|Pala Empire]].

kingdom-of-arrapha.t: A Hurrian kingdom around modern Kirkuk, vassal of Mitanni, whose town of Nuzi left thousands of tablets on family life, land and law.
kingdom-of-arrapha.o: Arrapha, the ancient name of [[e:kirkuk|Kirkuk]], became the capital of a Hurrian kingdom east of the [[e:tigris|Tigris]] in the 15th century BCE, when the region fell within the sphere of the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]]. Its kings ruled the plain between the [[e:little-zab|Lesser Zab]] and the [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]] foothills as Mitannian [[e:vassal|vassals]].
kingdom-of-arrapha.r: The best evidence comes from [[e:nuzi|Nuzi]] (Yorghan Tepe), a provincial town excavated in the 1920s and 1930s, where over 5,000 tablets were found. Written in a local Akkadian with many Hurrian words, they record family archives such as that of Tehip-tilla, adoptions used to transfer land, slave contracts, marriage settlements and lawsuits. Society was dominated by the palace and by [[e:chariot|chariot]]-owning families. Kings such as Kipi-Teshup and Ithi-Teshup are named in seal impressions and documents.
kingdom-of-arrapha.e: As [[e:mitanni|Mitanni]] weakened in the mid-14th century BCE, [[e:nuzi|Nuzi]] was burnt around 1340 BCE, probably by Assyrian forces, and Arrapha was soon absorbed by the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]], later becoming an Assyrian province.

kwanyama-kingdom.t: The largest Ovambo kingdom, straddling the Angola–Namibia border, whose last king Mandume ya Ndemufayo fought both Portugal and South Africa.
kwanyama-kingdom.o: Oukwanyama formed by the 18th century on the floodplains around the [[e:kunene-river|Kunene]] and Cuvelai rivers, under kings drawn from a royal matriclan. It grew into the most populous of the [[e:ovambo-people|Ovambo]] kingdoms, with its royal seat in the area of modern [[e:ondjiva|Ondjiva]].
kwanyama-kingdom.r: Kings held wide power over land and justice, ruling through district headmen and maintaining armed retainers. The economy combined [[e:millet|millet]] farming, [[e:cattle|cattle]], salt and iron, and in the 19th century the kingdom traded cattle and captives for guns and horses with Portuguese and [[e:boers|Boer]] traders. German and Finnish missionaries worked in the kingdom from the 1880s.
kwanyama-kingdom.e: [[e:mandume-ya-ndemufayo|Mandume ya Ndemufayo]], king from 1911, resisted Portuguese advances, but after the Portuguese victory at [[e:battle-of-mongua|Mongua]] in 1915 he withdrew south. He was killed fighting South African forces in 1917, and the kingdom was divided between [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]] and [[s:south-west-africa|South West Africa]].

kapurthala-state.t: The Ahluwalia Sikh state of the Doaba region of Punjab, known for its Francophile Maharaja Jagatjit Singh and his Versailles-style palace.
kapurthala-state.o: [[e:jassa-singh-ahluwalia|Jassa Singh Ahluwalia]], leader of the [[e:ahluwalia-misl|Ahluwalia misl]] and a commander of the [[s:sikh-misls|Dal Khalsa]], briefly held [[e:lahore|Lahore]] in 1761 and took Kapurthala in the 1770s. His successor [[e:fateh-singh-ahluwalia|Fateh Singh Ahluwalia]] was an ally of [[e:ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]].
kapurthala-state.r: Kapurthala sided with the British after the First Anglo-Sikh War and in 1857, gaining estates in [[e:awadh|Awadh]]. [[e:jagatjit-singh|Jagatjit Singh]] (1877–1949) travelled widely, admired [[e:france|France]] and built the [[e:jagatjit-palace|Jagatjit Palace]] modelled on [[e:versailles|Versailles]]. Unusually the [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] ruler governed a majority-Muslim population, and the state was known for [[e:religious-tolerance|religious tolerance]], including a Moorish-style mosque he funded.
kapurthala-state.e: Kapurthala acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1947 amid Partition violence and in 1948 joined the [[s:patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union|Patiala and East Punjab States Union]], which merged into [[e:punjab|Punjab]] in 1956.

kingdom-of-khurda.t: The Odia kingdom that kept the Gajapati title and guarded the Jagannath temple at Puri under Mughal, Maratha and British overlords.
kingdom-of-khurda.o: After the [[e:karrani-dynasty|Karrani Afghans]] overthrew independent [[e:odisha|Odisha]] in 1568, [[e:ramachandra-deva-i|Ramachandra Deva I]], of the Bhoi family, established himself at Khurda near Puri. [[e:akbar|Akbar's]] general [[e:man-singh-i|Man Singh]] recognised him as Raja of Khurda in 1592, and his successors took the Gajapati title of the former kings.
kingdom-of-khurda.r: The Khurda rajas were acknowledged as the first servants of [[e:jagannath|Jagannath]] at Puri, a role that gave them prestige across [[e:odisha|Odisha]]. They ruled a small hill-and-forest territory with paika militia soldiers who held land for service. They paid tribute to the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] and, from 1751, to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] of [[e:nagpur|Nagpur]].
kingdom-of-khurda.e: The British [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] took [[e:odisha|Odisha]] in 1803. The raja [[e:mukunda-deva-ii|Mukunda Deva II]] joined a revolt and Khurda was annexed in 1804. Resentment over land settlements led to the Paika Rebellion of 1817. The Puri Gajapati family still holds ritual rights at the [[e:jagannath|Jagannath]] temple.

kathiri-sultanate.t: The sultanate of the Kathiri tribe in Wadi Hadramawt, which ruled Seiyun and Tarim for centuries and was absorbed into South Yemen in 1967.
kathiri-sultanate.o: The Kathiri tribe rose in [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]] in the late 14th and 15th centuries, taking control of the valley's towns. In the 16th century [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:badr-abu-tuwayriq|Badr Abu Tuwayriq]] expanded Kathiri rule across Hadramawt and into [[e:dhofar|Dhofar]], using firearms and troops obtained through Ottoman contacts.
kathiri-sultanate.r: Kathiri sultans ruled from [[e:seiyun|Seiyun]], whose mud-brick palace still dominates the town, and from [[e:tarim-yemen|Tarim]], the religious centre of the valley's sayyid families and [[e:shafii-school|Shafi'i]] scholarship. Their power depended on tribal alliances and later on remittances from Hadrami emigrants in [[e:java|Java]], [[s:singapore|Singapore]] and [[e:hyderabad|Hyderabad]]. In the 19th century they lost the coast and much of the valley to the [[s:quaiti-sultanate|Qu'aiti Sultanate]].
kathiri-sultanate.e: An agreement of 1918 with the [[s:quaiti-sultanate|Qu'aiti]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] placed the sultanate within the British sphere, later the [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]]. In 1967 the [[e:national-liberation-front-south-yemen|National Liberation Front]] took over [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]], abolished the sultanate and incorporated it into [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]].
