kingdom-of-afghanistan.t: The Afghan monarchy of Amanullah and Zahir Shah, which pursued modernisation and neutrality for nearly half a century.
kingdom-of-afghanistan.o: [[e:amanullah-khan|Amanullah Khan]], who had won full independence from [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1919, took the title king (padishah) in 1926, turning the [[s:saqqawist-emirate|Emirate of Afghanistan]] into a kingdom. He launched ambitious reforms, including a constitution, schools for girls and the unveiling of women, inspired by [[e:mustafa-kemal-ataturk|Atatürk]]'s [[e:turkey|Turkey]].
kingdom-of-afghanistan.r: [[e:amanullah-khan|Amanullah]]'s reforms provoked a revolt that drove him out in 1929, and after the brief [[s:saqqawist-emirate|Saqqawist Emirate]], [[e:mohammad-nadir-shah|Mohammad Nadir Shah]] took the throne. After his assassination in 1933 his son [[e:mohammad-zahir-shah|Mohammad Zahir Shah]] reigned for forty years, at first through his uncles and then his cousin [[e:mohammad-daoud-khan|Mohammad Daoud Khan]] as prime minister. [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-2021-present|Afghanistan]] stayed neutral in the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]], received aid from both the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]], and adopted a liberal constitution in 1964.
kingdom-of-afghanistan.e: In July 1973, while [[e:mohammad-zahir-shah|Zahir Shah]] was in [[e:italy|Italy]], [[e:mohammad-daoud-khan|Daoud Khan]] seized power in a bloodless coup and abolished the monarchy, proclaiming the [[s:republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978|Republic of Afghanistan]] (1973-1978).

kingdom-of-anga.t: An eastern kingdom with its capital at the river port of Champa, the first great conquest of Magadha.
kingdom-of-anga.o: Anga lay east of [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] in modern [[e:bihar|Bihar]], around [[s:champa|Champa]] near [[e:bhagalpur|Bhagalpur]] on the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]]. It is mentioned in the [[e:atharvaveda|Atharvaveda]] as a distant eastern people and by the 6th century BCE it was listed among the sixteen mahajanapadas. Buddhist texts say Anga once dominated [[e:magadha|Magadha]], and a king named Brahmadatta is said to have defeated [[e:bimbisara|Bimbisara's]] father.
kingdom-of-anga.r: [[s:champa|Champa]] was counted among the six great cities of the [[e:gautama-buddha|Buddha]]'s day. It was a river port from which merchants were said to sail to [[s:suphannaphum|Suvarnabhumi]] in [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and its wealth rested on trade and the farming of the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]]. Little is known of its government beyond the names of a few kings in Buddhist and [[e:jainism|Jain]] tradition.
kingdom-of-anga.e: Around 540 BCE the young [[e:bimbisara|Bimbisara]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Kingdom of Magadha]] conquered Anga, and [[s:champa|Champa]] was governed for a time by his son [[e:ajatashatru|Ajatashatru]]. The conquest began [[e:magadha|Magadha's]] rise to dominance over the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] valley.

klaipeda-region.t: The Memel Territory, detached from Germany after the First World War, seized by Lithuania in 1923 and annexed by Hitler in 1939.
klaipeda-region.o: The [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]] separated the land north of the [[e:neman|Neman]], including the port of [[e:klaipeda|Memel]] (Klaipėda), from [[e:germany|Germany]], placing it under the [[e:allies|Allies]] in 1920 with a French administration. In January 1923 Lithuanian irregulars staged the [[e:klaipeda-revolt|Klaipėda Revolt]], and the Allies accepted Lithuanian [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]].
klaipeda-region.r: Under the [[e:klaipeda-convention|Klaipėda Convention]] of 1924, the region was an autonomous part of the [[s:republic-of-lithuania-1918-1940|Republic of Lithuania]], with its own parliament and directorate. Most inhabitants were German-speaking or bilingual [[e:lietuvininkai|Lietuvininkai]], and conflicts between German parties and the Lithuanian governor were constant. The port was [[e:lithuania|Lithuania's]] only outlet to the sea.
klaipeda-region.e: Nazi groups grew strong in the 1930s. In March 1939 [[e:germany|Germany]] issued an ultimatum, and [[s:republic-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] ceded the region, which was annexed to the Reich on 23 March 1939. After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] it became part of the [[s:lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic|Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic]], and its German population fled or was expelled.

kiautschou-bay-concession.t: Germany's naval colony on the Shandong coast, centred on Tsingtao, whose transfer to Japan in 1919 triggered China's May Fourth Movement.
kiautschou-bay-concession.o: Using the murder of two German missionaries in [[e:shandong|Shandong]] in 1897 as a pretext, [[e:germany|Germany]] occupied [[e:jiaozhou-bay|Kiautschou Bay]] and in 1898 forced the [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]] to grant a ninety-nine-year lease, together with railway and mining rights in Shandong.
kiautschou-bay-concession.r: Uniquely among German colonies, it was run by the navy, with a naval officer as governor. Tsingtao was planned as a model colony, with modern harbour works, sewerage, schools, German-style architecture and a brewery founded in 1903, and the railway to Jinan opened in 1904. Chinese and European residential areas were kept separate.
kiautschou-bay-concession.e: When the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] began, [[e:japan|Japan]], supported by British troops, besieged Tsingtao, which Governor [[e:alfred-meyer-waldeck|Alfred Meyer-Waldeck]] surrendered in November 1914. The [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]] gave German rights to Japan, provoking the May Fourth protests of 1919; Japan returned the territory to [[e:china|China]] in 1922.

kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.t: A kingdom without a king, created by Germany and Austria-Hungary in occupied Poland during the First World War, which handed power to Pilsudski in 1918.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.o: After driving the Russians out of [[s:congress-poland|Congress Poland]] in 1915, the [[e:central-powers|Central Powers]] proclaimed an independent Kingdom of Poland by the Act of 5 November 1916, hoping to recruit Polish soldiers. Its borders and future king were left undecided.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.r: A Provisional Council of State, including [[e:jozef-pilsudski|Jozef Pilsudski]], was set up in 1917, but real power remained with the German governor-general in [[e:warsaw|Warsaw]]. When Pilsudski's legionnaires refused an oath of loyalty to the [[e:central-powers|Central Powers]], he was interned at [[e:magdeburg|Magdeburg]]. A [[e:regency-council-kingdom-of-poland|Regency Council]] of Archbishop [[e:aleksander-kakowski|Aleksander Kakowski]], Prince [[e:zdzislaw-lubomirski|Zdzislaw Lubomirski]] and [[e:jozef-ostrowski|Jozef Ostrowski]] then governed, building Polish courts, schools and offices.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.e: As [[e:germany|Germany]] collapsed in November 1918, the [[e:regency-council-kingdom-of-poland|Regency Council]] handed command of the army and then all authority to Pilsudski, freshly released, and dissolved itself. Its institutions passed to the [[s:second-polish-republic|Second Polish Republic]].

kingdom-of-buganda.t: The largest and most centralised of the Great Lakes kingdoms, which gave its name to Uganda and still survives as a cultural monarchy.
kingdom-of-buganda.o: Buganda began around the 14th century as a small state on the northern shore of [[e:lake-victoria|Lake Victoria]], near modern [[e:kampala|Kampala]]. Its traditions trace the royal line to [[e:kintu|Kintu]], the first man, and Kato Kimera. It was long overshadowed by [[s:kingdom-of-bunyoro|Bunyoro]], but from the 17th century the kabakas (kings) steadily expanded their territory at Bunyoro's expense.
kingdom-of-buganda.r: The kabaka ruled through appointed chiefs rather than hereditary clan heads, giving Buganda an unusually centralised government with a large standing army and a war-canoe fleet on [[e:lake-victoria|Lake Victoria]]. Plantains provided a reliable food base. In the 19th century [[e:mutesa-i-of-buganda|Mutesa I]] admitted Arab traders and Christian missionaries, and rivalry among Muslim, Catholic and Protestant factions led to civil war under [[e:mwanga-ii|Mwanga II]].
kingdom-of-buganda.e: The [[e:buganda-agreement|Buganda Agreement]] of 1900 made the kingdom a privileged part of the [[s:uganda-protectorate|Uganda Protectorate]]. Its kabaka [[e:mutesa-ii-of-buganda|Mutesa II]] became the first president of independent [[s:uganda|Uganda]], but in 1966 [[e:milton-obote|Milton Obote]] attacked the palace and in 1967 abolished the monarchies. Buganda was restored as a cultural kingdom in 1993 under [[e:ronald-muwenda-mutebi-ii|Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II]].

kanva-dynasty.t: A short-lived Brahmin dynasty of four kings that ruled Magadha after the Shungas, in the twilight of Pataliputra's ancient power.
kanva-dynasty.o: Around 73 BCE [[e:vasudeva-kanva|Vasudeva Kanva]], a [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] minister of the last [[e:shunga-empire|Shunga]] king, [[e:devabhuti|Devabhuti]], had his master killed and took the throne. The Kanvas inherited a shrunken kingdom in [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] and the middle [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]], ruled from [[e:pataliputra|Pataliputra]].
kanva-dynasty.r: The dynasty is known almost entirely from the [[e:puranas|Puranas]], which list four kings, [[e:vasudeva-kanva|Vasudeva]], [[e:bhumimitra|Bhumimitra]], Narayana and [[e:susharman|Susharman]], ruling for a total of 45 years. Coins bearing the name Bhumimitra may belong to the second king. Nothing reliable is known of their government.
kanva-dynasty.e: According to the [[e:puranas|Puranas]], [[e:susharman|Susharman]] was killed around 28 BCE by a king of the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Andhras]], usually taken to be a ruler of the Satavahana dynasty. [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] then broke into small local principalities until the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]] revived it in the 4th century.

kingdom-of-connacht.t: Western Irish province-kingdom whose O'Connor kings, Toirdelbach and Ruaidrí, became high kings before Anglo-Norman conquest reduced it.
kingdom-of-connacht.o: The [[e:connachta|Connachta]], who gave the province its name, claimed descent from [[e:conn-of-the-hundred-battles|Conn of the Hundred Battles]]. By the 6th century their branches, the [[e:ui-briuin|Uí Briúin]] and [[e:ui-fiachrach|Uí Fiachrach]], ruled the west, with kings inaugurated at [[e:rathcroghan|Cruachan]], the great ritual site of Rathcroghan in [[e:county-roscommon|Roscommon]]. The Uí Briúin gradually took control of the over-kingship.
kingdom-of-connacht.r: Kings ruled through a network of subject kingdoms such as the [[s:kingdom-of-ui-maine|Kingdom of Ui Maine]]. The [[e:ua-conchobair-dynasty|Ua Conchobair]], O'Connor, line rose in the 11th century; [[e:toirdelbach-ua-conchobair|Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair]], king from 1106 to 1156, built bridges and castles, divided [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] and claimed the high kingship. His son [[e:ruaidri-ua-conchobair|Ruaidrí]] became the last [[e:high-king-of-ireland|High King of Ireland]] and agreed the [[e:treaty-of-windsor-1175|Treaty of Windsor]] with [[e:henry-ii-of-england|Henry II]] in 1175.
kingdom-of-connacht.e: [[e:anglo-normans|Anglo-Norman]] lords led by the de Burghs received a grant of Connacht in 1227, and the [[e:ua-conchobair-dynasty|O'Connors]] were confined to [[e:county-roscommon|Roscommon]]. Splits between rival O'Connor branches in the 14th century weakened the kingship further, and the title faded out in the later 15th century.
kingdom-of-connacht.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-madanda.t: A small Shona kingdom in central Mozambique between the Buzi and Save rivers, on the edge of the Mutapa and Uteve world.
kingdom-of-madanda.o: Madanda emerged around 1500 as one of the [[e:shona|Shona]]-speaking states between the [[e:zimbabwean-plateau|Zimbabwe plateau]] and the coast, south of the [[s:kingdom-of-uteve|Kingdom of Uteve]]. Its rulers were probably linked by origin to the [[e:mutapa-empire|Mutapa]] dynasty, but the kingdom appears only occasionally in Portuguese records.
kingdom-of-madanda.r: Little is known of its government. Like its neighbours, it was probably ruled by a sacred king advised by [[e:spirit-medium|spirit mediums]], and its people farmed, herded [[e:cattle|cattle]] and traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and gold with Portuguese posts at [[e:sofala|Sofala]] and on the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]].
kingdom-of-madanda.e: In the 19th century Madanda came under the domination of the [[e:gaza-empire|Gaza Nguni]] state. In the 1890s its territory passed to the [[s:mozambique-company|Mozambique Company]] and was absorbed into [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]].

kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.t: Six centuries of Arakanese kingdoms in the Lemro river valley, between the fall of Waithali and the founding of Mrauk U.
kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.o: Rakhine chronicles date the start of the Lemro period to 818, when King Khittathin founded Pyinsa on the Lemro river after Waithali's decline. Over the following centuries the capital shifted between several towns in the valley, including Parein, Hkrit, Pyinsa again and finally Launggyet, founded in 1251.
kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.r: The Lemro kingdoms ruled the Rakhine coast through [[e:rice|rice]] cultivation and [[e:bay-of-bengal|Bay of Bengal]] trade, with strong links to [[e:bengal|Bengal]] and to the [[s:pagan-kingdom|Pagan Kingdom]], which at times claimed overlordship. [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada Buddhism]] became dominant, and kings built pagodas and patronised monks. Political history was turbulent, with frequent succession disputes and invasions.
kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.e: In 1406 forces of the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]] drove King [[e:min-saw-mon|Min Saw Mon]] from Launggyet into exile in [[e:bengal|Bengal]]. With help from the [[s:bengal-sultanate|Bengal Sultanate]] he regained the throne in 1429 and the next year founded a new capital at [[e:mrauk-u|Mrauk U]], opening the period of the [[s:mrauk-u-kingdom|Mrauk U Kingdom]].

kahuripan.t: The East Javanese kingdom of Airlangga, who rebuilt Javanese royal power after the fall of Medang in 1016.
kahuripan.o: When Haji Wurawari destroyed the court of [[e:dharmawangsa|Dharmawangsa Teguh]] of the [[s:medang-kingdom|Medang Kingdom]] in 1016, his young son-in-law [[e:airlangga|Airlangga]], a prince from [[e:bali|Bali]], fled to the forest with a few followers. In 1019 priests consecrated him king, and over the next two decades he reconquered [[e:east-java|East Java]] from rival lords.
kahuripan.r: [[e:airlangga|Airlangga's]] [[e:pucangan-inscription|Pucangan inscription]] of 1041 tells his story in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and [[e:old-javanese|Old Javanese]]. He built dams on the [[e:brantas-river|Brantas River]], encouraged trade through the port of [[e:hujung-galuh|Hujung Galuh]], and patronised [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Buddhist clergy. The poet [[e:mpu-kanwa|Mpu Kanwa]] wrote the [[e:arjunawiwaha|Arjunawiwaha]], seen as an allegory of his reign.
kahuripan.e: Before retiring as an ascetic, [[e:airlangga|Airlangga]] had his kingdom divided around 1045, tradition says by the sage [[e:mpu-bharada|Mpu Bharada]], between two sons: [[s:janggala|Janggala]] in the east and [[e:kediri-kingdom|Kediri]], or [[s:kediri-kingdom|Panjalu]], in the west. He died around 1049, and is believed to be buried at [[e:candi-belahan|Belahan]], on [[e:mount-penanggungan|Mount Penanggungan]].

kingdom-of-bussa.t: Borgu kingdom on the Niger where the Scottish explorer Mungo Park met his death in the rapids in 1806.
kingdom-of-bussa.o: Bussa was one of the kingdoms of [[e:borgu|Borgu]], a region straddling the middle [[e:niger-river|Niger]], and claimed seniority among them. Its rulers traced their descent to [[e:kisra-borgu-tradition|Kisra]], a legendary conqueror from the east whose story is shared across Borgu. The kingdom probably took shape by the 16th century.
kingdom-of-bussa.r: The king of Bussa ruled over Busa-speaking and [[e:bariba|Bariba]] subjects and controlled crossings and rapids on the [[e:niger-river|Niger]]. [[e:borgu|Borgu]] warriors were feared horsemen and [[e:archery|archers]], and the region resisted both the [[s:oyo-empire|Oyo Empire]] and the [[e:fulani-war|Fulani jihad]]. [[e:mungo-park|Mungo Park]] drowned in the Bussa rapids in 1806, and the Lander brothers passed through in 1830.
kingdom-of-bussa.e: Bussa was claimed by both [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and [[e:france|France]] and was assigned to [[e:britain|Britain]] by the [[e:anglo-french-convention-of-1898|Anglo-French Convention of 1898]], becoming part of [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Northern Nigeria]]. The old town was flooded by the [[e:kainji-dam|Kainji Dam]] in 1968, and its people moved to [[e:new-bussa|New Bussa]].

kalmar-union.t: Personal union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch, created by Queen Margaret I in 1397 and broken by Sweden's secession in 1523.
kalmar-union.o: [[e:margaret-i-of-denmark|Margaret I]], daughter of [[e:valdemar-iv-of-denmark|Valdemar IV of Denmark]] and widow of [[e:haakon-vi-of-norway|Haakon VI of Norway]], became ruler of [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and [[e:norway|Norway]] and, after defeating King Albert of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] in 1389, of [[e:sweden|Sweden]] too. In 1397 her great-nephew [[e:eric-of-pomerania|Eric of Pomerania]] was crowned king of all three realms at [[e:kalmar|Kalmar]].
kalmar-union.r: The union shared a monarch and foreign policy, but each kingdom kept its own laws, councils and nobility. Danish dominance and wars with the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]] and [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] caused resentment in [[e:sweden|Sweden]], where the [[e:engelbrekt-engelbrektsson|Engelbrekt]] rebellion of 1434 began a century of conflict. Swedish regents of the [[e:sture-family|Sture family]] often ruled in practice.
kalmar-union.e: [[e:christian-ii-of-denmark|Christian II]] reconquered [[e:sweden|Sweden]] in 1520 and executed some eighty nobles and clergy in the [[e:stockholm-bloodbath|Stockholm Bloodbath]], provoking a revolt led by [[e:gustav-i-of-sweden|Gustav Vasa]], who was elected king of Sweden in 1523. The union ended, while [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and [[e:norway|Norway]] continued together as [[s:denmark-norway|Denmark-Norway]].

kingdom-of-noricum.t: A Celtic kingdom in the eastern Alps, famed for its iron and steel, that became a Roman ally and then a Roman province without a major war.
kingdom-of-noricum.o: Noricum grew out of a union of Celtic tribes in the eastern [[e:alps|Alps]], led by the [[e:norici|Norici]], during the 2nd century BCE. Its core lay in modern [[e:carinthia|Carinthia]] and [[e:styria|Styria]], around the [[e:magdalensberg|Magdalensberg]] and a centre the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] called [[e:noreia|Noreia]]. In 113 BCE [[e:rome|Rome]] defended it against the migrating [[e:cimbri|Cimbri]], who defeated a Roman army at Noreia.
kingdom-of-noricum.r: The kingdom was ruled by kings over a federation of tribes and was known across the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] for ferrum Noricum, a high-quality [[e:steel|steel]] produced from local ores. Italian merchants settled at the [[e:magdalensberg|Magdalensberg]] trading post, and Noricum minted its own [[e:silver|silver]] coins. Close ties with [[e:rome|Rome]] made it a client kingdom; its king [[e:voccio|Voccio]] sent cavalry to [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] in 49 BCE.
kingdom-of-noricum.e: Around 16 BCE Noricum was absorbed peacefully into the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]], becoming the province of Noricum with towns such as [[e:virunum|Virunum]] and [[e:celje|Celeia]]. Roman rule lasted until the late 5th century, when the [[e:life-of-saint-severinus|Life of Saint Severinus]] records the last Roman communities before their evacuation in 488.

knidos.t: Dorian port city on a Carian peninsula, home of Praxiteles's Aphrodite, the astronomer Eudoxus and a renowned school of medicine.
knidos.o: [[e:dorians|Dorian Greeks]] settled Knidos at the tip of a long peninsula in south-west [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] in the early first millennium BCE. It belonged to the [[e:dorian-hexapolis|Dorian Hexapolis]] with Kos, [[s:halicarnassus|Halicarnassus]] and the three Rhodian cities of [[s:lindos|Lindos]], [[s:ialysos|Ialysos]] and [[s:kamiros|Kamiros]], which met at the sanctuary of [[e:apollo|Apollo]] at Triopion in Knidian territory.
knidos.r: Knidos was an oligarchy run by a council of sixty, and grew rich on trade, wine and its double harbour. When the Persian general [[e:harpagus|Harpagus]] advanced c. 545 BCE, the Knidians tried to cut through their isthmus but submitted. The city later produced the astronomer [[e:eudoxus-of-cnidus|Eudoxus]], the physician [[e:ctesias|Ctesias]] and [[e:sostratus-of-cnidus|Sostratus]], architect of the [[e:lighthouse-of-alexandria|Pharos of Alexandria]]; its treasury and clubhouse stood at [[s:delphi|Delphi]].
knidos.e: Off Knidos in 394 BCE [[e:conon|Conon's]] Persian-backed fleet destroyed Spartan sea power. In the 4th century BCE the city moved to the cape, where [[e:praxiteles|Praxiteles's]] nude Aphrodite drew visitors. It joined the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE as a free city.

kingdom-of-ailech.t: Kingdom of the northern Uí Néill based at the stone fort of Grianan of Aileach, whose Cenél nEógain kings often held the high kingship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-ailech.o: Ailech emerged in the early [[e:middle-ages|medieval period]] as the kingdom of the northern [[e:ui-neill|Uí Néill]], descendants of [[e:niall-of-the-nine-hostages|Niall of the Nine Hostages]] who expanded into the north-west in the 5th and 6th centuries. It took its name from the hilltop stone fort of [[e:grianan-of-aileach|Grianan of Aileach]] on the [[e:inishowen|Inishowen]] peninsula, which served as a royal centre.
kingdom-of-ailech.r: The kingdom was dominated by the [[e:cenel-neogain|Cenél nEógain]], who displaced the [[e:cenel-conaill|Cenél Conaill]] from the kingship in the 8th century and alternated the high kingship with the southern [[e:ui-neill|Uí Néill]]. Kings such as [[e:aed-findliath|Áed Findliath]] and [[e:niall-glundub|Niall Glúndub]], killed fighting the [[e:vikings|Vikings]] of [[e:dublin|Dublin]] in 919, were among the most powerful in Ireland. The [[e:mac-lochlainn-dynasty|Mac Lochlainn]] line, notably [[e:muirchertach-mac-lochlainn|Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn]], held the high kingship in the 12th century.
kingdom-of-ailech.e: In 1101 [[e:muirchertach-ua-briain|Muirchertach Ua Briain]] of [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] demolished [[e:grianan-of-aileach|Grianan of Aileach]] in revenge for an earlier attack on [[e:kincora|Kincora]]. Power within [[e:cenel-neogain|Cenél nEógain]] passed from the [[e:mac-lochlainn-dynasty|Mac Lochlainns]] to the [[e:o-neill-dynasty|Ua Néill]], and the kingdom of Ailech became the O'Neill kingdom of Tír Eógain, [[s:kingdom-of-tir-eoghain|Tyrone]].

kololo-kingdom.t: A Sotho conquest state on the upper Zambezi, visited by Livingstone, whose language still shapes Lozi speech.
kololo-kingdom.o: [[e:sebetwane|Sebetwane]] led the Kololo, a [[e:sotho-people|Sotho]] group displaced in the 1820s, on a long migration across [[e:botswana|Botswana]]. Around 1840 they conquered the [[e:lozi-people|Lozi]] kingdom of [[s:barotseland|Barotseland]] on the upper [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] floodplain, setting up their capital at [[e:linyanti|Linyanti]] in the Chobe swamps.
kololo-kingdom.r: [[e:sebetwane|Sebetwane]] ruled with skill, incorporating [[e:lozi-people|Lozi]] and other subjects and spreading his [[e:sotho-people|Sotho]] language, which became the basis of modern Silozi. The Kololo lived from [[e:cattle|cattle]], Lozi labour and tribute in grain, fish and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]]. [[e:david-livingstone|David Livingstone]] reached Sebetwane in 1851 and later travelled to the Atlantic and [[e:indian-ocean|Indian Ocean]] coasts with Kololo porters provided by [[e:sekeletu|Sekeletu]].
kololo-kingdom.e: [[e:sebetwane|Sebetwane]] died in 1851; under his sickly son [[e:sekeletu|Sekeletu]], malaria thinned the Kololo and loyalty collapsed. After Sekeletu's death in 1863 a [[e:lozi-people|Lozi]] rising led by [[e:sipopa|Sipopa]] killed most Kololo men in 1864, restoring the Lozi monarchy.

kingdom-of-middag.t: A multi-village alliance of indigenous peoples on Taiwan's central plain, called a kingdom by the Dutch, which kept its autonomy until the Qing crushed it in 1732.
kingdom-of-middag.o: The alliance, centred among the [[e:papora-people|Papora]], [[e:babuza-people|Babuza]], [[e:pazeh-people|Pazeh]] and other plains peoples around modern [[e:taichung|Taichung]], is known chiefly from [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] records of the 1640s. Its origins are obscure; it is traditionally said to have formed in the mid-16th century.
kingdom-of-middag.r: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] described a chief they called the [[e:kamachat-aslamie|King of Middag]], Kamachat Aslamie, who presided over some fifteen to twenty-seven villages. Villages kept their own leaders, while the paramount chief led in war and diplomacy. In 1645 the Dutch forced him to accept a treaty acknowledging their authority, though the alliance stayed largely self-governing.
kingdom-of-middag.e: Middag kept its autonomy under the [[s:kingdom-of-tungning|Kingdom of Tungning]] and early [[e:qing-empire|Qing]] rule. Rising Chinese settlement and labour demands provoked the Dajia-Shalu revolt of 1731, which Qing forces suppressed in 1732, ending the alliance.

kingdom-of-cambrai.t: Small Frankish kingdom around Cambrai, ruled by Clovis' kinsman Ragnachar until Clovis eliminated him.
kingdom-of-cambrai.o: [[s:prince-bishopric-of-cambrai|Cambrai]] was taken by the Salian king [[e:chlodio|Chlodio]] in the mid 5th century, and by the 480s it was the seat of a separate Frankish king, [[e:ragnachar|Ragnachar]], a relative of [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]]. Known almost only from [[e:gregory-of-tours|Gregory of Tours]].
kingdom-of-cambrai.r: [[e:ragnachar|Ragnachar]] joined [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]] against [[e:syagrius|Syagrius]] and the [[s:domain-of-soissons|Domain of Soissons]] in 486. [[e:gregory-of-tours|Gregory]] portrays him as a debauched ruler who lost the loyalty of his warriors.
kingdom-of-cambrai.e: Around 509 [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]] bribed [[e:ragnachar|Ragnachar's]] followers with armlets of gilded bronze passed off as gold, defeated him and killed him and his brother Richar with his own axe. [[s:prince-bishopric-of-cambrai|Cambrai]] was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-the-franks|Kingdom of the Franks]].

kingdom-of-prussia.t: Hohenzollern kingdom that rose from scattered lands to a great power, defeated Austria and France and united Germany under its rule.
kingdom-of-prussia.o: Elector [[e:frederick-i-of-prussia|Frederick III of Brandenburg]] crowned himself King in Prussia at [[e:konigsberg|Königsberg]] on 18 January 1701, with Emperor [[e:leopold-i-holy-roman-emperor|Leopold I]]'s consent. The title rested on the [[s:duchy-of-prussia|Duchy of Prussia]], outside the Empire, but it was applied to all [[e:house-of-hohenzollern|Hohenzollern]] lands, including [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] and territories in the [[e:rhineland|Rhineland]] and [[e:westphalia|Westphalia]].
kingdom-of-prussia.r: [[e:frederick-william-i-of-prussia|Frederick William I]] built a large army and efficient bureaucracy. Frederick II seized [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] in 1740 and survived the Seven Years' War, then gained [[e:west-prussia|West Prussia]] in the [[e:first-partition-of-poland|First Partition of Poland]]. After defeat at [[e:jena|Jena]] in 1806, the [[e:heinrich-friedrich-karl-vom-stein|Stein]] and [[e:karl-august-von-hardenberg|Hardenberg]] reforms modernised the state. Prussia gained the [[e:rhineland|Rhineland]] in 1815, led the [[e:zollverein|Zollverein]], and under Bismarck defeated [[e:denmark|Denmark]], [[e:austria|Austria]] and [[e:france|France]].
kingdom-of-prussia.e: In 1871 [[e:wilhelm-i|King William I]] became [[e:german-emperor|German Emperor]], and Prussia formed the dominant state of the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. [[e:wilhelm-ii|William II]] abdicated in November 1918, and Prussia became the [[s:free-state-of-prussia|Free State of Prussia]], abolished by the [[e:allies|Allies]] in 1947.

kushano-sasanian-kingdom.t: Sasanian princes who ruled the former Kushan lands of Bactria and Gandhara as 'Kushanshahs', blending Persian, Kushan and Buddhist traditions.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.o: After [[e:ardashir-i|Ardashir I]] founded the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]], he and his son [[e:shapur-i|Shapur I]] conquered [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]] and much of the [[s:kushan-empire|Kushan Empire]] in the mid-3rd century. Government of the region was entrusted to Sasanian princes who took the title Kushanshah, King of the Kushans, ruling from [[e:balkh|Balkh]].
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.r: The Kushanshahs issued gold and [[e:copper|copper]] coins in the Kushan style, often showing the god [[e:oesho|Oesho]] ([[e:shiva|Shiva]]) with the bull [[e:nandi-hinduism|Nandi]], alongside Sasanian crowns and [[e:middle-persian|Middle Persian]] or Bactrian legends. They held trade routes through the [[e:hindu-kush|Hindu Kush]], and Buddhist monasteries in [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]] continued to flourish under them. At times they acted nearly independently of the main Sasanian court.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.e: In the mid-4th century the [[s:chionites|Chionites]] and the [[s:kidarite-kingdom|Kidarite Kingdom]] overran [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]], ending Kushano-Sasanian rule. Their coinage strongly influenced the coin types of these later Hunnic rulers.

kalachuris-of-tripuri.t: A central Indian dynasty ruling the Chedi country from Tripuri near Jabalpur, which briefly became the strongest power in northern India under Lakshmikarna.
kalachuris-of-tripuri.o: The Kalachuris of Tripuri, who claimed descent from the legendary [[e:haihaya|Haihaya]] king [[e:kartavirya-arjuna|Kartavirya Arjuna]] and from the [[s:kalachuris-of-mahishmati|Kalachuris of Mahishmati]], rose in the late 9th century under [[e:kokalla-i|Kokalla I]]. He ruled the [[s:chedi|Chedi]] country around Tripuri, modern Tewar near [[e:jabalpur|Jabalpur]], and strengthened his position through marriage alliances with the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]].
kalachuris-of-tripuri.r: [[e:gangeyadeva|Gangeyadeva]] took the title Vikramaditya and expanded the kingdom in the early 11th century. His son [[e:lakshmikarna|Lakshmikarna]], ruling from about 1041 to 1073, campaigned in [[e:bengal|Bengal]], [[s:kingdom-of-kalinga|Kalinga]] and [[e:malwa|Malwa]] and helped defeat [[e:bhoja-paramara|Bhoja]] of the [[s:paramara-dynasty|Paramara dynasty]]. The Kalachuris patronised [[e:shaivism|Shaiva]] monasteries of the [[e:mattamayura|Mattamayura order]] and built temples such as the [[e:chausath-yogini-temple-jabalpur|Chausath Yogini]] temple at [[e:bheraghat|Bheraghat]]. They used the [[e:kalachuri-chedi-era|Kalachuri-Chedi era]] of 248.
kalachuris-of-tripuri.e: After [[e:lakshmikarna|Lakshmikarna]] the kingdom declined under pressure from the [[s:chandela-dynasty|Chandela dynasty]], the Paramaras and the [[e:gahadavala-dynasty|Gahadavalas]]. The last known king, Vijayasimha, ruled until about 1212, after which the region passed to the Chandelas and other powers.
