kingdom-of-kurda.t: A small kingdom of the Sinjar region known from the Mari letters, one of the rival states that filled the gap left by Shamshi-Adad's empire.
kingdom-of-kurda.o: Kurda lay in the [[e:sinjar-mountains|Sinjar]] plain of northern [[e:iraq|Iraq]], probably near [[s:kingdom-of-andarig|Andarig]] and [[s:kingdom-of-karana|Karana]]; its site is not identified. It emerged as an independent kingdom when the [[s:kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia|Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia]] dissolved around 1776 BCE.
kingdom-of-kurda.r: The [[s:mari|Mari]] letters name a king Simah-ilane and later a [[e:hammurabi-of-kurda|Hammurabi of Kurda]], not to be confused with his famous namesake of [[e:babylon|Babylon]]. Kurda's rulers concluded and broke oaths with [[e:mari|Mari]], [[s:kingdom-of-andarig|Andarig]], [[s:eshnunna|Eshnunna]] and Babylon, and their envoys appear at the courts of greater kings. Nothing is known of its institutions beyond this diplomatic record.
kingdom-of-kurda.e: After [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]] of [[e:babylon|Babylon]] conquered [[s:mari|Mari]] in 1761 BCE, the [[e:sinjar-mountains|Sinjar]] kingdoms fell under Babylonian control, and Kurda drops out of the record.

kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.t: The island-wide chiefdom of Kosrae in Micronesia, ruled from the basalt-walled royal town of Leluh, a sister site to Pohnpei's Nan Madol.
kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.o: Between about 1250 and 1400 the chiefdoms of [[e:kosrae|Kosrae]], the easternmost of the [[e:caroline-islands|Caroline Islands]], were probably unified under a single paramount ruler, the Tokosra. The capital was built on Leluh, a small island off the east coast that was enlarged with coral fill and covered with walled compounds of stacked basalt columns over the following centuries.
kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.r: [[e:kosrae|Kosrae]] was among the most centralised societies in [[e:micronesia|Micronesia]]. The Tokosra held ultimate title to land, and high chiefs living at Leluh administered the island's districts, drawing food from commoners who farmed breadfruit, taro and bananas on the main island. Royal tombs stood inside high walls, and canals ran through the town. Pohnpeian tradition makes Kosrae the [[e:bantustan|homeland]] of [[e:isokelekel|Isokelekel]], who overthrew the [[s:saudeleur-dynasty|Saudeleur dynasty]].
kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.e: Whalers, beginning in the 1830s, brought epidemics that reduced the population to a few hundred by the 1870s. American Protestant missionaries arrived in 1852, and the old kingship lost its authority. [[e:kosrae|Kosrae]] passed to [[e:spain|Spain]] in 1885, [[e:germany|Germany]] in 1899 and [[e:japan|Japan]] in 1914, and is now a state of the [[e:federated-states-of-micronesia|Federated States of Micronesia]].

kingdom-of-rarotonga.t: A chiefly kingdom on the main island of the Cook Islands, led by the Makea line, which sought British protection and became the core of the Cook Islands Federation.
kingdom-of-rarotonga.o: Rarotonga was divided among tribes led by hereditary ariki, including the Makea, Pa, Kainuku and Tinomana titles. After the [[e:london-missionary-society|London Missionary Society]] brought [[e:christianity|Christianity]] from 1823, through the Tahitian teacher [[e:papeiha|Papeiha]] and [[e:john-williams-missionary|John Williams]], the ariki governed with mission backing, and the Makea title holders of [[e:avarua|Avarua]] came to be regarded by outsiders as monarchs of the island.
kingdom-of-rarotonga.r: The ariki ruled through chiefly councils and mission-inspired law codes enforced by church judges. The island traded fruit, copra and [[e:cotton|cotton]] with [[s:kingdom-of-tahiti|Tahiti]] and [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]]. [[e:makea-takau-ariki|Makea Takau Ariki]], who held her title from 1871, was treated by visiting ships and governments as queen. Details of the kingdom's formal institutions before the 1880s are thinly documented.
kingdom-of-rarotonga.e: Fearing French annexation, the ariki requested British protection, and a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] was proclaimed in 1888. The British Resident [[e:frederick-moss|Frederick Moss]] set up a federal parliament, and Rarotonga became part of the [[s:cook-islands-federation|Cook Islands Federation]] in the early 1890s.

kotawaringin-sultanate.t: Malay sultanate of south-western Borneo founded by a prince of Banjarmasin, long the main power on the Lamandau and Arut rivers.
kotawaringin-sultanate.o: Kotawaringin was founded in the early 17th century by [[e:pangeran-dipati-anta-kasuma|Pangeran Dipati Anta-Kasuma]], a son of [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mustain Billah of the [[s:banjar-sultanate|Banjar Sultanate]], who was given the western lands of Banjar to rule. Its court was first at Kotawaringin Lama on the Lamandau river and moved to [[e:pangkalan-bun|Pangkalan Bun]] in the early 19th century.
kotawaringin-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled a Malay Muslim riverine elite that collected tribute from inland [[e:dayak-people|Dayak]] communities, trading forest goods such as rattan, resin, gold and birds nests to [[e:banjarmasin|Banjarmasin]] and [[e:java|Java]]. The court preserved Banjar customs and titles, and [[e:islam|Islam]] spread among coastal settlers while most of the interior remained Dayak.
kotawaringin-sultanate.e: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] brought Kotawaringin under contract in the 19th century as a self-governing domain of the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]]. The sultanate continued under colonial supervision and was absorbed into the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]] around 1948 to 1950. The royal palace in [[e:pangkalan-bun|Pangkalan Bun]] still stands.

kingdom-of-persis.t: The local kings of Fars, heartland of the Persians, who kept Achaemenid memory alive under Greek and Parthian overlords until one of them founded the Sasanian Empire.
kingdom-of-persis.o: After Alexander's conquest [[e:persis|Persis]] became part of the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]], but in the 3rd century BCE local dynasts called frataraka ('governor' or 'leader') began issuing their own coins from [[e:istakhr|Istakhr]] and [[e:persepolis|Persepolis]]. [[e:bagadates-i|Bagadates]] is often seen as the first independent frataraka, and his successors broke away from [[e:seleucid-empire|Seleucid]] control.
kingdom-of-persis.r: The frataraka coins show the ruler before a fire altar or Achaemenid-style monuments, with [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] legends, signalling continuity with the Persian past and Zoroastrian worship. From the mid-2nd century BCE [[e:persis|Persis]] became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:parthian-empire|Parthian Empire]], and its rulers took the title king (shah). Kings such as Darayan and Manchihr bore names drawn from Iranian epic. The land lived from agriculture in the valleys of the [[e:kor-river|Kur]] and [[e:pulvar-river|Pulvar]] rivers.
kingdom-of-persis.e: Around 205 CE [[e:papak|Pabag]], a local lord at [[e:istakhr|Istakhr]], seized power, and his son [[e:ardashir-i|Ardashir]] made himself king of [[e:persis|Persis]]. In 224 CE Ardashir defeated the Parthian king [[e:artabanus-iv|Artabanus IV]] and founded the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]].

kingdom-of-paphos.t: Ancient Cypriot kingdom centred on the great sanctuary of Aphrodite, whose kings served as the goddess's high priests for some eight centuries.
kingdom-of-paphos.o: Paphos grew at [[e:palaepaphos|Palaepaphos]], modern [[e:kouklia|Kouklia]], a [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]] town in south-west [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]]. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE [[e:aegean|Aegean]] settlers arrived, and Greek legend credited Agapenor of [[s:tegea|Tegea]] with founding the city after the [[e:trojan-war|Trojan War]]. An inscription of the 11th century BCE shows Greek already written there.
kingdom-of-paphos.r: Its kings combined royal power with the priesthood of the Paphian goddess, later identified with Aphrodite, whose open-air sanctuary with a conical stone drew pilgrims from across the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]]. Paphos used the Cypriot syllabary for Greek and struck its own coins. It paid tribute to [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and later to the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]], and joined the revolt against [[e:persia|Persia]] in 498 BCE.
kingdom-of-paphos.e: The last king, [[e:nicocles-of-paphos|Nicocles]], founded the harbour city of [[e:nea-paphos|Nea Paphos]], which became the capital of Ptolemaic and Roman [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]]. The kingdom was abolished when [[e:ptolemy-i-soter|Ptolemy I]] took the island, by c. 306 BCE, but the sanctuary of Aphrodite flourished into late antiquity.

kingdom-of-champasak.t: The southern Lao kingdom on the Mekong around Wat Phu, founded in 1713, whose princes later led the southern Lao nobility in modern Laos.
kingdom-of-champasak.o: In 1713 [[e:soysisamouth|Soysisamouth]], a grandson of [[e:sourigna-vongsa|Sourigna Vongsa]], was installed as king at Champasak in southern [[e:laos|Laos]] with the support of the monk Phra Khu Phonsamek, separating the south from the [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Kingdom of Vientiane]]. The region contained the ancient [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] temple of [[e:wat-phu|Wat Phu]].
kingdom-of-champasak.r: Champasak ruled the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]] plains of the south and upland areas with Mon-[[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] peoples, trading forest products, cardamom and slaves. From 1778 it became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of Siam, which later governed much of its territory directly. The kingdom's capital moved several times along the river near Bassac.
kingdom-of-champasak.e: After the Franco-Siamese treaties of 1893 and 1904, Champasak passed to [[s:french-protectorate-of-laos|French Laos]], the 1904 treaty adding its lands west of the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]]. [[e:boun-oum|Prince Boun Oum of Champasak]] renounced his dynastic claim in 1946 so that [[e:laos|Laos]] could be unified as the [[s:kingdom-of-laos|Kingdom of Laos]].

kirata-dynasty.t: The ancient Kirata kings of the Kathmandu Valley, remembered in Nepalese chronicles as the rulers who came before the Licchavis.
kirata-dynasty.o: The Kirata dynasty is known only from later Nepalese chronicles, above all the 14th-century [[e:gopalarajavamshavali|Gopalarajavamshavali]]. They say the [[e:kirata|Kiratas]], a people of the eastern [[e:himalayas|Himalaya]], took the [[e:kathmandu-valley|Kathmandu Valley]] from earlier cowherd dynasties, the Gopalas and Mahishapalas, and were ruled by a line of some 28 or 29 kings.
kirata-dynasty.r: No inscriptions or coins of the [[e:kirata|Kirata]] kings survive, so their government and society are unknown. The name links them to the Kiranti peoples of eastern [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]], such as the [[e:rai-people|Rai]] and [[e:limbu-people|Limbu]], who regard the dynasty as their ancestors. Indian epics and the Greek geographer Ptolemy mention Kiratas as a Himalayan people, and non-[[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] place names in early inscriptions may preserve their language.
kirata-dynasty.e: The chronicles say [[e:kirata|Kirata]] rule ended when kings from the south, followed by the [[e:licchavi|Licchavis]], took the valley. The [[s:licchavi-kingdom-of-nepal|Licchavi Kingdom of Nepal]] was established by the 5th century, when the first datable inscriptions of [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] appear.

kingdom-of-bangli.t: Landlocked kingdom of the Balinese highlands, home of the Kehen temple and the lands around Lake Batur.
kingdom-of-bangli.o: Bangli was the only Balinese kingdom without a coastline. Its ruling house was a branch of the noble lineages tied to the [[s:kingdom-of-klungkung|Kingdom of Klungkung]], and it emerged as a separate kingdom by about 1800. Its documented history is thin compared with the coastal courts.
kingdom-of-bangli.r: The kingdom stretched from the [[e:rice|rice]] terraces of central [[e:bali|Bali]] up to [[e:kintamani|Kintamani]] and [[e:lake-batur|Lake Batur]], where [[e:bali-aga|Bali Aga]] villages kept older customs. Its state temple, [[e:pura-kehen|Pura Kehen]], is one of the oldest on the island. Bangli was often at war with [[s:kingdom-of-gianyar|Gianyar]] and [[s:kingdom-of-klungkung|Klungkung]], and allied itself with whichever court served its interests.
kingdom-of-bangli.e: In 1909, after the conquests of [[s:kingdom-of-badung|Badung]], [[s:kingdom-of-tabanan|Tabanan]] and [[s:kingdom-of-klungkung|Klungkung]], Bangli accepted [[e:dutch|Dutch]] protection, with its ruler kept on as regent within the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]]. It is now a regency of [[e:bali|Bali]] province.

kingdom-of-alashiya.t: Late Bronze Age kingdom on Cyprus whose rulers traded copper with Egypt, the Hittites and Ugarit, as revealed by the Amarna letters.
kingdom-of-alashiya.o: Alashiya appears in Near Eastern texts from the 18th century BCE as a source of [[e:copper|copper]], and most scholars identify it with [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] or part of it. Cyprus developed urban centres in the Late Cypriot period from c. 1650 BCE, including [[e:enkomi|Enkomi]] on the east coast, Kalavasos and Alassa, though which was the royal seat is uncertain.
kingdom-of-alashiya.r: The king of Alashiya corresponded with [[e:pharaoh|Pharaoh]] [[e:akhenaten|Akhenaten]] as a 'brother' in the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]], sending [[e:copper-ingot|copper ingots]] in return for [[e:silver|silver]], oil and luxury goods. Clay analysis shows these letters were made on [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]]. [[e:enkomi|Enkomi]] had [[e:copper|copper]] workshops and ashlar buildings, and the island used the [[e:cypro-minoan-syllabary|Cypro-Minoan]] script. The [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] claimed overlordship in the 13th century BCE.
kingdom-of-alashiya.e: Letters from [[s:kingdom-of-ugarit|Ugarit]] describe enemy ships threatening Alashiya c. 1200 BCE, and [[e:suppiluliuma-ii|Suppiluliuma II]] fought naval battles off its coast. In the following century Cypriot towns declined or moved, [[e:aegean|Aegean]] settlers arrived, and the island reorganised into the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] kingdoms such as [[e:salamis-cyprus|Salamis]], [[s:kingdom-of-paphos|Paphos]] and [[s:kingdom-of-kition|Kition]].

khanate-of-urmia.t: A khanate of the Afshar tribe on the western shore of Lake Urmia, whose khan Fath Ali Khan Afshar contended for power in Iran after Nader Shah's death.
khanate-of-urmia.o: [[e:urmia|Urmia]] was home to a branch of the Turkic [[e:afshar-tribe|Afshar tribe]], kin of [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]]. After Nader's assassination in 1747 and the break-up of the [[s:afsharid-empire|Afsharid Empire]], Afshar chiefs held Urmia and its plain as a khanate.
khanate-of-urmia.r: [[e:fath-ali-khan-afshar|Fath Ali Khan Afshar]], the most ambitious of the khans, fought [[e:azad-khan-afghan|Azad Khan Afghan]] and [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan Zand]] for control of north-western [[e:iran|Iran]]. Karim Khan besieged and took [[e:urmia|Urmia]] in 1763, and Fath Ali Khan was later killed. The khanate continued under other [[e:afshar-tribe|Afshar]] khans as [[e:zand-dynasty|Zand]] [[e:vassal|vassals]]. Its population included Azerbaijani Turks, [[e:kurds|Kurds]] and Assyrian Christians, and the plain produced grain, fruit and tobacco.
khanate-of-urmia.e: [[e:agha-mohammad-khan-qajar|Agha Mohammad Khan]]'s [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]] took [[e:urmia|Urmia]] in the 1790s, and by 1797 the khanate was incorporated into the [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] province of [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].

khilchipur-state.t: A small Khichi Chauhan Rajput state in the Malwa region of central India, one of the minor states of the Bhopal Agency.
khilchipur-state.o: The ruling family belonged to the Khichi branch of the [[e:chauhan|Chauhan Rajputs]], and tradition dates the founding of the state to 1544. Little is reliably known of its early rulers.
khilchipur-state.r: Khilchipur was a small agricultural state on the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] plateau. It paid tribute to the [[e:scindias|Sindhia]] rulers of [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior State]] and came under British protection in the early 19th century. Its history is poorly recorded.
khilchipur-state.e: Khilchipur merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948, which became part of [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 1956. It is now in [[s:rajgarh-state|Rajgarh]] district.

kangju.t: A long-lived nomad kingdom of the middle Syr Darya, a rival of the Wusun and Dayuan that dominated the steppe north of Sogdiana for six centuries.
kangju.o: Kangju first appears in the account of the Han envoy [[e:zhang-qian|Zhang Qian]], who passed through around 128 BCE and reported a nomadic state north-west of [[s:kingdom-of-dayuan|Dayuan]] with some 80,000 to 90,000 [[e:archery|archers]]. Its people were Iranian-speaking pastoralists on the middle [[e:syr-darya|Syr Darya]] and the Talas and Chu valleys, part of the wider [[s:saka|Saka]] world.
kangju.r: According to the Han histories, the king had his seat at the city of Beitian and a separate winter residence, with five lesser kings beneath him. Kangju controlled routes between the steppe, [[s:principality-of-samarkand|Sogdiana]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-dayuan|Kingdom of Dayuan]], and at times held Sogdian towns as dependencies. In 36 BCE it sheltered the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]] [[e:chanyu|chanyu]] [[e:zhizhi|Zhizhi]], whom a Han army killed there.
kangju.e: Kangju is linked by archaeologists to the Kaunchi and Otrar-Karatau cultures. It weakened under pressure from the [[s:kidarite-kingdom|Kidarite Kingdom]], [[s:hephthalite-empire|Hephthalites]] and [[s:rouran-khaganate|Rouran]], and by the 5th century its name passed to [[s:principality-of-samarkand|Sogdiana]] itself, 'Kang' being the later Chinese name for [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]].

kingdom-of-tanahun.t: A Sen hill kingdom of central Nepal and one of the Chaubise Rajya, a neighbour and rival of Gorkha and Lamjung.
kingdom-of-tanahun.o: Tanahun was founded by a branch of the Sen dynasty of [[s:kingdom-of-palpa|Palpa]] in the early 16th century, after the realm of [[e:mukunda-sen|Mukunda Sen]] was divided among his heirs. It held hill country along the Marsyangdi and Seti rivers, east of the Kingdom of Palpa and south of the [[s:kingdom-of-lamjung|Kingdom of Lamjung]].
kingdom-of-tanahun.r: As one of the [[e:chaubise-rajya|Chaubise Rajya]], the twenty-four principalities of the central hills, Tanahun was ruled by Sen kings who were linked by marriage to other hill dynasties. Little is recorded of its administration. In the 18th century its ruler Trivikram Sen tried to resist [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha]] expansion through alliances with [[s:kingdom-of-lamjung|Lamjung]] and [[s:kingdom-of-palpa|Palpa]].
kingdom-of-tanahun.e: The [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha]] forces of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] annexed Tanahun in 1782 during the unification of [[e:nepal|Nepal]] under the regent [[e:bahadur-shah-of-nepal|Bahadur Shah]]. It is now Tanahun district.

kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.t: A northern kingdom of the Chu-Han war, first the place of exile for the Zhao king Zhao Xie and then the fief of Chen Yu, overrun by Han Xin.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.o: In 206 BCE [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] moved [[e:zhao-xie|Zhao Xie]], the restored king of Zhao, north to the frontier region of Dai, with its capital at Dai near modern [[e:yu-county-hebei|Yuxian]], [[e:hebei|Hebei]], so that [[e:zhang-er|Zhang Er]] could rule the Zhao heartland as the [[s:kingdom-of-changshan|Kingdom of Changshan]].
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.r: In 205 BCE [[e:chen-yu|Chen Yu]] drove out [[e:zhang-er|Zhang Er]] and brought [[e:zhao-xie|Zhao Xie]] back to Zhao; in thanks, Zhao Xie made Chen Yu King of Dai. Chen Yu stayed in Zhao as chief minister and governed Dai through his deputy [[e:xia-yue|Xia Yue]]. The kingdom was a frontier zone of herding and farming facing the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]].
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.e: In 205 BCE [[e:han-xin|Han Xin]] defeated and captured [[e:xia-yue|Xia Yue]], and in 204 BCE he destroyed the Zhao army at [[e:battle-of-jingxing|Jingxing]], where [[e:chen-yu|Chen Yu]] was killed. Dai passed to the [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and later became a Han kingdom held by [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang's]] son, the future [[e:emperor-wen-of-han|Emperor Wen]].

kathiwara-state.t: A small Rajput chiefship in the hills of western Malwa, under British supervision through the Bhopawar Agency.
kathiwara-state.o: Kathiwara was a small estate in the hills of western [[e:malwa|Malwa]] near [[s:jhabua-state|Jhabua]], held by a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family from around 1600. Its founding is not well documented.
kathiwara-state.r: Its chief ruled hilly, forested country with a largely [[e:bhils|Bhil]] population, paying tribute to more powerful neighbours. In the British period it was a minor state in the [[e:bhopawar-agency|Bhopawar Agency of Central India]]. Little else is recorded.
kathiwara-state.e: Kathiwara joined [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948, which became part of [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 1956.

kingdom-of-hazor.t: Hazor, the largest Canaanite city, which traded with Mari and Babylon and which the Bible calls the head of all those kingdoms.
kingdom-of-hazor.o: Hazor grew north of the [[e:sea-of-galilee|Sea of Galilee]] on the road from [[e:egypt|Egypt]] to [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. In the 18th century BCE a huge lower city was added to the old mound, creating a city of some 80 hectares. With [[e:tel-dan|Laish]], it is one of the only Canaanite cities named in the [[s:mari|Mari]] letters, which mention [[e:tin|tin]] sent to its king.
kingdom-of-hazor.r: Its kings ruled from a palace on the upper city with basalt orthostats and temples in Syrian style, and controlled much of northern [[e:canaan|Canaan]]. In the [[e:akhetaten|Amarna]] age King Abdi-Tirshi was a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]], though neighbours accused him of disloyalty. Excavations by [[e:yigael-yadin|Yigael Yadin]] and [[e:amnon-ben-tor|Amnon Ben-Tor]] uncovered statues and [[e:cuneiform|cuneiform]] tablets.
kingdom-of-hazor.e: In the 13th century BCE the Canaanite city was destroyed by fire, and its statues deliberately defaced. The [[e:book-of-joshua|Book of Joshua]] credits its destruction to the [[e:israelites|Israelites]]; scholars still debate who was responsible. A smaller fortified town later belonged to the [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Kingdom of Israel]].

kingdom-of-desmond.t: The MacCarthy kingdom of South Munster, created when Munster was split in 1118 and surviving in parts until the end of the 16th century.
kingdom-of-desmond.o: The [[e:treaty-of-glanmire|Treaty of Glanmire]] in 1118 divided [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]], giving the south, Deasmumu, to the [[e:charles-maccarthy|MacCarthys]], heirs of the [[e:eoganachta|Eoganacht]] kings of [[e:rock-of-cashel|Cashel]]. [[e:cormac-mac-carthaigh|Cormac MacCarthy]] ruled from [[e:cork|Cork]] and built [[e:cormacs-chapel|Cormac's Chapel]] on the Rock of Cashel, consecrated in 1134.
kingdom-of-desmond.r: Desmond's kings lost much of [[e:cork|Cork]] to the Normans after 1177, but [[e:finghin-mac-carthaigh|Finghin MacCarthy]]'s victory at [[e:battle-of-callann|Callann]] in 1261 halted the colonists. The [[e:charles-maccarthy|MacCarthy]] Mor branch then ruled from Pallis in [[s:ciarraige-luachra|Kerry]], with cadet lines in [[e:carbery-county-cork|Carbery]] and [[e:muskerry|Muskerry]]. The kingdom was an overlordship of Gaelic lords such as the [[e:osullivan-dynasty|O'Sullivans]] and O'Donoghues.
kingdom-of-desmond.e: [[e:donal-maccarthy-mor-1st-earl-of-clancare|Donal MacCarthy Mor]] became Earl of Clancare in 1565 under the [[s:kingdom-of-ireland|Kingdom of Ireland]]. His death without a legitimate male heir in 1596 ended the senior line, and its lands passed into English plantations.

cr.a: The original uploader was (Automated conversion) at English Wikipedia.

khanate-of-khoy.t: A khanate of the Kurdish Donboli family in north-western Iran whose last khan resisted the Qajars and ended his days ruling a khanate under Russia.
khanate-of-khoy.o: The Donboli, a Kurdish family long settled around [[e:khoy|Khoy]], held hereditary authority there under the [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]]. After [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah's]] death in 1747 they ruled Khoy and [[e:salmas|Salmas]] as a khanate. [[e:ahmad-khan-donboli|Ahmad Khan Donboli]] (r. 1763 to 1786) was the most powerful of the line, extending his influence over [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]].
khanate-of-khoy.r: [[e:khoy|Khoy]] lay on the main route between [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]] and the Ottoman frontier and was a prosperous trading town. The Donboli khans kept tribal cavalry and patronised building in the town. [[e:ahmad-khan-donboli|Ahmad Khan]] was murdered in 1786, and his son [[e:jafar-qoli-khan-donboli|Jafar Qoli Khan Donboli]] opposed the rising power of [[e:agha-mohammad-khan-qajar|Agha Mohammad Khan]].
khanate-of-khoy.e: [[e:agha-mohammad-khan-qajar|Agha Mohammad Khan]]'s [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]] took control of the region in the 1790s; [[e:jafar-qoli-khan-donboli|Jafar Qoli Khan]] fled north in 1799 and was later installed by [[e:russia|Russia]] as khan of [[e:shaki-azerbaijan|Sheki]]. [[e:khoy|Khoy]] became part of [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].

kingdom-of-mpororo.t: A short-lived pastoral kingdom between Uganda and Rwanda whose breakup left a patchwork of small chiefdoms later absorbed by Ankole.
kingdom-of-mpororo.o: Mpororo arose in the mid-17th century in the grasslands of south-western [[s:uganda|Uganda]] and northern [[s:kingdom-of-rwanda|Rwanda]], ruled by the Bashambo clan. Traditions connect its founding with the decline of the [[s:kingdom-of-ndorwa|Kingdom of Ndorwa]] and the rivalries of the Kingdom of Rwanda and the [[s:kingdom-of-ankole|Kingdom of Ankole]].
kingdom-of-mpororo.r: It was a [[e:cattle|cattle]]-keeping kingdom with a court and royal drums like its neighbours. Its power seems to have rested on the king's herds and on alliances with pastoral clans. Only fragments of its history survive in oral tradition.
kingdom-of-mpororo.e: In the mid-18th century Mpororo split into several small principalities, among them Rujumbura and Kajara. Under the [[e:ankole-agreement|Ankole Agreement]] of 1901 most of these were merged into the [[s:kingdom-of-ankole|Kingdom of Ankole]], while others went to [[e:kigezi|Kigezi]] district.

kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.t: Croatian kingdom in personal union with Hungary, governed by bans and a noble diet, until the disaster of Mohács led it to the Habsburgs.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.o: After the [[e:trpimirovic-dynasty|Trpimirović]] line ended and the last king fell at [[e:battle-of-gvozd-mountain|Gvozd]] in 1097, Coloman of [[e:hungary|Hungary]] was crowned king of [[e:croatia|Croatia]] and [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]] at [[e:biograd-na-moru|Biograd]] in 1102. Later tradition held that a pact ([[e:pacta-conventa-croatia|Pacta conventa]]) with Croatian nobles guaranteed their rights, though its authenticity is disputed.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.r: The kingdom kept its own institutions: a ban governed for the king, and the [[e:croatian-parliament|Sabor]] (diet) of nobles met separately. Great families such as the [[e:subic-family|Šubići of Bribir]] and the [[e:frankopan-family|Frankopans]] held vast lands; Ban [[e:paul-i-subic-of-bribir|Paul I Šubić]] was almost independent around 1300. [[e:venice|Venice]] and [[e:hungary|Hungary]] fought over [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]] for centuries, and in 1409 [[e:ladislaus-of-naples|Ladislaus of Naples]] sold his Dalmatian claims to Venice. Ottoman raids grew after 1463, with a heavy defeat at [[e:battle-of-krbava-field|Krbava Field]] in 1493.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.e: After [[e:louis-ii-of-hungary|Louis II]] died at [[e:battle-of-mohacs|Mohács]] in 1526, the Croatian nobles meeting at [[e:1527-election-in-cetin|Cetin]] in 1527 elected [[e:ferdinand-i-holy-roman-emperor|Ferdinand of Habsburg]] as king, beginning centuries of [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] rule.

kingdom-of-urartu.t: Urartu, a mountain kingdom around Lake Van, Assyria's great northern rival, famed for its fortresses, canals and bronze work.
kingdom-of-urartu.o: Urartu formed in the 9th century BCE when the chiefdoms of [[s:nairi|Nairi]] united under pressure from the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]]. Sarduri I built the fortress of Van, called [[e:tushpa|Tushpa]], on a rock above [[e:lake-van|Lake Van]] c. 840 BCE, and his successors pushed the kingdom into [[e:south-caucasus|Transcaucasia]] and north-western [[e:iran|Iran]].
kingdom-of-urartu.r: Kings governed through fortified centres with storerooms for grain and wine, linked by roads. [[e:menua|Menua]] built a canal over 50 km long that still waters Van, and [[e:argishti-i|Argishti I]] founded [[e:erebuni|Erebuni]] in 782 BCE, origin of [[e:yerevan|Yerevan]]. The god [[e:haldi|Haldi]] headed the pantheon; his temple at [[s:musasir|Musasir]] was famous for its treasures.
kingdom-of-urartu.e: [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] defeated [[e:rusa-i|Rusa I]] and sacked [[s:musasir|Musasir]] in 714 BCE. Urartu recovered under [[e:rusa-ii|Rusa II]] but collapsed in the early 6th century BCE, probably under attacks by the [[s:median-empire|Median Empire]] and [[e:scythians|Scythians]]. [[e:armenians|Armenians]] later occupied its lands.

kingdom-of-anshan.t: The small Persian kingdom in Fars ruled by the ancestors of Cyrus the Great, the springboard for the Achaemenid Empire.
kingdom-of-anshan.o: As the [[s:neo-elamite-kingdom|Neo-Elamite kingdom]] weakened under Assyrian attack in the 7th century BCE, Persian rulers took control of [[e:anshan|Anshan]], the old Elamite highland capital at Tall-i Malyan in [[e:fars|Fars]]. Assyrian texts mention Kurash of Parsumash, often identified with Cyrus I, sending his son as hostage to [[e:ashurbanipal|Ashurbanipal]] around 640 BCE.
kingdom-of-anshan.r: The [[e:cyrus-cylinder|Cyrus Cylinder]] gives the line of [[e:teispes|Teispes]], Cyrus I and [[e:cambyses-i|Cambyses I]], all 'king of [[e:anshan|Anshan]]'. The dynasty, called [[e:teispids|Teispid]] by historians, ruled a mixed Persian and Elamite society; a seal of Cyrus I follows Elamite style and Elamite remained a written language of administration. The kingdom was probably a [[e:vassal|vassal]] first of [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and then of the [[s:median-empire|Median Empire]], and [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] says Cambyses I married a Median princess.
kingdom-of-anshan.e: In 550 BCE [[e:cyrus-the-great|Cyrus II]], king of [[e:anshan|Anshan]], defeated the Median king [[e:astyages|Astyages]] and took [[e:ecbatana|Ecbatana]], then went on to found the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]]. Anshan's royal tradition lived on in the titles of Persian kings.

kahat.t: Kahat, a small kingdom of the upper Khabur plains in the age of Mari, one of many rival city-states of the region known as Ida-Maras.
kahat.o: Kahat grew at Tell Barri on the [[e:jaghjagh-river|Jaghjagh]] river in north-eastern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], a site inhabited since the 4th millennium BCE. By the 18th century BCE it was one of the minor kingdoms of the [[e:ida-maras|Ida-Maras]] district, between the larger powers of [[s:mari|Mari]], [[s:ashnakkum|Ashnakkum]] and [[s:apum|Shubat-Enlil]].
kahat.r: Known mainly from the [[s:mari|Mari]] letters, its kings swore alliances with [[e:zimri-lim|Zimri-Lim]] and switched sides as the balance of power shifted. Kahat was also a religious centre of the storm god, honoured in later Hurrian and Assyrian sources. Italian excavations since 1980 have explored the town.
kahat.e: The kingdom lost its independence when [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi's]] [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]] and later the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]] reshaped northern [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]]. Kahat survived as a town under [[e:mitanni|Mitanni]] and the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]].

kingdom-of-kasanje.t: An Imbangala kingdom on the Kwango whose fair channelled captives from the Lunda interior to Portuguese Luanda for two centuries.
kingdom-of-kasanje.o: Kasanje was founded around 1620 by an [[e:imbangala|Imbangala]] warband, formerly allied with [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]], which settled in the [[e:baixa-de-kasanje|Baixa de Kasanje]], the fertile [[e:kwango-river|Kwango]] valley. Its leader, Kasanje, and his successors combined Imbangala military traditions with [[e:mbundu|Mbundu]] lineage institutions to build a stable kingdom.
kingdom-of-kasanje.r: The king, titled the [[e:jaga|Jaga]] Kasanje, ruled through officials drawn from different lineages, and [[e:imbangala|Imbangala]] rituals shaped kingship. The kingdom's wealth came from its position as middleman: captives and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] from the [[s:lunda-empire|Lunda Empire]] passed through the Kasanje market to Portuguese traders, who kept a resident agent there. Kasanje jealously blocked direct contact between the coast and the interior.
kingdom-of-kasanje.e: The end of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] undermined Kasanje's economy, and wars with the Portuguese in the 1850s weakened it. Portuguese forces finally occupied the region in 1912, absorbing it into [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]].

kingdom-of-eile.t: Irish kingdom of the O'Carrolls around Birr, on the border of Munster and Leinster, which survived as Ely O'Carroll until the 16th century.
kingdom-of-eile.o: Éile was the territory of an early medieval people of the Irish midlands, in what is now south [[s:kingdom-of-ui-failge|Offaly]] and north [[e:county-tipperary|Tipperary]], counted as part of the [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Kingdom of Munster]]. Its ruling family claimed descent from the [[e:eoganachta|Eóganachta's]] kin, and from the 11th century the [[e:ocarrolls-of-ely|Ua Cerbaill]], O'Carroll, became the dominant line, giving the region its later name of [[e:ely-ocarroll|Ely O'Carroll]].
kingdom-of-eile.r: The kingdom lay on the boundary between [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] and [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Leinster]], which gave it strategic value and exposed it to raids. The monastery of [[e:birr|Birr]], founded by St [[e:brendan-of-birr|Brendan of Birr]] in the 6th century, produced the [[e:macregol-gospels|Book of MacRegol]], an illuminated gospel book of about 800. The [[e:ocarrolls-of-ely|O'Carrolls]] ruled from strongholds such as [[e:leap-castle|Leap Castle]] and Birr.
kingdom-of-eile.e: [[e:anglo-normans|Anglo-Norman]] settlers took part of the territory in the 13th century, but the [[e:ocarrolls-of-ely|O'Carrolls]] recovered much of it. In 1552 their chief [[e:tadhg-ocarroll-baron-of-ely|Tadhg O'Carroll]] surrendered his lands to the crown and was created Baron of Ely, and the region was later divided between [[e:county-offaly|King's County]] and [[e:county-tipperary|Tipperary]].
kingdom-of-eile.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-cusco.t: The small highland kingdom around Cusco from which the Incas rose to build the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas.
kingdom-of-cusco.o: [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] tradition says the founder [[e:manco-capac|Manco Capac]] emerged from [[e:lake-titicaca|Lake Titicaca]] or the cave of [[e:pacaritambo|Pacaritambo]] and led his people to the valley of [[e:cusco|Cusco]], founding the city around 1200. Archaeology shows the [[e:killke-culture|Killke culture]] in the valley from about 1000, which developed into the early Inca polity.
kingdom-of-cusco.r: The early [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] kingdom was one of several competing lordships in the region, led by a ruler called the [[e:sapa-inca|Sapa Inca]] and by royal lineages called panacas. [[e:cusco|Cusco]] was organised in two halves, Hanan and Hurin. Successive rulers such as [[e:sinchi-roca|Sinchi Roca]], [[e:mayta-capac|Mayta Capac]] and [[e:viracocha-inca|Viracocha Inca]] fought and allied with neighbours such as the [[e:ayarmaca|Ayarmaca]]. The economy depended on [[e:maize|maize]] terraces and herding.
kingdom-of-cusco.e: According to [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] tradition, around 1438 [[e:pachacuti|Cusi Yupanqui]] repelled the [[s:chanka-confederation|Chanka Confederation]], deposed his father [[e:viracocha-inca|Viracocha Inca]] and took the name Pachacuti. He rebuilt [[e:cusco|Cusco]] and began the conquests that created the [[s:inca-empire|Inca Empire]].

karkiya-dynasty.t: A Shia dynasty of eastern Gilan, centred on Lahijan, that sheltered the boy who became Shah Ismail I, founder of the Safavid state.
karkiya-dynasty.o: [[e:sayyid-ali-kiya|Sayyid Ali Kiya]], a Zaydi sayyid supported by the [[s:marashi-dynasty|Mar'ashi dynasty]] of [[e:mazandaran|Mazandaran]], took [[e:lahijan|Lahijan]] and eastern [[e:gilan|Gilan]] (Biyapish) around 1370. His descendants, the Kar-Kiya, ruled this part of Gilan east of the [[e:sefidrud|Sefidrud]].
karkiya-dynasty.r: The Karkiya combined religious authority as sayyids with princely rule over a wet, forested land of [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]] and fishing. They long followed [[e:zaydism|Zaydi Shia Islam]], later adopting [[e:twelver-shiism|Twelver Shi'ism]], and fought the [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] [[s:ishaqid-dynasty|Ishaqid dynasty]] of western [[e:gilan|Gilan]]. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:ali-mirza-karkiya|Ali Mirza Karkiya]] gave refuge at [[e:lahijan|Lahijan]] from 1494 to 1499 to the young Ismail, heir of the Safavid order, who left from there to found the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]].
karkiya-dynasty.e: [[e:khan-ahmad-khan|Khan Ahmad Khan]], the last ruler, quarrelled with [[e:abbas-i-of-persia|Shah Abbas I]], who conquered [[e:gilan|Gilan]] in 1592; Khan Ahmad fled to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]].

khyrim-state.t: A Khasi state of the Meghalaya plateau with its seat at Smit, home of the annual Nongkrem dance held by its Syiem.
khyrim-state.o: Hima Khyrim emerged as one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the [[e:shillong|Shillong]] plateau; its origins are known from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
khyrim-state.r: Khyrim was headed by a [[e:syiem|Syiem]] chosen from a royal clan, with succession through the female line, and ruled with clan elders in a dorbar. The Syiem also had ritual duties: the annual [[e:nongkrem-dance|Shad Nongkrem]], a dance and thanksgiving at Smit, is held by the Syiem and the high priestess (Syiem Sad) of Khyrim.
khyrim-state.e: Khyrim came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1948, joining [[e:assam|Assam]]. It is now part of [[e:meghalaya|Meghalaya]], where the [[e:nongkrem-dance|Nongkrem]] festival continues.

kalachuris-of-ratanpur.t: A Kalachuri branch that ruled Chhattisgarh from Ratanpur for over seven centuries, from the 11th century until the Maratha conquest.
kalachuris-of-ratanpur.o: Around 1000 Kalingaraja, a member of the [[s:kalachuris-of-tripuri|Kalachuris of Tripuri]], conquered the region of [[e:dakshina-kosala|Dakshina Kosala]], in modern [[e:chhattisgarh|Chhattisgarh]], and settled at Tummana. His grandson Ratnaraja I founded [[e:ratanpur|Ratanpur]], which became the capital, and the family gradually became independent of the Tripuri line.
kalachuris-of-ratanpur.r: [[e:jajalladeva-i|Jajalladeva I]] and [[e:prithvideva-ii|Prithvideva II]] extended the kingdom and fought the [[s:eastern-ganga-dynasty|Eastern Ganga dynasty]] and other neighbours. The kings, [[e:shaivism|Shaivas]], built temples and tanks at [[e:ratanpur|Ratanpur]] and Malhar, and inscriptions show a structured administration with ministers and district chiefs. In later centuries the kingdom split into the Ratanpur and [[e:raipur|Raipur]] branches, and it is often linked with the name [[e:chhattisgarh|Chhattisgarh]], thirty-six forts.
kalachuris-of-ratanpur.e: The [[e:haihaya|Haihaya]] rajas survived as a regional power, acknowledging the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]] in name. In 1741 the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Bhonsles of Nagpur]], under their general [[e:bhaskar-ram-kolhatkar|Bhaskar Pant]], conquered [[e:ratanpur|Ratanpur]], and the last raja was pensioned off.

kenedougou-kingdom.t: A Senufo and Dyula kingdom ruled from walled Sikasso, which held off Samori Toure and fell to the French only after a bloody siege in 1898.
kenedougou-kingdom.o: Kenedougou formed among [[e:senufo|Senufo]] farming communities in what is now southern [[e:mali|Mali]] and western [[e:burkina-faso|Burkina Faso]], where [[e:wangara|Dyula]] traders of the Traore clan established a ruling dynasty, traditionally from the late 17th century. For long it was a loose chiefdom; it became a strong kingdom only in the 19th century, when [[e:tieba-traore|Tieba Traore]] expanded it and moved the capital to [[e:sikasso|Sikasso]].
kenedougou-kingdom.r: Its kings ruled through a court of warriors, [[e:senufo|Senufo]] village chiefs and a Muslim [[e:wangara|Dyula]] merchant class, while most subjects kept Senufo traditional religion. [[e:sikasso|Sikasso]] was ringed by a massive earthen tata wall several kilometres long. Kenedougou drew wealth from kola, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and the trade between the savanna and the forest, and bought firearms through the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic trade]].
kenedougou-kingdom.e: [[e:samori-ture|Samori Toure]] besieged [[e:sikasso|Sikasso]] in 1887 and 1888 without success, and [[e:tieba-traore|Tieba]] allied with the French. His brother [[e:babemba-traore|Babemba Traore]] refused French demands, and on 1 May 1898 a French column stormed the city; Babemba died rather than surrender. The land became part of [[s:french-sudan|French Sudan]].
kenedougou-kingdom.re: Senufo traditional religion and Sunni Islam

kingdom-of-dayuan.t: The ancient kingdom of the Ferghana valley, famed in China for its 'heavenly horses', which provoked the Han dynasty's longest-range war.
kingdom-of-dayuan.o: Dayuan, the Chinese name for the farming people of the [[s:principality-of-ferghana|Ferghana]] valley, was described by the envoy [[e:zhang-qian|Zhang Qian]] around 128 BCE as a land of over 70 walled towns and several hundred thousand people. Its population may have included descendants of Greek settlers from Alexander's era, though this is debated.
kingdom-of-dayuan.r: The people grew [[e:rice|rice]], wheat and grapes, made wine and bred tall, fast horses that the Han court prized as 'blood-sweating' heavenly horses. A king ruled with nobles from the capital [[e:ershi|Ershi]]. In 104 BCE Dayuan refused to supply horses, and [[e:emperor-wu-of-han|Emperor Wu]] sent the general [[e:li-guangli|Li Guangli]], who after two campaigns besieged Ershi in 102 BCE, forcing the nobles to kill their king Wugua and hand over horses.
kingdom-of-dayuan.e: Dayuan remained a tributary of the Han for a time and appears in Chinese records into the 3rd century CE. Thereafter [[s:principality-of-ferghana|Ferghana]] was ruled by local dynasties that became the later Principality of [[e:fergana-valley|Ferghana]], still noted for its horses.

kingdom-of-the-regni.t: Client kingdom of Togidubnus in Sussex and Hampshire, a loyal ally of Rome after the conquest whose seat may have been the palace at Fishbourne.
kingdom-of-the-regni.o: After the Roman invasion of 43, much of the former realm of the [[s:atrebates-britain|Atrebates (Britain)]] was entrusted to [[e:togidubnus|Togidubnus]], a British noble loyal to [[e:rome|Rome]]. [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] says that certain states were given to him and that he remained faithful down to his own day, and the region became a base for Roman operations along the south coast.
kingdom-of-the-regni.r: An inscription from [[e:chichester|Chichester]] dedicating a temple to [[e:neptune|Neptune]] and [[e:minerva|Minerva]] names [[e:togidubnus|Tiberius Claudius Togidubnus]] as great king in [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], showing that he held Roman citizenship and royal status. His capital, [[e:noviomagus-reginorum|Noviomagus Reginorum]], grew into a Roman-style town, and the lavish villa at [[e:fishbourne-roman-palace|Fishbourne]], with mosaics and formal gardens, has often been linked to him. The kingdom provided [[e:rome|Rome]] with a stable and Romanised territory.
kingdom-of-the-regni.e: When [[e:togidubnus|Togidubnus]] died, probably around 80, the client kingdom was absorbed into the province of [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]]. Its lands were divided into civitates, the [[e:regni|Regni]] around [[e:chichester|Chichester]] and probably the [[s:belgae-britain|Belgae (Britain)]] around [[e:winchester|Winchester]]. Chichester remains the main town of the region.

kingdom-of-the-heruli.t: A short-lived East Germanic kingdom on the middle Danube, briefly dominant over the Lombards before a crushing defeat around 508.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.o: The Heruli had been in the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] region and under Hunnic rule; after the [[e:huns|Huns]]' collapse following the [[e:battle-of-nedao|Battle of Nedao]] in 454, one group settled near the middle [[e:danube|Danube]], probably in southern [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]], western [[e:slovakia|Slovakia]] and [[e:lower-austria|Lower Austria]]. By about 490 they had a strong kingdom that took tribute from the [[e:lombards|Lombards]].
kingdom-of-the-heruli.r: [[e:procopius|Procopius]] describes the Heruli as fierce warriors who kept old pagan customs, including the sacrifice of elderly people and the suicide of widows. Their king [[e:rodulf-king-of-the-heruli|Rodulf]] allied with [[e:theodoric-the-great|Theodoric the Great]], who adopted him as a 'son in arms' around 507. The kingdom rested on warrior power and tribute rather than settled institutions.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.e: Around 508 [[e:rodulf-king-of-the-heruli|Rodulf]] attacked the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombards]] under Tato and was killed in a heavy defeat. The Heruli scattered: some moved into Roman territory and became federates in [[e:illyricum-roman-province|Illyricum]], others went to [[e:scandinavia|Scandinavia]] according to [[e:procopius|Procopius]]. Herul soldiers later fought for Justinian in [[e:italy|Italy]] and [[e:persia|Persia]].

kingdom-of-bavaria.t: Wittelsbach kingdom created by Napoleon, the largest German state after Prussia and home of the fairy-tale castles of Ludwig II.
kingdom-of-bavaria.o: [[e:maximilian-i-joseph-of-bavaria|Elector Maximilian IV Joseph]], allied with [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], was proclaimed King Maximilian I of [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] on 1 January 1806. Napoleon's settlements added [[e:franconia|Franconia]], Swabian lands and imperial cities, creating a state of mixed religion and identity.
kingdom-of-bavaria.r: Minister [[e:maximilian-von-montgelas|Montgelas]] modernised the administration, and the constitution of 1818 established a parliament. [[e:ludwig-i-of-bavaria|Ludwig I]] turned [[e:munich|Munich]] into a city of classical architecture and museums before abdicating in 1848 over the [[e:lola-montez|Lola Montez]] affair. [[e:ludwig-ii-of-bavaria|Ludwig II]], patron of [[e:richard-wagner|Wagner]], built [[e:neuschwanstein-castle|Neuschwanstein]] and [[e:linderhof-palace|Linderhof]] and was deposed in 1886; his uncle [[e:luitpold-prince-regent-of-bavaria|Luitpold]] ruled as regent. [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] kept its own army and railway in the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]].
kingdom-of-bavaria.e: [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] sided with [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1866 but joined the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] in 1871. In November 1918 [[e:kurt-eisner|Kurt Eisner]] proclaimed a republic in [[e:munich|Munich]] and [[e:ludwig-iii-of-bavaria|Ludwig III]] fled, ending the monarchy; the state became the [[s:free-state-of-bavaria|Free State of Bavaria]].

kii-domain.t: One of the three Tokugawa branch houses, ruling from Wakayama, which gave Japan two shoguns, Yoshimune and Iemochi.
kii-domain.o: In 1619 the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] moved [[e:tokugawa-yorinobu|Tokugawa Yorinobu]], the tenth son of [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], to [[e:wakayama|Wakayama]], giving him Kii province and part of [[e:ise-province|Ise]] with about 555,000 koku. Kii became one of the three [[e:gosanke|Gosanke]] houses entitled to supply a shogun.
kii-domain.r: The domain controlled the Kii peninsula, with forests of the [[e:kumano|Kumano]] region, mandarin orange orchards, fisheries and the soy sauce makers of [[e:yuasa-wakayama|Yuasa]]. When the main line of [[e:shogun|shoguns]] ended in 1716, the Kii lord [[e:tokugawa-yoshimune|Tokugawa Yoshimune]] became the eighth shogun and launched the [[e:kyoho-reforms|Kyoho reforms]]. In 1858 another Kii lord, Yoshitomi, became Shogun [[e:tokugawa-iemochi|Tokugawa Iemochi]].
kii-domain.e: Kii submitted to the new government in 1868 and carried out military reforms. After abolition in 1871 it became [[e:wakayama-prefecture|Wakayama Prefecture]]; the diplomat [[e:mutsu-munemitsu|Mutsu Munemitsu]] came from Kii.

kuru-kingdom.t: The leading kingdom of the Middle Vedic period, where the Vedic hymns were collected and the ritual order of early Hinduism took shape.
kuru-kingdom.o: The Kuru tribe formed in the upper [[e:ganges-yamuna-doab|Ganges-Yamuna Doab]] around 1200 BCE, when the [[e:bharatas|Bharata]] and [[e:purus|Puru]] clans merged into a single polity. Under kings remembered in the [[e:atharvaveda|Atharvaveda]] and the [[e:brahmanas|Brahmanas]], notably [[e:parikshit|Parikshit]] and his son [[e:janamejaya|Janamejaya]], it became the dominant power of northern [[e:india|India]], with centres at Asandivat and [[e:hastinapura|Hastinapura]]. Many historians regard it as the first state-level society in [[e:south-asia|South Asia]].
kuru-kingdom.r: Kuru kings patronised [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] priests, who arranged the hymns of the [[e:rigveda|Rigveda]] into collections and developed the [[e:samaveda|Samaveda]] and [[e:yajurveda|Yajurveda]]. Royal consecration rites such as the [[e:rajasuya|Rajasuya]] and the horse sacrifice reinforced kingship, and society was ordered into the four [[e:varna|varnas]]. The economy rested on [[e:cattle|cattle]] herding, barley and [[e:rice|rice]] farming, and the early use of iron. Memories of the kingdom later formed the backdrop of the [[e:mahabharata|Mahabharata]].
kuru-kingdom.e: Tradition says a flood of the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] drove the court from [[e:hastinapura|Hastinapura]] to [[e:kausambi|Kaushambi]]. By the 6th century BCE the Kurus were a minor mahajanapada, partly ruled as a sangha, overshadowed by [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kosala]] and [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]]. Their territory was absorbed by the [[s:nanda-empire|Nanda Empire]] in the 4th century BCE.

kingdom-of-cottius.t: Alpine client kingdom around Susa whose ruler Cottius allied with Augustus and gave his name to the Cottian Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.o: In the 1st century BCE the Segusini and neighbouring Alpine peoples around the [[e:montgenevre-pass|Mont Genèvre]] pass were ruled by a king named [[e:donnus|Donnus]], who appears in Caesar's time. His son, [[e:marcus-julius-cottius|Marcus Julius Cottius]], chose to make peace with Augustus rather than resist the Roman conquest of the [[e:alps|Alps]].
kingdom-of-cottius.r: [[e:marcus-julius-cottius|Cottius]] governed fourteen Alpine communities as a Roman prefect while keeping royal status locally. He built and maintained the road over the [[e:montgenevre-pass|Mont Genèvre]] pass, a key route between [[e:italy|Italy]] and [[e:gaul|Gaul]]. In 9–8 BCE he erected the [[e:arch-of-augustus-susa|Arch of Augustus]] at [[e:susa-piedmont|Segusio]] (Susa), whose inscription lists his peoples. The kingdom combined Celtic traditions with Roman administration.
kingdom-of-cottius.e: [[e:claudius|Claudius]] restored the royal title to [[e:marcus-julius-cottius|Cottius's]] son, [[e:marcus-julius-cottius-ii|Marcus Julius Cottius II]], in 44 CE. When he died without an heir around 63 CE, [[e:nero|Nero]] annexed the kingdom as the province of the [[e:cottian-alps|Alpes Cottiae]]. The name survives in the Cottian [[e:alps|Alps]].

kingdom-of-moylurg.t: A Gaelic lordship of north Roscommon ruled by the MacDermots from their island fortress on Lough Key.
kingdom-of-moylurg.o: Magh Luirg was the territory of a branch of the [[e:sil-muiredaig|Sil Muiredaig]], the ruling kindred of [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]]. In the 12th century the [[e:macdermot|MacDermot]] family, descended from Diarmait mac Taidg, emerged as its rulers and as marshals of the [[e:ua-conchobair-dynasty|O'Connor]] kings of Connacht.
kingdom-of-moylurg.r: The [[e:macdermot|MacDermots]] ruled from the Rock of Lough Ce, an island fortress on [[e:lough-key|Lough Key]], and patronised the abbey of [[e:boyle-abbey|Boyle]] and the learned families who compiled the [[e:annals-of-loch-ce|Annals of Loch Ce]]. Their lordship was based on [[e:cattle|cattle]], clients and armed retainers, and they served as kingmakers in [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]] politics.
kingdom-of-moylurg.e: The [[e:composition-of-connacht|Composition of Connacht]] in 1585 brought the lordship under English land law. The [[e:macdermot|MacDermots]] kept part of their lands and their title, the MacDermot, Prince of Coolavin, has been recognised into modern times.

kievan-rus.t: The first great East Slavic state, ruled by the Rurikid princes from Kiev, which brought Orthodox Christianity to the lands of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.
kievan-rus.o: In 882, according to the [[e:primary-chronicle|Primary Chronicle]], [[e:oleg-of-novgorod|Oleg of Novgorod]] seized [[e:kyiv|Kiev]] and joined the northern and southern ends of the river route from the [[e:varangians|Varangians]] to the [[e:greeks|Greeks]]. His successors [[e:igor-of-kiev|Igor]], [[e:olga-of-kiev|Olga]] and [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav I]] forced the [[e:east-slavs|East Slavic]] tribes into tribute, destroyed the [[s:khazar-khaganate|Khazar Khaganate]] and raided [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]].
kievan-rus.r: The state was a family enterprise of the [[e:rurik-dynasty|Rurikid]] princes, who shared out towns among themselves, with [[e:kyiv|Kiev]] as the senior seat. [[e:vladimir-the-great|Vladimir the Great]] accepted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] from [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] in 988, bringing churches, Church Slavonic writing and Byzantine art. [[e:yaroslav-the-wise|Yaroslav the Wise]] issued the law code known as the [[e:russkaya-pravda|Russkaya Pravda]] and built the [[e:saint-sophia-cathedral-kyiv|Cathedral of Saint Sophia]].
kievan-rus.e: After [[e:vladimir-ii-monomakh|Vladimir Monomakh]] and his son Mstislav, who died in 1132, Rus' broke into rival principalities such as [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]], [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]] and the [[s:novgorod-republic|Novgorod Republic]]. The Mongol invasion ended it, sacking [[e:kyiv|Kiev]] in 1240. [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]], [[e:belarus|Belarus]] and [[e:russia|Russia]] all trace their history to Rus'.

khanate-of-qaradagh.t: A mountain khanate north of Tabriz, centred on Ahar, that emerged after Nader Shah's death and was gradually absorbed by the Qajars.
khanate-of-qaradagh.o: Qaradagh, the 'Black Mountain' country between [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]] and the [[e:aras-river|Aras]] river, became a separate khanate after the assassination of [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] in 1747 broke up the [[s:afsharid-empire|Afsharid Empire]]. Local tribal chiefs ruled from [[e:ahar-iran|Ahar]], a town known for the shrine of the [[e:sufism|Sufi]] Sheikh Shihab al-Din.
khanate-of-qaradagh.r: The khanate was a land of mountain villages and pastoral tribes, with [[e:copper|copper]] and other mineral resources. Its khans, of whom Kazem Khan Qaradaghi is among the best known, competed with the neighbouring [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]] and [[e:karabakh|Karabakh]] khanates and paid tribute to whichever power dominated [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]]. Records of its internal government are sparse.
khanate-of-qaradagh.e: [[e:agha-mohammad-khan-qajar|Agha Mohammad Khan]]'s [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]] brought Qaradagh under its control in the 1790s. After the [[e:russo-persian-war-1826-1828|Russo-Persian War]] ended with the [[e:treaty-of-turkmenchay|Treaty of Turkmenchay]] in 1828, the [[e:aras-river|Aras]] became the border, and Qaradagh remained within [[e:iran|Iran]] as a governorate.

kingdom-of-karagwe.t: A kingdom west of Lake Victoria whose ruler Rumanyika welcomed the explorers Speke and Grant on their way to the source of the Nile.
kingdom-of-karagwe.o: Karagwe emerged around the 15th or 16th century, ruled by the [[e:hinda-dynasty|Hinda dynasty]] that also ruled [[s:kingdom-of-ankole|Ankole]] and other states of the region. It lay in the hills of north-western [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]], between [[e:lake-victoria|Lake Victoria]] and the [[e:kagera-river|Kagera river]], and traced its royal line to the legendary [[e:ruhinda|Ruhinda]].
kingdom-of-karagwe.r: The mukama (king) ruled with chiefs over pastoral [[e:bahima|Bahima]] and farming [[e:bairu|Bairu]]. Karagwe grew rich in the 19th century as a staging post on the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] linking [[s:kingdom-of-buganda|Buganda]] with [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] traders, trading [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] for cloth and firearms. King Rumanyika I hosted [[e:john-hanning-speke|John Hanning Speke]] and [[e:james-augustus-grant|James Grant]] in 1861, and their accounts made Karagwe known in [[e:europe|Europe]].
kingdom-of-karagwe.e: Succession wars and disease weakened the kingdom in the late 19th century, and it was absorbed into [[s:german-east-africa|German East Africa]] and then [[s:tanganyika-territory|Tanganyika Territory]] as a native authority. The chiefdom was abolished by the government of independent [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] in 1963.

kingdom-of-lapethos.t: North Cypriot kingdom where Phoenician kings ruled a Greek population in the Classical age, until Ptolemy I deposed the last king in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-lapethos.o: Lapethos lay on the north coast of [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] near modern [[e:lambousa|Lambousa]], facing [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. Greek tradition said it was founded by Praxandros from [[e:laconia|Laconia]] after the [[e:trojan-war|Trojan War]]. A city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE, it had close ties with the Phoenician coast.
kingdom-of-lapethos.r: In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE Lapethos was ruled by a dynasty with Phoenician names, such as Sidqmelek, who issued coins with Phoenician legends; Phoenician inscriptions from the town honour [[e:melqart|Melqart]] and other gods. The economy rested on farming, fishing and trade, and the city had a good harbour.
kingdom-of-lapethos.e: Its last king, Praxippos, supported [[e:antigonus-i-monophthalmus|Antigonus]] against [[e:ptolemy-i-soter|Ptolemy I]], who removed him in 312 BCE and annexed the kingdom. Lapethos continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman town, later called [[e:lambousa|Lambousa]], abandoned after Arab raids in the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.t: Self-governing Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary, a time of rapid growth and Budapest's rise, and of tension with the kingdom's many nationalities.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.o: [[e:austria|Austria's]] defeat by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1866 forced [[e:franz-joseph-i|Franz Joseph]] to settle with the Hungarian leaders [[e:ferenc-deak|Ferenc Deák]] and [[e:gyula-andrassy|Gyula Andrássy]]. The [[e:austro-hungarian-compromise-of-1867|Compromise of 1867]] restored [[e:hungary|Hungary's]] constitution and parliament, with the emperor crowned king, and created [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]], sharing only the monarch, foreign policy, the army and common finances. The [[e:croatian-hungarian-settlement|Croatian-Hungarian Settlement]] of 1868 gave [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia|Croatia-Slavonia]] autonomy within it.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.r: Parliament was dominated by the landed nobility and [[e:gentry|gentry]] under a narrow franchise, led by premiers such as [[e:kalman-tisza|Kálmán Tisza]] and [[e:istvan-tisza|István Tisza]]. [[e:pest-hungary|Pest]], [[e:buda|Buda]] and [[e:obuda|Óbuda]] merged into [[e:budapest|Budapest]] in 1873, which grew into a major industrial city, celebrated in the Millennium of 1896. Policies of [[e:magyarisation|Magyarisation]], such as the Apponyi school laws of 1907, angered Slovaks, [[e:romanians|Romanians]] and [[e:serbs|Serbs]].
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.e: Defeat in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] brought the [[e:aster-revolution|Aster Revolution]] of October 1918, and the [[s:hungarian-democratic-republic|Hungarian Democratic Republic]] was proclaimed in November. The [[e:treaty-of-trianon|Treaty of Trianon]] in 1920 transferred two-thirds of the former kingdom to its neighbours.

kingdom-of-damot.t: A powerful non-Christian kingdom of the southwestern Ethiopian highlands that rivalled Shewa and the Muslim sultanates in the 13th century.
kingdom-of-damot.o: Damot is known mainly from Ethiopian Christian traditions and hagiographies. In the 13th century it was a strong kingdom south of the [[e:blue-nile|Abay]] (Blue [[e:nile|Nile]]), and tradition says its ruler, remembered under the title Motalami, forced Muslim and Christian neighbours in [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]] to pay tribute.
kingdom-of-damot.r: Little is known of its government or society. Its people followed traditional religions, and saints' lives describe the missionary [[e:tekle-haymanot-saint|Tekle Haymanot]], founder of [[e:debre-libanos|Debre Libanos]], preaching there. Damot lay on routes that brought gold and slaves from the southwest to the highland and coastal markets.
kingdom-of-damot.e: The Solomonic emperor [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] conquered Damot around 1316 and made it a province of the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]]. The name lived on as a province, and from the 16th century [[e:oromo-migrations|Oromo migrations]] transformed the region.

kingdom-of-kashi.t: The ancient kingdom of Varanasi on the Ganges, an early centre of Vedic learning and a prize fought over by Kosala and Magadha.
kingdom-of-kashi.o: Kashi grew around [[e:varanasi|Varanasi]], where the [[e:varuna-river|Varuna]] meets the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]], in the Later Vedic period. The [[e:brihadaranyaka-upanishad|Brihadaranyaka Upanishad]] names a learned king, [[e:ajatashatru-of-kashi|Ajatashatru of Kashi]], who taught the [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] Gargya about the nature of the self. By the 6th century BCE it was listed among the sixteen mahajanapadas of Buddhist texts.
kingdom-of-kashi.r: Its wealth came from river trade, fine textiles and its sacred standing, for [[e:varanasi|Varanasi]] was already a place of pilgrimage and teaching. The [[e:jataka-tales|Jataka tales]] set many stories in the reigns of kings called Brahmadatta of Varanasi, and [[e:jainism|Jain]] tradition makes the 23rd tirthankara, [[e:parshvanatha|Parshvanatha]], the son of a Kashi king. The [[e:gautama-buddha|Buddha]] gave his first sermon at nearby [[e:sarnath|Sarnath]].
kingdom-of-kashi.e: Kashi lost a long rivalry with its neighbour, the [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kingdom of Kosala]], in the 6th century BCE. Revenue from a Kashi village formed the dowry of a Kosalan princess who married [[e:bimbisara|Bimbisara of Magadha]], and the quarrel over it led to war; the territory passed to [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] under [[e:ajatashatru|Ajatashatru]]. [[e:varanasi|Varanasi]] remains [[e:hinduism|Hinduism's]] holiest city.

kingdom-of-kosala.t: A great kingdom of the middle Ganges plain, ruled from Shravasti, where the Buddha spent much of his teaching life before Magadha swallowed it.
kingdom-of-kosala.o: Kosala appears in Later Vedic texts as a kingdom east of [[s:panchala|Panchala]], between the [[e:gomti-river|Gomti]] and the [[e:sarayu-river|Sarayu]] rivers, with early centres at [[e:ayodhya|Ayodhya]] and [[e:saketa|Saketa]]. Its kings claimed descent from the solar [[e:ikshvaku|Ikshvaku]] line, the lineage of [[e:rama|Rama]] in the [[e:ramayana|Ramayana]]. By the 7th and 6th centuries BCE it had become one of the strongest of the sixteen mahajanapadas, with its capital at [[e:shravasti|Shravasti]].
kingdom-of-kosala.r: King Mahakosala annexed the [[s:kingdom-of-kashi|Kingdom of Kashi]] and held the Shakya and Koliya republics as dependants. His son [[e:prasenajit|Prasenajit]] was a lay follower of the [[e:gautama-buddha|Buddha]], and the merchant [[e:anathapindika|Anathapindika]] gave the [[e:jetavana|Jetavana]] grove at [[e:shravasti|Shravasti]], where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons. Shravasti and [[e:saketa|Saketa]] were wealthy trading cities on the northern route. Kosala's rivalry with [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] was eased for a time by royal marriages.
kingdom-of-kosala.e: [[e:prasenajit|Prasenajit]] was overthrown by his son [[e:vidudabha|Vidudabha]], who destroyed the [[s:shakya-republic|Shakyas]] around the time of the [[e:gautama-buddha|Buddha]]'s death. Soon after, Kosala was absorbed by the [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Kingdom of Magadha]] under [[e:ajatashatru|Ajatashatru]] or his successors in the 5th century BCE. [[e:ayodhya|Ayodhya's]] place in the [[e:ramayana|Ramayana]] kept the name Kosala alive in Indian tradition.

kingdom-of-pylos.t: Mycenaean kingdom of Messenia whose burnt palace preserved more than a thousand Linear B tablets, the fullest record of a Bronze Age Greek state.
kingdom-of-pylos.o: Pylos grew on the Englianos ridge in western [[s:messene|Messenia]], where rich shaft and tholos tombs show an emerging elite by c. 1650 BCE, including the [[e:griffin-warrior-tomb|Griffin Warrior]] burial found in 2015. By the 14th and 13th centuries BCE its rulers had unified Messenia into a single kingdom divided into two provinces.
kingdom-of-pylos.r: The palace, linked by [[e:homer|Homer]] with King [[e:nestor|Nestor]], was headed by a wanax with a lawagetas below him. Its [[e:linear-b|Linear B]] archive records taxation of some 16 districts, landholding, bronze-smiths, [[e:flax|flax]] and perfumed oil production, rowers for the fleet and offerings to [[e:poseidon|Poseidon]], [[e:zeus|Zeus]], [[e:hera|Hera]] and the [[e:potnia|Potnia]]. Frescoes and a well-preserved throne room survive.
kingdom-of-pylos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire c. 1180 BCE, apparently while preparing coastal defences, and the region largely depopulated. Its tablets, baked by the fire, were found by [[e:carl-blegen|Carl Blegen]] in 1939 and helped [[e:michael-ventris|Michael Ventris]] show in 1952 that [[e:linear-b|Linear B]] was Greek.

kingdom-of-egypt.t: Egypt's constitutional monarchy under Fuad I and Farouk, independent in name but under British influence, overthrown by the Free Officers.
kingdom-of-egypt.o: [[e:britain|Britain's]] declaration of February 1922 ended the [[s:sultanate-of-egypt|Sultanate of Egypt]], recognising [[e:egypt|Egypt]] as independent while reserving defence, communications, foreign interests and [[e:sudan|Sudan]]. [[e:fuad-i-of-egypt|Fuad I]] took the title of king, and a constitution followed in 1923.
kingdom-of-egypt.r: Parliamentary politics were dominated by the struggle between the popular [[e:wafd-party|Wafd]] party, the palace and the British. The [[e:anglo-egyptian-treaty-of-1936|Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936]] kept British troops in the [[s:panama-canal-zone|Canal Zone]]. In 1942 British tanks surrounded [[e:abdeen-palace|Abdeen Palace]] to force [[e:farouk-of-egypt|Farouk]] to appoint a Wafd government, and the [[e:axis-powers|Axis]] advance was halted at [[e:el-alamein|El Alamein]]. Defeat in the 1948 war against [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] discredited the regime.
kingdom-of-egypt.e: After the [[e:cairo|Cairo]] riots of January 1952, the [[e:free-officers-movement-egypt|Free Officers]] led by [[e:muhammad-naguib|Muhammad Naguib]] and [[e:gamal-abdel-nasser|Gamal Abdel Nasser]] seized power in July. [[e:farouk-of-egypt|Farouk]] abdicated for his infant son [[e:fuad-ii-of-egypt|Fuad II]], and the monarchy was abolished in June 1953, creating the [[s:republic-of-egypt|Republic of Egypt]].

kingdom-of-baguirmi.t: Sultanate of the lower Chari river in Chad, a slave-raiding state caught between the larger powers of Bornu and Wadai.
kingdom-of-baguirmi.o: Baguirmi was founded in the early 16th century, traditionally in 1522, by a dynasty that established its capital at [[e:massenya|Massenya]], south-east of [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]]. Its rulers took the title mbang. [[e:islam|Islam]] was adopted at court under Mbang [[e:abdullah-of-baguirmi|Abdullah]], who reigned in the late 16th century.
kingdom-of-baguirmi.r: The mbang ruled with a court of officials, many of them [[e:eunuch|eunuchs]], and a cavalry force that raided the peoples to the south for slaves, who were traded north and used on Baguirmi farms. The kingdom paid tribute at times to the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]] and later to the [[s:wadai-empire|Wadai Empire]].
kingdom-of-baguirmi.e: In 1871 [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]] sacked [[e:massenya|Massenya]], and in the 1890s [[s:rabih-az-zubayrs-state|Rabih az-Zubayr]] devastated the country. Mbang Gaourang II accepted a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1897, and Baguirmi became part of French colonial [[e:chad|Chad]]. The sultanate survives as a traditional office.
