kingdom-of-brega.t: A kingdom of the southern Ui Neill on the fertile plain north of Dublin, home to Tara, Knowth and Newgrange and rival of Mide.
kingdom-of-brega.o: Brega emerged in the 7th century when the [[e:sil-naedo-slaine|Sil nAedo Slaine]], descendants of [[e:aed-slaine|Aed Slaine]] of the southern [[e:ui-neill|Ui Neill]], established themselves in the plain of Brega, stretching from the [[e:river-liffey|Liffey]] northwards across the [[e:river-boyne|Boyne]]. Their rulers made the ancient passage tomb at [[e:knowth|Knowth]] into a royal residence.
kingdom-of-brega.r: Brega's kings shared the kingship of [[e:hill-of-tara|Tara]] with [[s:kingdom-of-mide|Clann Cholmain]] and the northern [[e:ui-neill|Ui Neill]], holding it often in the 7th and early 8th centuries and once more under [[e:congalach-cnogba|Congalach Cnogba]] in the 10th. The kingdom split into northern and southern parts. It contained monasteries such as [[e:slane|Slane]], [[e:duleek|Duleek]] and [[e:monasterboice|Monasterboice]], and from the 9th century suffered heavy pressure from the Norse of the [[s:kingdom-of-dublin|Kingdom of Dublin]].
kingdom-of-brega.e: By the 11th century Brega was fragmented and dominated by Mide, [[e:dublin|Dublin]] and [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Leinster]]. Its lands passed into the [[s:lordship-of-meath|Lordship of Meath]] granted to [[e:hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath|Hugh de Lacy]] in 1172, and its name survives in Irish place-names.

kunihar-state.t: One of the smallest of the Simla Hill States, a Rajput chiefship near Shimla restored under British protection after the Gurkha wars.
kunihar-state.o: Tradition holds that the ruling family came from [[e:akhnoor|Akhnoor]] near [[e:jammu|Jammu]] and founded the state around 1154.
kunihar-state.r: Kunihar consisted of a few villages in the hills west of [[e:shimla|Shimla]], ruled by a Thakur or Rana. Like its neighbours it was occupied by the [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] in the early 19th century; little else is recorded of its history.
kunihar-state.e: The British restored the ruler by sanad in 1815. Kunihar merged into [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948 and is now in Solan district.

kingdom-of-belgium.t: The kingdom born of the 1830 revolution, an early industrial power and colonial ruler of the Congo, now a federal state and home of the EU's institutions.
kingdom-of-belgium.o: In August 1830 a revolt in [[e:brussels|Brussels]] against the [[s:united-kingdom-of-the-netherlands|United Kingdom of the Netherlands]] spread across the south. A provisional government declared independence in October, a congress adopted a liberal constitution in 1831, and [[e:leopold-i-of-belgium|Leopold of Saxe-Coburg]] became king. The [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] recognised [[e:belgium|Belgium]] in the [[e:treaty-of-london-1839|Treaty of London]] of 1839, which also guaranteed its neutrality.
kingdom-of-belgium.r: [[e:belgium|Belgium]] became continental [[e:europe|Europe's]] first industrial nation, with [[e:coal|coal]], iron and railways in [[e:wallonia|Wallonia]]. [[e:leopold-ii|Leopold II]] ruled the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]] as a personal possession, notorious for forced labour, until Belgium annexed it in 1908. [[e:germany|Germany]] invaded in 1914 and 1940; [[e:albert-i-of-belgium|King Albert I]] led resistance in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]]. Tension between French and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] speakers grew steadily.
kingdom-of-belgium.e: After 1945 [[e:belgium|Belgium]] co-founded [[e:benelux|Benelux]], [[e:nato|NATO]] and the [[e:european-communities|European Communities]], and [[e:brussels|Brussels]] hosts the EU and NATO headquarters. The Congo became independent in 1960. Language conflicts led to reforms that made Belgium a federal state of regions and communities in 1993.

kingdom-of-nikki.t: The leading Bariba kingdom of Borgu, famed for its cavalry aristocracy and the Gaani festival still celebrated in northern Benin.
kingdom-of-nikki.o: Nikki was founded by Wasangari horsemen who imposed their rule on [[e:bariba|Bariba]] farming communities of eastern [[e:borgu|Borgu]], probably in the 16th century. Its kings traced descent from Sunon Sero and through him to the legendary conqueror [[e:kisra-borgu-tradition|Kisra]]. Nikki came to be recognised as the most powerful of the Borgu states, alongside the [[s:kingdom-of-bussa|Kingdom of Bussa]].
kingdom-of-nikki.r: The Sina Boko, the king of Nikki, ruled with princes and Wasangari warriors who held provinces and lived from tribute and raiding. [[e:borgu|Borgu]] cavalry checked the [[s:oyo-empire|Oyo Empire]] and later the [[e:fula|Fulani]]; Sero Kpera of Nikki died fighting the [[s:ilorin-emirate|Ilorin]] forces in the 1830s. The annual Gaani festival renewed loyalty to the king.
kingdom-of-nikki.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and [[e:france|France]] raced to sign treaties at Nikki in 1894, and the Anglo-French Convention of 1898 assigned it to France. It became part of [[s:french-dahomey|French Dahomey]], and the king of Nikki remains a respected traditional ruler in [[e:benin-empire|Benin]].

kingdom-of-tylis.t: Celtic kingdom in eastern Thrace that extorted heavy tribute from Byzantium after the great Celtic invasion of 279 BCE.
kingdom-of-tylis.o: [[e:celts|Celts]] who had invaded the [[e:balkans|Balkans]] in 279 BCE, defeating [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]], settled in eastern [[e:thrace|Thrace]] under their leader [[e:comontorius|Comontorius]] around 277 BCE. They founded a kingdom with its capital at Tylis, whose exact location near the [[e:balkan-mountains|Haemus]] or [[e:strandzha|Strandzha]] mountains is still debated.
kingdom-of-tylis.r: The kingdom lived largely from tribute. According to [[e:polybius|Polybius]], [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] paid it ever larger sums, rising to 80 [[e:talent|talents]] a year. Celtic warriors ruled over a Thracian population, and coins of the last king, [[e:cavarus|Cavarus]], are known. Cavarus was praised as a statesman and mediated in the war between [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantium]] and [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] in 220 BCE.
kingdom-of-tylis.e: Around 212 BCE the local [[e:thracians|Thracians]] rose against Celtic rule and destroyed the kingdom. Thracian dynasts reasserted themselves in the region, which later came under Macedonian and Roman influence.

kingdom-of-northumbria.t: The kingdom of the Angles north of the Humber, home of Bede, Lindisfarne and the Northumbrian Renaissance, later carved up by the Vikings.
kingdom-of-northumbria.o: Northumbria grew out of the union of the [[s:kingdom-of-bernicia|Kingdom of Bernicia]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-deira|Kingdom of Deira]], which became lasting under [[e:oswiu|Oswiu]] after his victory over [[e:penda-of-mercia|Penda]] at the [[e:battle-of-the-winwaed|Winwaed]] in 655. At its height it stretched from the [[e:humber|Humber]] to the [[e:firth-of-forth|Firth of Forth]] and west to the [[e:irish-sea|Irish Sea]].
kingdom-of-northumbria.r: Northumbrian kings were Christian patrons of monasteries such as [[e:lindisfarne|Lindisfarne]], [[e:monkwearmouth-jarrow-abbey|Wearmouth-Jarrow]] and [[e:whitby-abbey|Whitby]], where the Synod of 664 chose Roman over Irish church practice. This produced the [[e:lindisfarne-gospels|Lindisfarne Gospels]], the [[e:codex-amiatinus|Codex Amiatinus]] and the works of [[e:bede|Bede]] and [[e:alcuin-of-york|Alcuin]]. The 8th century was marked by frequent royal murders and depositions.
kingdom-of-northumbria.e: Defeat by the [[e:picts|Picts]] at [[e:battle-of-dun-nechtain|Nechtansmere]] in 685 checked its northward growth, and [[e:vikings|Vikings]] sacked [[e:lindisfarne|Lindisfarne]] in 793. In 867 the [[e:great-heathen-army|Great Heathen Army]] took [[e:york|York]], creating the [[s:kingdom-of-york|Kingdom of York]], while English rulers held out at [[s:earldom-of-bamburgh|Bamburgh]]. The last Viking king, [[e:eric-bloodaxe|Eric Bloodaxe]], was expelled in 954.

kingdom-of-thomond.t: The O'Brien kingdom of North Munster, descendant of Brian Boru's power base, which kept its independence until 1543.
kingdom-of-thomond.o: Thomond arose from the [[e:dal-cais|Dal Cais]] lands in [[e:county-clare|Clare]] and [[e:limerick|Limerick]]. In 1118 the [[e:treaty-of-glanmire|Treaty of Glanmire]], imposed by [[e:toirdelbach-ua-conchobair|Turlough O'Connor]], split [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]], leaving the [[e:obrien-dynasty|O'Briens]] with the north, Tuadmumu. Their capital was Limerick, the former [[s:kingdom-of-limerick|Kingdom of Limerick]].
kingdom-of-thomond.r: The [[e:obrien-dynasty|O'Brien]] kings were patrons of churches such as [[e:holy-cross-abbey|Holy Cross]], [[e:killaloe|Killaloe]] and [[e:limerick|Limerick's]] cathedral, founded by [[e:domnall-mor-ua-briain|Domnall Mor O'Brien]]. After losing Limerick to the Normans in the 1190s, they ruled from Clonroad near [[e:ennis|Ennis]]. In 1318 [[e:muirchertach-o-briain-d-1343|Muirchertach O'Brien]] defeated the Normans at [[e:battle-of-dysert-odea|Dysert O'Dea]], preserving Gaelic rule west of the [[e:river-shannon|Shannon]].
kingdom-of-thomond.e: In 1543 [[e:murrough-obrien-1st-earl-of-thomond|Murrough O'Brien]] surrendered his kingship to [[e:henry-viii-of-england|Henry VIII]] and became Earl of Thomond under the [[s:kingdom-of-ireland|Kingdom of Ireland]]. His lands became [[e:county-clare|County Clare]] in the 1570s.

kasadi-sultanate.t: A dynasty of Yafa'i origin that ruled the Hadrami port of Mukalla until the Qu'aiti sultans took it in 1881.
kasadi-sultanate.o: The Kasadi were a family of the [[e:yafa|Yafa]] tribal confederation, whose men served as soldiers across [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]]. In the 18th century they established themselves as naqibs, or governors, of the port of [[e:mukalla|Mukalla]] on the coast of Hadramawt and ruled it as a small independent state.
kasadi-sultanate.r: [[e:mukalla|Mukalla]] was the main outlet of [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]] to the sea, and the Kasadi lived from customs on trade with [[e:india|India]], [[e:east-africa|East Africa]] and the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]], including slaves and dates. Their rule was contested by [[s:kathiri-sultanate|Kathiri]] and other [[e:yafa|Yafa]]'i rivals and depended on armed retainers. Little is recorded about their internal administration.
kasadi-sultanate.e: In the 19th century the Kasadi came into conflict with the rising [[s:quaiti-sultanate|Qu'aiti Sultanate]]. With British support the Qu'aiti took [[e:mukalla|Mukalla]] in 1881, and the Kasadi naqib went into exile in [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]]. Mukalla became the Qu'aiti capital.

kingdom-of-gojjam.t: A royal province of north-western Ethiopia whose rulers, Negus Tekle Haymanot and Ras Hailu, were among the empire's most powerful vassals.
kingdom-of-gojjam.o: In 1881 Emperor [[e:yohannes-iv|Yohannes IV]] crowned [[e:tekle-haymanot-of-gojjam|Ras Adal]] Tessema, the ruler of Gojjam, as Negus [[e:tekle-haymanot-saint|Tekle Haymanot]] of Gojjam and [[s:kingdom-of-kaffa|Kaffa]], partly to balance the power of [[e:menelik-ii|Menelik]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Kingdom of Shewa]]. The two kings soon clashed over the rich lands south of the [[e:blue-nile|Abay]], and Menelik defeated Tekle Haymanot at the [[e:battle-of-embabo|Battle of Embabo]] in 1882.
kingdom-of-gojjam.r: Gojjam was a highland province of farmers and [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] monasteries, with its capital at [[e:debre-markos|Debre Markos]]. Its king kept his own court and army and collected taxes and tribute. [[e:tekle-haymanot-of-gojjam|Tekle Haymanot]] fought at the [[e:battle-of-adwa|Battle of Adwa]] in 1896. His son [[e:hailu-tekle-haymanot|Ras Hailu]] [[e:tekle-haymanot-saint|Tekle Haymanot]] later ruled Gojjam as one of the empire's wealthiest lords.
kingdom-of-gojjam.e: In 1932 [[e:hailu-tekle-haymanot|Ras Hailu]] was arrested for helping the deposed emperor [[e:iyasu-v|Lij Iyasu]] escape, and [[e:haile-selassie|Haile Selassie]] ended Gojjam's autonomy, placing it under a governor and fully integrating it into the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]].

kel-adagh.t: The Tuareg confederation of the Adrar des Ifoghas mountains around Kidal, led by the Ifoghas lineage and central to Tuareg politics in Mali.
kel-adagh.o: The Kel Adagh, meaning the people of the mountain, formed in the [[e:adrar-des-ifoghas|Adrar des Ifoghas]] massif of north-eastern [[e:mali|Mali]]. By the 18th century the Ifoghas, a lineage of religious prestige, had become the leading group, providing the confederation's amenokal.
kel-adagh.r: The confederation united noble, [[e:vassal|vassal]] and dependent groups of [[e:camel|camel]] and goat herders who moved between [[e:well|wells]] and pastures in a harsh environment. It traded livestock and salt with the [[e:niger-river|Niger]] valley and the [[e:sahara|Sahara]], and maintained shifting relations with the [[s:kel-ahaggar|Kel Ahaggar]] and the [[s:iwellemmeden-kel-ataram|Iwellemmeden Kel Ataram]]. Islamic scholarship gave the Ifoghas authority.
kel-adagh.e: French forces occupied the [[e:adrar-des-ifoghas|Adrar des Ifoghas]] around 1908 to 1910 and ruled through the amenokal. The confederation became part of [[s:french-sudan|French Sudan]], and after independence [[e:kidal|Kidal]] was the centre of repeated [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] rebellions in [[e:mali|Mali]].

kingdom-of-adansi.t: Early Akan kingdom of the central forest, remembered as one of the first Akan states before its conquest by Denkyira.
kingdom-of-adansi.o: Adansi lay in the forest south of present-day [[e:kumasi|Kumasi]], with its capital at Fomena. [[e:akan|Akan]] tradition regards it as one of the earliest organised Akan states, and its name is linked in tradition with building, as its people were said to be the first to construct houses in the forest.
kingdom-of-adansi.r: Its rulers controlled gold mining and the trade routes from the central forest toward the coast and northern markets. Several [[e:akan|Akan]] clans trace their early migrations through Adansi, and its political forms, including the stool and matrilineal succession, were shared by later states.
kingdom-of-adansi.e: In the 17th century Adansi was conquered by [[s:denkyira|Denkyira]] and then passed under the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]]. Fomena later gave its name to the 1874 treaty that ended the Anglo-[[e:ashanti-empire|Ashanti]] war, and Adansi remains a traditional area in Ghana.

kingdom-of-derge.t: The leading kingdom of eastern Tibet (Kham), renowned for the Derge printing house and as the cradle of the 19th-century Rime religious movement.
kingdom-of-derge.o: The royal house of Derge claimed descent from [[e:gar-tongtsen|Gar Tongtsen]], minister of the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]]. The family rose in the 15th century around the [[s:sakya-regime|Sakya]] monastery of [[e:derge-gonchen-monastery|Lhundrup Teng]], which became the royal seat, and gradually extended its rule over large parts of the upper [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] valley in [[e:kham|Kham]].
kingdom-of-derge.r: Its kings combined secular and religious authority and ruled through hereditary officials over farming valleys and nomad pastures. King [[e:tenpa-tsering|Tenpa Tsering]] founded the [[e:derge-parkhang|Derge Parkhang]] [[e:printing-press|printing]] house in 1729, which carved woodblocks for the Buddhist canon still used today. In the 19th century Derge patronised the non-sectarian [[e:rime-movement|Rime movement]] of teachers such as [[e:jamgon-kongtrul|Jamgön Kongtrul]]. Derge recognised [[e:qing-empire|Qing]] suzerainty while remaining close to [[e:lhasa|Lhasa]].
kingdom-of-derge.e: From 1848 Derge was occupied by the warlord [[e:gonpo-namgyal|Gönpo Namgyal]] of Nyarong until [[e:lhasa|Lhasa's]] troops expelled him in 1865. In 1909 the [[e:qing-empire|Qing]] commander [[e:zhao-erfeng|Zhao Erfeng]] deposed the king and placed Derge under direct Chinese administration.

kingdom-of-kakongo.t: A small Kongo coastal kingdom between Loango and Ngoyo whose port of Malemba was a busy Atlantic slave-trading harbour.
kingdom-of-kakongo.o: Kakongo was one of the [[e:kongo-language|Kikongo]]-speaking kingdoms north of the [[e:congo-river|Congo]] estuary that recognised the senior [[s:kingdom-of-loango|Kingdom of Loango]] in early times. By the mid-16th century it had its own king, ruling from Kinguele, with lands between the coast and the [[e:mayombe|Mayombe]] forest.
kingdom-of-kakongo.r: Its sacred king was elected by senior lineages and surrounded by ritual restrictions, and regional chiefs controlled much of the land. In the 18th century the port of [[e:malembo|Malemba]] became a major market for French and English slavers, and the Abbe Proyart's history of [[s:kingdom-of-loango|Loango]] and Kakongo (1776), based on French missionaries' reports, described the court and customs.
kingdom-of-kakongo.e: With the end of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] Kakongo declined into a cluster of chiefdoms. In 1885 its lands were divided between [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]], where they formed part of [[s:portuguese-congo|Cabinda]], and the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]].

kingdom-of-italy.t: The united Italian monarchy of the House of Savoy, which completed unification, fought two world wars and fell to a referendum in 1946.
kingdom-of-italy.o: On 17 March 1861 the parliament in [[e:turin|Turin]] proclaimed [[e:victor-emmanuel-ii|Victor Emmanuel II]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]] king of [[e:italy|Italy]], after the annexation of [[e:lombardy|Lombardy]], central Italy and the [[s:kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies|Kingdom of the Two Sicilies]]. [[e:venetia|Venetia]] was added in 1866 and [[e:rome|Rome]] taken from the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]] in 1870.
kingdom-of-italy.r: The capital moved from [[e:turin|Turin]] to [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] in 1865 and to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 1871. Under the [[e:statuto-albertino|Statuto Albertino]], liberal governments led by [[e:agostino-depretis|Agostino Depretis]], [[e:francesco-crispi|Francesco Crispi]] and Giovanni Giolitti industrialised the north while millions emigrated. [[e:italy|Italy]] entered the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] in 1915. [[e:benito-mussolini|Benito Mussolini]] took power in 1922, built a Fascist dictatorship, signed the [[e:lateran-treaty|Lateran Treaty]] in 1929, conquered [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] in 1936 and allied with [[s:nazi-germany|Nazi Germany]].
kingdom-of-italy.e: Defeat led the king to dismiss [[e:benito-mussolini|Mussolini]] in 1943 and sign an armistice with the [[e:allies|Allies]]. On 2 June 1946 a referendum abolished the monarchy, creating the [[s:italian-republic|Italian Republic]].

cr.a: F l a n k e r

kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.t: Habsburg-ruled Kingdom of Hungary, from the narrow frontier strip of Royal Hungary to the reconquered kingdom that won self-government in 1867.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.o: After the death of [[e:louis-ii-of-hungary|Louis II]] at [[e:battle-of-mohacs|Mohács]] in 1526, a diet at [[e:bratislava|Pozsony]] elected [[e:ferdinand-i-holy-roman-emperor|Ferdinand of Habsburg]] king, against the rival [[e:john-zapolya|John Zápolya]]. The Ottoman capture of [[e:buda|Buda]] in 1541 left the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] with only a western and northern strip, [[e:royal-hungary|Royal Hungary]], governed from Pressburg, where diets met and kings were crowned.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.r: [[e:hungary|Hungary]] kept its own diet, counties and noble privileges while the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] controlled war and foreign affairs from [[e:vienna|Vienna]]. [[e:latin|Latin]] was the official language until 1844. Ottoman wars dominated until the reconquest of [[e:buda|Buda]] in 1686 and the [[e:treaty-of-karlowitz|Treaty of Karlowitz]] in 1699. Revolts by Bocskai, [[e:imre-thokoly|Thököly]] and Rákóczi defended Protestant and noble rights; the Reform Era brought [[e:istvan-szechenyi|Széchenyi]]'s modernisation.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.e: The revolution of 1848 and the war of independence were crushed in 1849 with Russian help, followed by direct rule from [[e:vienna|Vienna]]. Defeat by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1866 forced the [[e:austro-hungarian-compromise-of-1867|Compromise of 1867]], which created [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] and the self-governing [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1867-1918).

kingdom-of-lagos.t: Yoruba island kingdom under the authority of Benin that became a major 19th century slave port before Britain annexed it in 1861.
kingdom-of-lagos.o: [[e:lagos|Lagos]], known locally as Eko, began as a settlement of [[e:awori|Awori]] [[e:yoruba|Yoruba]] on the lagoon islands. In the 16th or early 17th century the [[s:benin-empire|Benin Empire]] established a war camp there, and Ashipa, recognised by the [[e:oba-dynasty|Oba of Benin]], founded the line of [[e:oba-of-lagos|Obas of Lagos]].
kingdom-of-lagos.r: The [[e:oba-dynasty|Oba]] ruled with [[e:yoruba|Yoruba]] white-cap chiefs and paid tribute to [[e:benin-empire|Benin]]. [[e:lagos|Lagos]] grew into a leading slave port in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. A succession struggle between [[e:kosoko|Kosoko]] and his uncle [[e:akitoye|Akitoye]] drew in the British, who bombarded Lagos in 1851, deposed Kosoko and installed Akitoye.
kingdom-of-lagos.e: Under pressure from [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], [[e:oba-dynasty|Oba]] [[e:dosunmu|Dosunmu]] signed a treaty ceding [[e:lagos|Lagos]] in 1861, and it became [[s:lagos-colony|Lagos Colony]]. Lagos grew into [[e:nigeria|Nigeria's]] largest city, and the [[e:oba-of-lagos|Oba of Lagos]] remains its traditional ruler.

kaulonia.t: Achaean Greek city on the Calabrian coast, a dependency of Croton, destroyed by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 389 BCE.
kaulonia.o: Kaulonia was founded in the 7th century BCE on the Ionian coast of [[e:calabria|Calabria]], near modern Monasterace Marina, by Achaean settlers, probably sent out by [[s:croton|Croton]], to secure its southern border against [[s:locri-epizephyrii|Locri]].
kaulonia.r: Kaulonia remained closely tied to [[s:croton|Croton]]. Its [[e:silver|silver]] coins, showing [[e:apollo|Apollo]] carrying a small running figure and a deer, are among the finest of [[e:magna-graecia|Magna Graecia]]. Excavations have uncovered a Doric temple, walls and houses, and a large floor mosaic with a dragon of the 3rd century BCE. Little is known of its government.
kaulonia.e: After defeating the [[s:italiote-league|Italiote League]] at the [[e:battle-of-the-elleporus|Elleporus]] river in 389 BCE, [[e:dionysius-i-of-syracuse|Dionysius I]] took Kaulonia, moved its people to [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] and gave its land to [[s:locri-epizephyrii|Locri]]. A smaller town revived later but was destroyed during the wars with [[e:pyrrhus-of-epirus|Pyrrhus]] and [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]], and by the Roman period the site was deserted.

kingdom-of-ladakh.t: A Tibetan Buddhist kingdom high in the western Himalaya that lasted nine centuries, ruled from Leh by the Namgyal kings until the Dogra conquest.
kingdom-of-ladakh.o: After the collapse of the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]], [[e:kyide-nyimagon|Nyimagon]], a descendant of the Tibetan royal line, founded a kingdom in western [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] around 930. His son received Maryul, the upper [[e:indus|Indus]] valley around Leh, which became the core of Ladakh. [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] revived there in the 11th century, when the translator [[e:rinchen-zangpo|Rinchen Zangpo]] is credited with founding many temples.
kingdom-of-ladakh.r: The kingdom lived on trade between [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]], [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] and [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]], especially in [[e:shawl|pashmina]] wool, and on irrigated barley farming. Monasteries such as [[e:alchi-monastery|Alchi]], [[e:hemis-monastery|Hemis]] and [[e:thiksey-monastery|Thiksey]] held great influence. The [[e:namgyal-dynasty|Namgyal dynasty]] took power in the 15th century; its greatest king, [[e:sengge-namgyal|Sengge Namgyal]], built [[e:leh-palace|Leh Palace]] and patronised Hemis. After a war with [[e:tibet|Tibet]], the [[e:treaty-of-tingmosgang|Treaty of Tingmosgang]] of 1684 fixed Ladakh's borders, with Mughal help on Ladakh's side.
kingdom-of-ladakh.e: Between 1834 and 1842 the [[e:dogras|Dogra]] general [[e:zorawar-singh|Zorawar Singh]] conquered Ladakh for [[e:gulab-singh|Gulab Singh]], and it became part of the princely state of [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir]]. The [[e:namgyal-dynasty|Namgyal]] family kept the palace at [[e:stok-palace|Stok]], and Ladakh is now a union territory of [[e:india|India]].

cr.a: A.H. Francke, S.S.Gergan and F.M. Hassnan

kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.t: Akan kingdom of the eastern Gold Coast forest, a partner of Akyem Abuakwa in the wars against Akwamu and Ashanti.
kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.o: Akyem Kotoku was one of the three [[s:akyem-abuakwa|Akyem]] states formed in the Birim and [[e:pra-river|Pra]] forests by the 17th century, alongside Akyem Abuakwa and Akyem Bosome. Its ruling house traced descent from the [[e:akan|Akan]] clans that migrated south from the region of [[s:kingdom-of-adansi|Adansi]].
kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.r: The Kotokuhene ruled with divisional chiefs, queen mothers and councils in the usual [[e:akan|Akan]] form. The kingdom mined and traded gold. In 1730 it joined [[s:akyem-abuakwa|Akyem Abuakwa]] and the Ga in defeating [[s:akwamu|Akwamu]], and it fought the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]] repeatedly over the following century, at times being driven from its lands.
kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.e: Akyem Kotoku allied with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] against [[e:ashanti-empire|Ashanti]] and came under British rule with the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast Colony]] in 1874. Its capital was fixed at [[e:akim-oda|Oda]] in the 19th century, and the Kotokuhene still reigns there.

kingdom-of-abemama.t: A small Gilbertese kingdom whose rulers conquered neighbouring atolls and controlled the copra trade, famed through Robert Louis Stevenson's portrait of Tem Binoka.
kingdom-of-abemama.o: The chiefs of Abemama in the central [[e:gilbert-islands|Gilbert Islands]] built up their power in the mid-19th century. [[e:tem-baiteke|Tem Baiteke]], using firearms obtained from traders, brought the nearby atolls of [[e:aranuka|Aranuka]] and [[e:kuria-kiribati|Kuria]] under his rule, creating a small island kingdom unlike the council-based societies of the other [[e:humphrey-gilbert|Gilberts]].
kingdom-of-abemama.r: Under [[e:tem-binoka|Tem Binoka]], who succeeded in the 1870s, Abemama was an [[e:autocracy|autocracy]]: the king controlled land, labour and trade, and he dealt directly with European ships, selling copra and buying goods for himself. Foreign residents were strictly limited. [[e:robert-louis-stevenson|Robert Louis Stevenson]], who stayed on the island in 1889, described Binoka in 'In the South Seas' as a shrewd and formidable ruler. Little else is documented in detail.
kingdom-of-abemama.e: [[e:tem-binoka|Binoka]] died in 1891, and in 1892 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] declared a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the [[e:gilbert-islands|Gilbert Islands]], absorbing Abemama into what became the [[s:gilbert-and-ellice-islands|Gilbert and Ellice Islands]]. Captain Davis of HMS Royalist proclaimed the protectorate there. The atoll is now part of [[e:kiribati|Kiribati]].

kingdom-of-ennarea.t: A gold-rich kingdom of south-western Ethiopia beyond the Gibe river that paid tribute to the emperors and briefly adopted Christianity.
kingdom-of-ennarea.o: Ennarea emerged by the 14th century among the Gonga-speaking peoples of the [[e:gibe-river|Gibe]] region, related to the people of the [[s:kingdom-of-kaffa|Kingdom of Kaffa]]. Ethiopian chronicles record it as a tributary land from the 15th century, valued as the main source of the gold and civet that reached the highlands and the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]].
kingdom-of-ennarea.r: Ennarea was ruled by a sacred king who traded gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], slaves and [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] northward. Its rulers paid tribute in gold to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]], and in the late 16th century, under Emperor [[e:sarsa-dengel|Sarsa Dengel]], its king and court were baptised. Portuguese [[e:jesuits|Jesuits]] passed through in the early 17th century, describing it as a major market.
kingdom-of-ennarea.e: Cut off from the highlands by the [[e:oromo-migrations|Oromo migrations]], Ennarea was gradually overrun, and in the early 18th century its old dynasty fled south to [[s:kingdom-of-kaffa|Kaffa]]. [[e:oromo|Oromo]] rulers later founded [[s:limmu-ennarea|Limmu-Ennarea]] on its former territory.

kingdom-of-iraq.t: The Hashemite monarchy that ruled Iraq from 1921 until the revolution of 1958, balancing British influence, Arab nationalism and a divided society.
kingdom-of-iraq.o: [[e:faisal-i-of-iraq|Faisal I]], son of [[e:hussein-bin-ali-king-of-hejaz|Sharif Hussein]] of [[e:mecca|Mecca]] and leader of the Arab Revolt, was crowned king of [[e:iraq|Iraq]] in August 1921 under the British mandate. The monarchy gained formal independence when [[s:mandatory-iraq|Mandatory Iraq]] ended in 1932.
kingdom-of-iraq.r: [[e:iraq|Iraq]] was a [[e:constitutional-monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] with a parliament dominated by landowners, tribal sheikhs and ex-Ottoman officers, while [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] kept bases and influence. [[e:faisal-i-of-iraq|Faisal I]] died in 1933 and was followed by [[e:ghazi|Ghazi]] and the boy king [[e:faisal-ii-of-iraq|Faisal II]], under the regent [[e:abd-al-ilah|Abd al-Ilah]]. The period saw the [[e:simele-massacre|Simele massacre]] of [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyrians]] in 1933, the Arab world's first military coup in 1936, and in 1941 [[e:rashid-ali-al-gaylani|Rashid Ali]]'s pro-[[e:axis-powers|Axis]] coup, the [[e:anglo-iraqi-war|Anglo-Iraqi War]] and the [[e:farhud|Farhud]] pogrom against [[e:baghdad|Baghdad's]] [[e:jews|Jews]]. Oil revenue funded development, and [[e:nuri-al-said|Nuri al-Said]] dominated politics.
kingdom-of-iraq.e: In 1955 [[e:iraq|Iraq]] joined the [[e:baghdad-pact|Baghdad Pact]], and in 1958 it formed the [[s:arab-federation|Arab Federation]] with [[s:hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan|Jordan]]. On 14 July 1958 army officers led by [[e:abd-al-karim-qasim|Abd al-Karim Qasim]] overthrew the monarchy; [[e:faisal-ii-of-iraq|Faisal II]] and much of the royal family were killed, and the [[s:republic-of-iraq|Republic of Iraq]] was proclaimed.

karakalpakstan.t: The autonomous republic of the Karakalpak people on the lower Amu Darya, now part of Uzbekistan and at the heart of the Aral Sea disaster.
karakalpakstan.o: The [[e:karakalpaks|Karakalpaks]], a [[e:kipchak-languages|Kipchak Turkic]] people living in the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]] delta under the [[s:khanate-of-khiva|Khanate of Khiva]], received their own [[e:karakalpak-autonomous-oblast|Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast]] in 1925, created from lands of the [[s:khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic|Khorezm People's Soviet Republic]] and attached to the [[s:kazakh-assr|Kazakh ASSR]]. In 1932 it became the Karakalpak ASSR within [[e:russia|Russia]], and in 1936 it was transferred to the [[s:uzbek-ssr|Uzbek SSR]].
karakalpakstan.r: Its capital moved from [[e:turtkul|Turtkul]] to [[e:nukus|Nukus]] in 1939. The economy was based on irrigated [[e:cotton|cotton]] and [[e:rice|rice]], along with fishing on the [[e:aral-sea|Aral Sea]]. Massive Soviet irrigation from the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]] caused the sea to shrink from the 1960s, destroying the fishing industry of [[e:moynaq|Moynaq]] and bringing salt storms, polluted water and high rates of disease. The [[e:savitsky-museum|Savitsky museum]] in Nukus preserved banned Soviet avant-garde art.
karakalpakstan.e: Karakalpakstan declared [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] in 1990 and joined independent [[s:uzbekistan|Uzbekistan]] in 1993 as a sovereign republic with a constitutional right to secede. In 2022 proposals to remove that right sparked deadly protests in [[e:nukus|Nukus]], and the plan was withdrawn.

cr.a: No machine-readable author provided. Urmas assumed (based on copyright claims).

kingdom-of-gobir.t: Warlike northern Hausa kingdom whose clash with the scholar Usman dan Fodio set off the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate.
kingdom-of-gobir.o: [[e:gobir|Gobir]], one of the [[s:hausa-kingdoms|Hausa Bakwai]], is believed to have formed further north, near the Air massif, and moved south under [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] pressure. Its rulers were known as the frontier guards of Hausaland. By the 15th century it occupied the lands of present-day southern [[e:niger-river|Niger]] and north-western [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]].
kingdom-of-gobir.r: [[e:gobir|Gobir]] was a military state relying on cavalry. In 1762 its king Babari sacked [[e:birnin-zamfara|Birnin Zamfara]] and moved Gobir's capital to [[e:alkalawa|Alkalawa]]. Its rulers were Muslim but tolerated older practices, which the [[e:fula|Fulani]] scholar [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio]], once tutor at the court of [[e:bawa-jan-gwarzo|Bawa Jan Gwarzo]], condemned in his preaching.
kingdom-of-gobir.e: When Sarkin [[e:gobir|Gobir]] [[e:yunfa|Yunfa]] moved against [[e:usman-dan-fodio|dan Fodio's]] community in 1804, the scholar declared [[e:jihad|jihad]]. [[e:alkalawa|Alkalawa]] fell in 1808 and Yunfa was killed. Gobir loyalists withdrew north and founded the [[s:sultanate-of-tsibiri|Sultanate of Tsibiri]], and the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]] took over the old Gobir lands.

kingdom-of-rheged.t: A British kingdom of the 'Old North' around the Solway, celebrated in Welsh poetry for King Urien and his battles against the Angles.
kingdom-of-rheged.o: Rheged emerged in the 6th century among the Brittonic kingdoms of northern [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. Its location is uncertain, but scholars usually place it around [[e:carlisle|Carlisle]], [[e:cumbria|Cumbria]] and [[s:lordship-of-galloway|Galloway]]. Its fame rests on poems attributed to [[e:taliesin|Taliesin]] praising [[e:urien-rheged|Urien Rheged]], and on the [[e:historia-brittonum|Historia Brittonum]].
kingdom-of-rheged.r: [[e:urien-rheged|Urien]] is remembered as a leader of a coalition of British kings that besieged the [[e:angles|Angles]] of [[s:kingdom-of-bernicia|Bernicia]] on [[e:lindisfarne|Lindisfarne]] in the late 6th century, before he was murdered by a rival. Welsh tradition remembers the court as a centre of bardic patronage. Its society and economy are otherwise almost unknown.
kingdom-of-rheged.e: Rheged seems to have passed peacefully to [[s:kingdom-of-northumbria|Northumbria]], perhaps through the marriage of [[e:oswiu|Oswiu]] to Rhiainfellt, a descendant of [[e:urien-rheged|Urien]], around 638. Its memory lived on in Welsh poetry and Arthurian romance, where Urien and his son Owain became famous figures.

kingdom-of-tonga.t: The only Pacific island state never formally colonised, a constitutional monarchy founded by George Tupou I that still rules today.
kingdom-of-tonga.o: Tonga had long been ruled through the sacred [[s:tu-i-tonga-empire|Tuʻi Tonga Empire]] and related chiefly lines, but civil wars broke out in the early 19th century. [[e:george-tupou-i|Tāufaʻāhau]], a chief from Haʻapai converted by Wesleyan missionaries, united the islands by 1845 and took the name George Tupou I, with [[e:nukualofa|Nukuʻalofa]] as his capital.
kingdom-of-tonga.r: [[e:george-tupou-i|George Tupou I]] issued codes freeing commoners from chiefly obligations in 1862 and granted a constitution in 1875, assisted by the missionary [[e:shirley-baker|Shirley Baker]], which remains in force in amended form; later land laws guaranteed every adult male a plot. The [[s:tu-i-tonga-empire|Tuʻi Tonga]] line was ended in 1865. [[e:methodism|Methodism]] became the dominant faith. From 1900 to 1970 Tonga was a British protected state, governing itself internally, and Queen [[e:salote-tupou-iii|Sālote Tupou III]] became widely admired.
kingdom-of-tonga.e: Tonga regained full independence in 1970 and joined the Commonwealth. Riots in 2006 hastened reforms, and since 2010 most of parliament has been elected by the people. King [[e:tupou-vi|Tupou VI]] has reigned since 2012.

kanoman-sultanate.t: Junior branch of the divided Cirebon Sultanate, ruled by the Sultan Anom from a palace in the heart of old Cirebon.
kanoman-sultanate.o: Kanoman was created in 1677 when [[e:sultan-ageng-tirtayasa|Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa]] of the [[s:banten-sultanate|Banten Sultanate]] partitioned [[e:cirebon|Cirebon]] among the sons of [[e:panembahan-girilaya|Panembahan Girilaya]], who had died as a hostage of [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]]. The younger son, Pangeran Kartawijaya, became [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Anom, the junior sultan, alongside his elder brother in the [[s:kasepuhan-sultanate|Kasepuhan Sultanate]], and built the [[e:keraton-kanoman|Keraton Kanoman]] as his seat.
kanoman-sultanate.r: The two sultans shared authority over [[e:cirebon|Cirebon]], a port and pilgrimage centre around the grave of [[e:sunan-gunung-jati|Sunan Gunung Jati]], and rivalry between their houses invited outside arbitration. From 1681 both accepted the protection of the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]], which controlled their trade in [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:indigo|indigo]] and textiles. A further split in 1807 created the Kacirebonan line.
kanoman-sultanate.e: Reforms under [[e:herman-willem-daendels|Herman Willem Daendels]] and the British during [[s:british-java|British Java]] removed the sultans political powers by 1815, leaving them pensions and ceremonial roles. The [[e:keraton-kanoman|Keraton Kanoman]] survives, still hosting traditional rites and markets.

kingdom-of-cochin.t: The Kerala kingdom of Kochi, whose early alliance with the Portuguese made its harbour the first European foothold in India and whose rulers reigned until 1949.
kingdom-of-cochin.o: The ruling house, the Perumpadappu Swaroopam, emerged as one of the successor chiefdoms after the [[s:chera-perumals-of-makotai|Chera Perumals of Makotai]] collapsed in the early 12th century. In the 14th century, after a flood of the [[e:periyar-river|Periyar]] opened a new harbour, the dynasty made [[e:kochi|Kochi]] its centre, and the port grew as older [[e:muziris|Muziris]] declined.
kingdom-of-cochin.r: [[e:kochi|Cochin's]] rulers were long overshadowed by the [[e:zamorin|Zamorins]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-calicut|Kingdom of Calicut]], so in 1500 they welcomed the Portuguese, who built [[e:fort-manuel|Fort Manuel]] at Kochi in 1503. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] replaced them in 1663. [[e:pepper|Pepper]] and [[e:spice-trade|spices]] drove the economy, and Kochi was home to Syrian Christians, [[e:jews|Jews]] and Konkani merchants. [[e:sakthan-thampuran|Sakthan Thampuran]] (r. 1790–1805) curbed the nobles and rebuilt [[e:thrissur|Thrissur]].
kingdom-of-cochin.e: After invasions by Mysore, [[e:kochi|Cochin]] became a British subsidiary ally from 1791 and was known for its schools and administration. In 1949 it merged with [[s:travancore|Travancore]] to form [[s:travancore-cochin|Travancore-Cochin]], which became part of [[e:kerala|Kerala]] in 1956.

kingdom-of-kano.t: The largest Hausa kingdom, a walled market city whose dyed cloth and leather were traded across the Sahara and the Sudan.
kingdom-of-kano.o: The [[e:kano-chronicle|Kano Chronicle]] dates the kingdom to [[e:bagauda|Bagauda]], said to have become king in 999 among communities of farmers and ironworkers around [[e:dala-hill|Dala hill]]. Over the following centuries the rulers extended their authority over the surrounding plain and built the earthen walls that enclosed farmland as well as the city, making [[e:kano|Kano]] defensible in long sieges.
kingdom-of-kano.r: [[e:islam|Islam]] was adopted at court under [[e:ali-yaji|Ali Yaji]] in the 14th century, brought by [[e:wangara|Wangara]] traders from [[e:mali|Mali]]. [[e:muhammad-rumfa|Muhammad Rumfa]], ruling in the late 15th century, built the [[e:gidan-rumfa|Gidan Rumfa]] palace and the Kurmi market and took advice from the scholar al-Maghili on Islamic government. [[e:kano|Kano]] prospered on textiles, [[e:indigo|indigo]] dyeing, leather and the caravan trade, at times paying tribute to the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]].
kingdom-of-kano.e: In 1805 [[e:fula|Fulani]] reformers of [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio's]] [[e:jihad|jihad]] drove out the last [[e:hausa|Hausa]] king, [[e:muhammad-alwali-ii|Muhammad Alwali II]], and [[e:kano|Kano]] became the [[s:kano-emirate|Kano Emirate]] within the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]]. The city remained the commercial heart of northern [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]], and its emir still reigns.

kwantung-leased-territory.t: Japan's foothold at the tip of the Liaodong peninsula, base of the South Manchuria Railway and of the Kwantung Army that seized Manchuria in 1931.
kwantung-leased-territory.o: By the [[e:treaty-of-portsmouth|Treaty of Portsmouth]] in 1905 [[e:japan|Japan]] took over [[e:russia|Russia's]] lease of [[s:kwantung-oblast|Kwantung Oblast]], including [[e:lushunkou|Port Arthur]] (Ryojun) and [[e:dalian|Dalny]] (Dairen), together with the railway south of [[e:changchun|Changchun]]. A [[e:kwantung-government-general|Kwantung Government-General]] was set up in 1906 under [[e:oshima-yoshimasa|Ōshima Yoshimasa]].
kwantung-leased-territory.r: [[e:dalian|Dairen]] became one of [[e:east-asia|East Asia's]] busiest ports and the headquarters of the [[e:south-manchuria-railway|South Manchuria Railway Company]], which ran mines, hotels, research bureaus and towns along its line. The Twenty-One Demands of 1915 extended the lease to ninety-nine years. The garrison, renamed the [[e:kwantung-army|Kwantung Army]] in 1919, acted with growing independence and in 1931 staged the [[e:mukden-incident|Mukden Incident]], leading to the creation of [[s:manchukuo|Manchukuo]].
kwantung-leased-territory.e: Soviet troops occupied the territory in August 1945. The [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] kept a naval base at [[e:lushunkou|Port Arthur]] until 1955, when the area was handed to the [[s:peoples-republic-of-china|People's Republic of China]]; it is now part of [[e:dalian|Dalian]].
kwantung-leased-territory.re: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, State Shinto

kingdom-of-iberia.t: The eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli, centred on Mtskheta, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century and laid the foundations of Georgian statehood and letters.
kingdom-of-iberia.o: Georgian chronicles credit [[e:pharnavaz-i-of-iberia|Pharnavaz I]] with uniting [[s:kingdom-of-kartli|Kartli]] around 302 BCE after the collapse of Achaemenid power, establishing his seat at [[e:mtskheta|Mtskheta]] and organising the land into duchies. Classical authors knew the kingdom as [[e:iberia|Iberia]], a well-organised state on the [[e:kura-river|Mtkvari]] river guarding key passes across the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]].
kingdom-of-iberia.r: Kings ruled through regional eristavis, with a priestly and military aristocracy above a farming population. [[e:iberia|Iberia]] balanced between [[e:rome|Rome]] and [[e:persia|Persia]], submitting to [[e:pompey|Pompey]] after his invasion in 65 BCE and later serving as a Roman client. King [[e:mirian-iii-of-iberia|Mirian III]] adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in the 330s through the mission of St [[e:saint-nino|Nino]], and the Georgian alphabet appeared by the 5th century.
kingdom-of-iberia.e: [[e:vakhtang-i-of-iberia|Vakhtang I Gorgasali]] fought the [[e:persians|Persians]] and is traditionally credited with founding [[e:tbilisi|Tbilisi]], which became the capital under his successors, but Sasanian pressure grew. In 580 the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] abolished the monarchy, and the land passed to local aristocrats who formed the [[s:principality-of-iberia|Principality of Iberia]].

kingdom-of-valencia.t: A realm of the Crown of Aragon created by James I's conquest, famed for its rice and silk, its 15th-century golden age and its own laws.
kingdom-of-valencia.o: [[e:james-i-of-aragon|James I of Aragon]] conquered the [[s:third-taifa-of-valencia|Third Taifa of Valencia]] between 1232 and 1245, taking the city in 1238. He made it a separate kingdom with its own legal code, the [[e:furs-of-valencia|Furs of Valencia]], rather than attaching it to [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] or [[s:principality-of-catalonia|Catalonia]].
kingdom-of-valencia.r: Catalan and Aragonese settlers lived alongside a large Muslim population that farmed the irrigated [[e:huerta|huertas]], producing [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and [[e:silk|silk]]. In the 15th century [[e:valencia|Valencia]] was the Crown's largest city, building the Silk Exchange and producing writers such as [[e:ausias-march|Ausiàs March]] and [[e:joanot-martorell|Joanot Martorell]]. The [[e:revolt-of-the-brotherhoods|Germanies]] revolt of 1519-1523 and the expulsion of the [[e:moriscos|Moriscos]] in 1609 brought upheaval.
kingdom-of-valencia.e: [[e:valencia|Valencia]] backed the [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] claimant in the [[e:war-of-the-spanish-succession|War of the Spanish Succession]]. After the [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] victory at [[e:battle-of-almansa|Almansa]] in 1707, Philip V abolished its [[e:fur-trade|Furs]] by the [[e:nueva-planta-decrees|Nueva Planta decrees]], absorbing it into [[s:bourbon-spain|Bourbon Spain]].

kingdom-of-mide.t: The midland kingdom around the sacred hill of Uisnech, ruled by the Clann Cholmain kings who often held the kingship of Tara.
kingdom-of-mide.o: Mide formed in the 6th century as the southern [[e:ui-neill|Ui Neill]] dynasties established themselves in the Irish midlands. The Clann Cholmain branch, descended from [[e:colman-mor|Colman Mor]], emerged as its dominant line by the 8th century, ruling in what is now [[e:county-westmeath|Westmeath]] with [[e:hill-of-uisneach|Uisnech]] as its symbolic centre.
kingdom-of-mide.r: Clann Cholmain kings alternated the kingship of [[e:hill-of-tara|Tara]] with the northern [[e:ui-neill|Ui Neill]]. [[e:mael-sechnaill-mac-maele-ruanaid|Mael Sechnaill mac Maele Ruanaid]] and [[e:mael-sechnaill-mac-domnaill|Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill]] were among the most powerful kings in Ireland. The kingdom contained great monasteries such as [[e:durrow-abbey|Durrow]] and [[e:clonard-abbey|Clonard]], and royal sites at [[e:lough-ennell|Lough Ennell]].
kingdom-of-mide.e: After [[e:brian-boru|Brian Boru's]] rise, Mide was repeatedly partitioned by rival provincial kings. In 1172 [[e:henry-ii-of-england|Henry II]] granted it to [[e:hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath|Hugh de Lacy]], creating the [[s:lordship-of-meath|Lordship of Meath]], and the native line survived only as minor lords.

kizzuwatna.t: Kizzuwatna, a Hurrian-Luwian kingdom of the Cilician plain, through whose priests Hurrian gods and rituals entered Hittite religion.
kizzuwatna.o: Kizzuwatna arose in the plain of [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]] and the [[e:taurus-mountains|Taurus]] mountains after the Hittite [[s:old-kingdom-of-egypt|Old Kingdom]] weakened in the 16th century BCE. Its kings ruled from [[e:kummanni|Kummanni]] and other centres such as [[e:adana|Adaniya]] and [[e:lawazantiya|Lawazantiya]], and balanced between the [[e:hittite-empire|Hittites]] and the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]].
kizzuwatna.r: Its kings, such as [[e:isputahsu|Isputahsu]], [[e:pilliya|Pilliya]] and [[e:sunassura|Sunassura]], concluded treaties with Hittite rulers and with [[e:idrimi|Idrimi]] of [[s:kingdom-of-mukish|Mukish]]. The population mixed Luwian and Hurrian elements, and its temples of [[e:teshub|Teshub]] and [[e:hebat|Hebat]] and its priests specialised in purification rituals.
kizzuwatna.e: Around 1400 BCE [[e:sunassura|Sunassura]] accepted Hittite overlordship, and Kizzuwatna was soon absorbed into the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]]. Its cults passed to the Hittite court; Queen [[e:puduhepa|Puduhepa]] was a priest's daughter from [[e:lawazantiya|Lawazantiya]]. The region later became Que.

kingdom-of-elmet.t: Small British kingdom around Leeds that held out against the Angles until Edwin of Northumbria expelled its king Ceretic around 617.
kingdom-of-elmet.o: Elmet emerged after Roman rule ended as a British kingdom in the area of modern [[e:west-yorkshire|West Yorkshire]], between the [[e:pennines|Pennines]] and the [[e:vale-of-york|Vale of York]]. It is remembered in place names such as [[e:sherburn-in-elmet|Sherburn-in-Elmet]] and [[e:barwick-in-elmet|Barwick-in-Elmet]], and a 6th-century memorial stone at [[e:llanaelhaearn|Llanaelhaearn]] in [[s:kingdom-of-gwynedd|Gwynedd]] names a man of Elmet.
kingdom-of-elmet.r: Very little is known of its government. Welsh poetry praises a king [[e:gwallawg-ap-lleenog|Gwallawg]], possibly of Elmet, who fought alongside [[e:urien-rheged|Urien of Rheged]] against the [[e:angles|Angles]]. The kingdom survived surrounded by the growing Anglian powers of [[s:kingdom-of-deira|Deira]] and [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]], perhaps protected by its wooded and marshy terrain and by dyke systems such as those near [[e:barwick-in-elmet|Barwick]].
kingdom-of-elmet.e: The [[e:historia-brittonum|Historia Brittonum]] records that [[e:edwin-of-northumbria|Edwin of Northumbria]] seized Elmet and expelled its king [[e:ceretic-of-elmet|Ceretic]], usually dated around 617. The district appears in the [[e:tribal-hidage|Tribal Hidage]] as the Elmetsæte, and its people were absorbed into [[s:kingdom-of-northumbria|Northumbria]].

kingdom-of-sumenep.t: The kingdom of eastern Madura, whose first ruler Arya Wiraraja helped found Majapahit and whose princes ruled until 1883.
kingdom-of-sumenep.o: Tradition dates Sumenep's founding to 1269, when [[e:kertanegara|Kertanegara of Singhasari]] appointed [[e:arya-wiraraja|Arya Wiraraja]] as its adipati. Wiraraja is a well-known figure in Javanese chronicles: he advised [[e:jayakatwang|Jayakatwang]] and then helped [[e:raden-wijaya|Raden Wijaya]] defeat him and expel the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1293, opening the way for [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]].
kingdom-of-sumenep.r: Sumenep was a dry land of salt pans, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and seafaring traders. Its rulers converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 16th century and later accepted the overlordship of [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]] and, from 1705, the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]]. [[e:panembahan-somala|Panembahan Somala]] built the Great Mosque and the palace in the late 18th century, and [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abdurrahman was a noted scholar of Javanese and [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] texts.
kingdom-of-sumenep.e: Sumenep's princes served the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] as regents, supplying troops for colonial wars. In 1883 the colonial government abolished the royal title and ruled through ordinary regents. The palace and mosque remain landmarks of Madurese culture.

kingdom-of-dahomey.t: Fon kingdom of the Abomey plateau, famed for its female soldiers and royal palaces, and a major power of the Atlantic slave trade.
kingdom-of-dahomey.o: Dahomey arose in the early 17th century when a branch of the royal family of the [[s:kingdom-of-allada|Kingdom of Allada]] settled on the [[e:abomey|Abomey]] plateau among the [[e:fon-people|Fon]]. Under [[e:houegbadja|Houegbadja]] in the mid-17th century the kingdom was consolidated with Abomey as its capital. [[e:agaja|King Agaja]] conquered [[e:allada|Allada]] in 1724 and the [[s:kingdom-of-whydah|Kingdom of Whydah]] in 1727, gaining access to the coast.
kingdom-of-dahomey.r: The king ruled through an exceptionally centralised administration, with a female corps of soldiers known to Europeans as the [[e:amazon|Amazons]], a royal monopoly on the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] and annual customs honouring the royal ancestors. Dahomey paid tribute to the [[s:oyo-empire|Oyo Empire]] from the 1730s until [[e:ghezo|Ghezo]] ended it in 1823. After the slave trade declined, [[e:palm-oil|palm oil]] plantations grew.
kingdom-of-dahomey.e: [[e:behanzin|King Behanzin]] fought [[e:france|France]] from 1890 and surrendered in 1894. France installed a puppet king and absorbed the kingdom into [[s:french-dahomey|French Dahomey]], which became independent in 1960 and took the name [[e:benin-empire|Benin]] in 1975. The [[e:royal-palaces-of-abomey|Royal Palaces of Abomey]] are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].

kaga-domain.t: The richest domain of Tokugawa Japan, held by the Maeda family at Kanazawa and famed as the million-koku domain of Kaga.
kaga-domain.o: [[e:maeda-toshiie|Maeda Toshiie]], a comrade of [[e:oda-nobunaga|Oda Nobunaga]] and [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]], received northern [[e:kaga-province|Kaga]] after the defeat of [[e:shibata-katsuie|Shibata Katsuie]] in 1583 and moved into [[e:kanazawa|Kanazawa]] castle. His son [[e:maeda-toshinaga|Toshinaga]] sided with [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] in 1600 and was rewarded with lands covering Kaga, [[e:noto-province|Noto]] and [[e:etchu-province|Etchu]].
kaga-domain.r: Assessed at over a million koku, the domain was second only to the [[e:shogun|shogun]]'s own holdings. As outside (tozama) lords the [[e:maeda-clan|Maeda]] were watched carefully, and they spent heavily on culture rather than armies to reassure the shogunate. [[e:maeda-tsunanori|Maeda Tsunanori]] patronised scholarship and crafts, and [[e:kanazawa|Kanazawa]] became a centre of gold leaf, Kutani [[e:porcelain|porcelain]] and [[e:kaga-province|Kaga]] yuzen dyeing, with the [[e:kenroku-en|Kenroku-en]] garden.
kaga-domain.e: The domain stayed cautious during the [[e:boshin-war|Boshin War]] and joined the new government. It was abolished in 1871, becoming the core of [[e:ishikawa-prefecture|Ishikawa Prefecture]], and [[e:kanazawa|Kanazawa]] remains a cultural centre.

kingdom-of-dumnonia.t: Post-Roman British kingdom of Devon and Cornwall, with its high-status site at Tintagel, which slowly gave way to the West Saxons.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.o: Dumnonia grew from the Roman civitas of the [[s:dumnonii|Dumnonii]] after Roman rule ended around 410, covering [[e:cornwall|Cornwall]], [[e:devon|Devon]] and parts of [[e:somerset|Somerset]]. In the 6th century [[e:gildas|Gildas]] denounced its king Constantine for murder and sacrilege. Many [[e:britons-celtic-people|Britons]] from the region emigrated to [[e:armorica|Armorica]], where the district of [[s:domnonee|Domnonée]] in [[s:duchy-of-brittany|Brittany]] carries the same name.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.r: Little is recorded of its government. Imported [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] pottery and glass at [[e:tintagel|Tintagel]], and at sites such as [[e:bantham|Bantham]], show trade with the Byzantine world, probably for [[e:tin|tin]], in the 5th and 6th centuries. [[e:christianity|Christianity]] was organised around local saints and monasteries, and inscribed memorial stones in [[e:latin|Latin]] and ogham mark the burials of its elite.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.e: The West [[s:saxons|Saxons]] pushed westward through [[e:somerset|Somerset]] and [[e:devon|Devon]] in the 7th century, and around 705 [[e:aldhelm|Aldhelm]] wrote to King [[e:geraint-of-dumnonia|Geraint]] urging Roman practice on [[e:easter-controversy|Easter]]. In 710 [[e:ine-of-wessex|Ine of Wessex]] fought Geraint, and Devon was gradually absorbed. A smaller British kingdom of [[e:cornwall|Cornwall]] survived until the 9th century.

kingdom-of-breifne.t: A Gaelic kingdom of the drumlin country of Leitrim and Cavan, ruled by the O'Rourkes, whose king Tigernan Ua Ruairc helped bring about the Norman invasion of 1169.
kingdom-of-breifne.o: Breifne emerged in the 8th century among the [[e:ui-briuin|Ui Briuin]] of [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]], whose branch, the [[e:ui-briuin-breifne|Ui Briuin Breifne]], settled the lakes and hills of later [[e:county-leitrim|Leitrim]] and Cavan. The [[e:o-ruairc|O'Rourke]] family became its leading dynasty by the 10th century.
kingdom-of-breifne.r: Breifne was an upland kingdom of [[e:cattle|cattle]], lakes and crannog dwellings. Its kings occasionally claimed the kingship of [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]]. [[e:tigernan-ua-ruairc|Tigernan Ua Ruairc]], ruler from about 1124 to 1172, fought [[e:diarmait-mac-murchada|Diarmait Mac Murchada]] of [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Leinster]], who had abducted his wife [[e:derbforgaill|Derbforgaill]]; their feud helped bring the Normans to Ireland. Tigernan was killed at [[e:hill-of-ward|Tlachtga]] in 1172.
kingdom-of-breifne.e: After the death of its king in 1256, Breifne split between the [[e:o-ruairc|O'Rourkes]] of [[s:west-breifne|West Breifne]] and the [[e:o-raghallaigh|O'Reillys]] of [[s:east-breifne|East Breifne]]. Both survived until the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

kingdom-of-africa.t: The Norman Kingdom of Sicily's string of coastal conquests in Ifriqiya, a short-lived Christian dominion over Muslim ports from Tripoli to Mahdia.
kingdom-of-africa.o: Under [[e:roger-ii-of-sicily|Roger II]], the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]] exploited famine and the collapse of the [[s:zirid-emirate|Zirid emirate]] to seize the North African coast. His admiral [[e:george-of-antioch|George of Antioch]] took [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] in 1146, and in 1148 [[e:mahdia|Mahdia]], [[e:sousse|Sousse]] and [[e:sfax|Sfax]] fell as the [[e:zirid-dynasty|Zirid]] ruler al-Hasan fled. [[e:gabes|Gabès]] and other towns accepted Sicilian overlordship, forming what Roger styled his realm of [[e:africa|Africa]].
kingdom-of-africa.r: The Normans ruled indirectly, as they did with the Muslims of [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. Local [[e:qadi|qadis]] and governors stayed in place, Islamic law and worship continued, and the towns paid tribute to [[e:palermo|Palermo]]. Garrisons held the ports, and the aim was control of grain and the sea lanes between Sicily and [[e:africa|Africa]] rather than settlement or conversion.
kingdom-of-africa.e: After Roger's death in 1154 the towns revolted, starting with [[e:sfax|Sfax]] in 1156. The [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] [[e:caliphate|caliph]] [[e:abd-al-mumin|Abd al-Mu'min]] marched east, besieged [[e:mahdia|Mahdia]] and took it in January 1160, ending Christian rule. The episode foreshadowed later European footholds on the [[e:maghreb|Maghreb]] coast.

kingdom-of-lundu.t: A Manganja kingdom of the lower Shire valley, a southern offshoot of the Maravi confederacy linked to the feared Zimba warriors.
kingdom-of-lundu.o: The Lundu title was held by a branch of the Phiri ruling clan of the [[s:kingdom-of-maravi|Kingdom of Maravi]], which settled in the lower Shire valley among the [[e:manganja|Manganja]]. By the late 16th century the Lundu was a powerful independent ruler, and Portuguese writers associated him with the [[e:zimba|Zimba]], warrior bands that attacked Portuguese posts on the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] and coastal towns.
kingdom-of-lundu.r: The Lundu controlled routes carrying [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] from the interior to the coast near [[e:quelimane|Quelimane]] and [[e:mozambique-island|Mozambique Island]] and drew tribute from [[e:manganja|Manganja]] chiefs. Religious authority was closely tied to the [[e:mbona|Mbona]] rain shrine at Khulubvi, a cult the Lundu dynasty is said to have taken over and reshaped.
kingdom-of-lundu.e: The kingdom was brought back under Maravi overlordship by [[e:kalonga-masula|Kalonga Masula]] in the early 17th century and gradually lost power to chiefs and Afro-Portuguese prazo holders. By around 1800 it had broken up, and 19th-century [[s:kololo-kingdom|Kololo]] and Yao incursions completed its decline.

khanate-of-khiva.t: The Uzbek khanate of Khwarazm, ruled from the walled city of Khiva for four centuries, notorious for its slave markets and finally a Russian protectorate.
khanate-of-khiva.o: In 1511 Ilbars and Balbars, descendants of Arab Shah of the Shibanid line, took [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]] after the [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]] had briefly seized it from [[e:muhammad-shaybani|Muhammad Shaybani]]. The [[e:arabshahid-dynasty|Arabshahid dynasty]] ruled at first from [[e:gurganj|Urgench]] and later from [[e:khiva|Khiva]], which became the capital in the 17th century as the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]] changed course.
khanate-of-khiva.r: The khanate ruled [[e:uzbeks|Uzbek]] tribes, [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] and settled [[e:sarts|Sarts]] along the irrigated lower [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]]. The khan and historian [[e:abul-ghazi-bahadur|Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur]] wrote a genealogical history of the Turks. Slave trading of [[e:persians|Persians]] and Russians captured by Turkmen raiders was central to the economy. From 1804 the Qungrat dynasty, whose founders had been inaks, ruled as khans, building much of [[e:itchan-kala|Itchan Kala]].
khanate-of-khiva.e: Russian forces captured [[e:khiva|Khiva]] in 1873 and made it a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. In 1920 the [[e:red-army|Red Army]] and the [[e:young-khivans|Young Khivans]] deposed the last khan, Said Abdullah, creating the [[s:khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic|Khorezm People's Soviet Republic]].

kingdom-of-tiryns.t: Mycenaean citadel near the Argolic Gulf whose Cyclopean walls, among the most massive of the Bronze Age, so impressed later Greeks that they credited them to giants.
kingdom-of-tiryns.o: Tiryns stands on a low rock near the coast of the [[e:argolid|Argolid]], settled from the [[e:early-bronze-age|Early Bronze Age]], when a large circular building was erected on its summit. Mycenaean rulers built a fortified palace from c. 1600 BCE, and in the 14th and 13th centuries BCE the citadel was enclosed by walls up to 8 metres thick, with vaulted galleries.
kingdom-of-tiryns.r: The palace had a megaron with painted floors and frescoes of women in procession and boar hunts. Tiryns probably served as the harbour and partner, or subordinate, of nearby [[s:kingdom-of-mycenae|Mycenae]]. A few [[e:linear-b|Linear B]] tablets and inscribed jars show palace administration. Greek myth tied it to Perseus and to [[e:heracles|Heracles]], who served King [[e:eurystheus|Eurystheus]].
kingdom-of-tiryns.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1200 BCE, but unlike most centres Tiryns continued, with a large lower town and a rebuilt hall into the 12th century BCE. It later became a small city absorbed by [[s:argos|Argos]] c. 470 BCE. Its walls are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] together with [[s:kingdom-of-mycenae|Mycenae]].

kingdom-of-taxila.t: The kingdom of King Ambhi, who welcomed Alexander the Great to Taxila in 326 BCE and joined him against his rival Porus.
kingdom-of-taxila.o: After Achaemenid control of the [[e:indus|Indus]] region faded in the 4th century BCE, a local kingdom emerged around [[e:taxila|Taxila]], the old capital of the [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Kingdom of Gandhara]], between the Indus and the [[e:jhelum|Jhelum]]. Its ruler, known to the [[e:greeks|Greeks]] as [[e:ambhi|Taxiles]] and in Indian tradition as Ambhi, was at odds with the neighbouring [[s:paurava-kingdom|Paurava kingdom]].
kingdom-of-taxila.r: [[e:taxila|Taxila]] was a wealthy city on the trade route from [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]] to the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] and a famous centre of learning; tradition says [[e:chanakya|Chanakya]], adviser to [[e:chandragupta-maurya|Chandragupta Maurya]], taught there. Greek writers described its customs, including the exposure of the dead to vultures and the sale of girls in marriage markets. When Alexander arrived in 326 BCE, [[e:ambhi|Ambhi]] submitted with gifts and provided troops and elephants for the campaign.
kingdom-of-taxila.e: Alexander confirmed [[e:ambhi|Ambhi]] as ruler under Macedonian oversight. After Alexander's death the Greek commanders left the region, and around 317 BCE [[e:taxila|Taxila]] was absorbed by Chandragupta's [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]], becoming the seat of its north-western province.

kingdom-of-kyamutwara.t: A Haya kingdom west of Lake Victoria that split around 1800, giving rise to the kingdoms of Kianja and Bugabo.
kingdom-of-kyamutwara.o: Kyamutwara arose in the 17th century in the [[e:kagera-region|Kagera region]], near today's [[e:bukoba|Bukoba]], among the [[e:haya-people|Haya people]]. Traditions describe a dynasty of the Bankango clan later displaced by the [[e:hinda-dynasty|Hinda]], who were related to the rulers of the [[s:kingdom-of-karagwe|Kingdom of Karagwe]].
kingdom-of-kyamutwara.r: The kingdom had the [[e:sacred-kingship|sacred kingship]], chiefs and banana-and-[[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] farming economy shared by the [[e:haya-people|Haya]] states. Around 1800 succession disputes split it, and the [[s:kingdom-of-kianja|Kingdom of Kianja]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-bugabo|Kingdom of Bugabo]] became separate states, leaving a reduced Kyamutwara.
kingdom-of-kyamutwara.e: The remaining kingdom passed under [[s:german-east-africa|German East Africa]] and then [[e:tanganyika-territory|British Tanganyika Territory]] as a native authority. The chieftaincies were abolished by independent [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] in 1963.

kingdom-of-bugesera.t: A small kingdom between Rwanda and Burundi whose lands were divided between its two powerful neighbours in the late 18th century.
kingdom-of-bugesera.o: Bugesera lay in the lake-strewn lowlands around Lakes Cyohoha and Rweru, on today's border between [[s:kingdom-of-rwanda|Rwanda]] and [[s:kingdom-of-burundi|Burundi]]. Its royal clan, the Bahondogo, are remembered in Rwandan and Burundian traditions as rulers of one of the older kingdoms of the region, dating to at least the 16th century.
kingdom-of-bugesera.r: Little is known of its government beyond royal rituals and drums similar to those of its neighbours. It was a land of [[e:cattle|cattle]] and farming, and its rulers engaged in alliances and wars with the [[s:kingdom-of-rwanda|Kingdom of Rwanda]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-burundi|Kingdom of Burundi]].
kingdom-of-bugesera.e: Bugesera was conquered and partitioned around the end of the 18th century, with the northern part absorbed by [[s:kingdom-of-rwanda|Rwanda]] and the southern by [[s:kingdom-of-burundi|Burundi]]. Bugesera survives as a district name in Rwanda.

kingdom-of-avanti.t: The kingdom of Malwa with its capital at Ujjain, ruled by the fierce Chanda Pradyota and one of the four great powers of the Buddha's time.
kingdom-of-avanti.o: Avanti occupied the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] plateau of western central [[e:india|India]], with [[e:ujjain|Ujjain]] in the north and [[e:mahishmati|Mahishmati]] on the [[e:narmada-river|Narmada]] in the south. By the 6th century BCE it was one of the four leading kingdoms alongside [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]], [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kosala]] and [[s:kingdom-of-vatsa|Vatsa]]. Puranic tradition says the [[e:pradyota-dynasty|Pradyota dynasty]] seized the throne after the last king of an older line was killed by his minister Pulika.
kingdom-of-avanti.r: [[e:pradyota|Chanda Pradyota]] Mahasena, a contemporary of the [[e:gautama-buddha|Buddha]], was remembered as violent and ambitious; he threatened [[e:rajgir|Rajagriha]] and fought [[e:udayana-of-vatsa|Udayana of Vatsa]], who eloped with his daughter [[e:vasavadatta|Vasavadatta]]. [[e:ujjain|Ujjain]] grew rich on the routes linking the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]] with the western ports, and Avanti later became a centre of [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] through the monk [[e:mahakaccana|Mahakaccana]], a native of Ujjain.
kingdom-of-avanti.e: Around 400 BCE Avanti was conquered by [[e:shishunaga|Shishunaga]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Kingdom of Magadha]], ending its independence. [[e:ujjain|Ujjain]] remained a provincial capital under the [[e:maurya-empire|Mauryas]], where [[e:ashoka|Ashoka]] served as [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]], and later became the seat of the [[s:western-satraps|Western Satraps]].

kingdom-of-bosnia.t: Medieval Bosnian kingdom of the Kotromanić dynasty, briefly the strongest Balkan state, until the Ottomans conquered it in 1463.
kingdom-of-bosnia.o: Ban [[e:tvrtko-i-of-bosnia|Tvrtko I]] of the [[s:banate-of-bosnia|Banate of Bosnia]], having won lands in western [[s:serbia|Serbia]], was crowned king of the [[e:serbs|Serbs]] and [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] in 1377 at Mile near [[e:visoko|Visoko]], claiming descent from the [[e:nemanjic-dynasty|Nemanjić dynasty]].
kingdom-of-bosnia.r: [[e:tvrtko-i-of-bosnia|Tvrtko]] expanded to the Adriatic, taking [[s:commune-of-kotor|Kotor]] and much of [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]] and [[e:croatia|Croatia]] by his death in 1391. Royal power then weakened as great nobles such as [[e:hrvoje-vukcic-hrvatinic|Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić]] and [[e:stjepan-vukcic-kosaca|Stjepan Vukčić Kosača]], whose lands became [[e:herzegovina|Herzegovina]], made and unmade kings. [[e:silver|Silver]] from [[e:srebrenica|Srebrenica]] supported the state, and the [[e:bosnian-church|Bosnian Church]], [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] and Orthodoxy coexisted. Carved tombstones called stećci mark the burials of the period.
kingdom-of-bosnia.e: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took parts of the kingdom from the 1430s. In 1463 [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] invaded, captured [[e:bobovac|Bobovac]] and executed the last king, [[e:stephen-tomasevic|Stephen Tomašević]], at [[e:jajce|Jajce]]. Most of [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] became an Ottoman province, while [[e:hungary|Hungary]] held a northern banate around Jajce until 1527.
